item.title: 视频模型是渲染器，但它没有 HTML/CSS 那种可控接口：NeurCo 自动探测它「到底能可靠执行什么」 ｜ Neural Rendering Compiler: Generative Video Models as Programmable Renderers
item.description:
一句话：能力隐式地从训练中涌现，所以没人说得清它可靠执行哪些语义要求。

要点：

  • 问题定得准：生成式视频模型正成为强大的渲染器，但**缺少 HTML/CSS 引擎或 Blender 那种可预测的控制接口**；它们的能力**隐式地从训练中涌现**，于是难以判断「哪些事情它一定能可靠执行」
  • NeurCo（Neural Rendering Compiler）的做法是**自动探测冻结的视频模型**，为每个模型构造一份**专属的「能力手册」**，写明它能可靠满足哪些语义要求
  • 有了这份手册，调用方（上游程序/代码）就能像对编译器那样，只发它能兑现的指令——即把「生成式渲染器」变成可编程的

为什么值得看：这是「引擎出代理、模型出渲染」这条主线最关键的一块缺失：**接口契约**。此前几期都在解决「状态放哪」「记忆怎么留」，而这条路解决的是「我们怎么知道这个渲染器能干什么」。没有它，AI 渲染进管线就只能靠试。

中文摘要：生成式视频模型正在成为强大的渲染器，但它们缺少 HTML/CSS 引擎或 Blender 那样可预测的控制接口：能力是从训练中隐式涌现的，因此很难判断某个模型究竟能可靠执行哪些语义要求。Neural Rendering Compiler（NeurCo）因此提出自动探测冻结的视频模型，为每个模型构建一份专属的「能力手册」，说明它能可靠满足哪些语义要求。有了这份手册，上层程序就可以像调用编译器那样，只发出模型能兑现的指令，从而把「生成式渲染器」变成真正可编程的组件。对想把 AI 渲染接进生产管线的团队，这条补的是接口契约这一层。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

Neural Rendering Compiler: Generative Video Models as Programmable Renderers

Abstract

Generative video models are becoming powerful renderers, yet lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional systems such as HTML/CSS engines or Blender. Their capabilities emerge implicitly from training, making it difficult to determine what they can reliably execute. We present Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which automatically probes frozen video models to construct model-specific capability manuals describing which semantic requirements they can reliably satisfy. NeurCo represents user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, then compiles it into model-specific execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while unreliable ones are selectively rewritten or compiled into alternative execution strategies. We introduce VComBench, a benchmark of 380 compositional, multi-requirement tasks spanning text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation. NeurCo improves requirement satisfaction from 46.8% to 52.3% on Wan and from 66.5% to 69.3% on Minimax H3, and achieves further gains when combined with prompt enhancers, including on Seedance 2.5. Our analysis reveals model-specific differences in control capabilities and trade-offs between controllability and photorealism, highlighting capability-guided compilation as a promising approach to programmable generative video rendering.

1 Introduction

Rendering is more than producing convincing visuals. It requires precise, composable control over how they are created. In conventional engines such as Blender, operations have well-defined semantics [3]. Moving a camera changes the viewpoint without altering scene geometry, while changing a material leaves an object’s motion intact. Such predictable effects allow complex scenes to be programmed. Generative video models instead synthesize rich scenes and motion directly from text or visual references [47, 44, 20, 38], but offer no comparable execution contract [14]. The effective control capabilities emerge implicitly from training and vary across models and conditioning modes [15, 53, 16]. Figure 1 illustrates this contrast between explicit and empirically discovered rendering controls. This raises a fundamental question: How can we program a generative renderer whose instruction set is unknown in advance?

Existing approaches improve the controllability of video generation from different directions. Prompt enhancers refine user instructions [17, 6], agentic pipelines [30, 25] decompose requests into plans or tool calls, and control-conditioned models introduce explicit camera or motion controls [14, 42]. However, they do not systematically characterize which requirements a given model can reliably execute or how control strategies should adapt to its capabilities. Consequently, they may unnecessarily rewrite requirements already satisfied by the model while failing to identify when alternative execution strategies are needed.

We approach this problem from a compiler perspective, treating generative video models as rendering backends [51, 21]. Conventional compilers target instruction sets with well-defined semantics, whereas generative renderers lack explicit execution specifications and exhibit uneven control capabilities [15, 37, 16]. Rather than imposing a universal interface, we systematically probe frozen models using a shared vocabulary of semantic primitives to identify which requirements they can reliably satisfy. The resulting model-specific capability manual guides the compilation of high-level user intent into appropriate execution strategies. Reliable requirements are preserved, while challenging ones are selectively rewritten or lowered into alternative controls [14, 12, 34]. Thus, while the primitive vocabulary is predefined, each renderer’s effective instruction set is discovered rather than assumed.

We introduce Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which treats frozen video models as black-box rendering backends. As illustrated in Figure 2, NeurCo systematically probes each model to construct a capability manual characterizing the reliability of semantic controls across conditioning modes. Given a user request, NeurCo identifies individual semantic requirements and consults the manual to determine appropriate execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while challenging ones are selectively rewritten or lowered into alternative controls, including reference images, first frames, and proxy videos. Unchanged inputs reuse native outputs, and the same compilation framework adapts to different rendering backends. We further introduce VComBench, comprising 380 challenging compositional tasks across text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation, evaluating multiple interacting requirements across conditioning modes. It measures both individual requirement satisfaction and whether all requirements are jointly satisfied, revealing potential interference between controls.

We evaluate NeurCo on three video model families: MiniMax-H3, Wan, and Seedance 2.5. On H3 and Wan, NeurCo achieves substantial improvements in requirement satisfaction, with larger gains on less capable backends. It also complements existing prompt enhancement methods, delivering further improvements on Seedance 2.5 across all three benchmarks. Rather than indiscriminately rewriting prompts, NeurCo selectively targets challenging requirements while preserving native generation when no intervention is needed. Our analysis further reveals that different execution strategies offer varying benefits across task types, while auxiliary controls can improve controllability at the cost of photorealism. Together, these findings highlight the value of capability-guided compilation and underscore the need for empirical specifications that characterize not only what generative renderers can reliably execute, but also the limitations and trade-offs that compilers must account for.

2 Related Work

2.1 Video Generation Evaluation

Video generation evaluation has shifted from distribution-level metrics such as FVD [39] toward capability diagnosis. FETV [28] categorizes prompts by content, attribute, and complexity; EvalCrafter [29] and VBench [15] assess visual quality, motion, temporal consistency, and prompt alignment, with VBench++ [16] adding image-to-video generation and VBench-2.0 [53] covering human fidelity, controllability, physics, and commonsense. Targeted benchmarks probe compositionality [37], temporal change [8], consecutive events [41], physical commonsense and laws [1, 27], scientific causality [49], and rule adherence and goal realization [31]. ETVA [13] checks fine-grained alignment, and PEBench [36] evaluates enhanced prompts.

2.2 Prompt Enhancement for Video Generation

Prompt enhancement improves video generation by adapting user descriptions. Existing methods employ preference learning and reward-guided rewriting [17, 6], retrieval-augmented optimization [10], and iterative feedback from generated videos [11, 18]. Recent approaches further explore cinematic planning and reasoning-based rewriting [56, 31], multi-agent refinement and semantic verification [30, 45], reusable optimization rules [54], and reference-guided prompt refinement [52]. Unlike these approaches, which primarily optimize prompt formulation, NeurCo uses empirically discovered, model-specific capabilities to selectively preserve, rewrite, or lower requirements into alternative execution strategies.

2.3 Structured and Programmatic Video Control

Structured video control uses layouts and interaction graphs to specify scenes and relationships [23, 26, 35], while image and reference conditioning improve appearance and temporal consistency [44, 50, 33, 19, 4]. Explicit camera, motion, and structural controls further enable fine-grained manipulation [42, 14, 48, 46, 5, 37]. Agentic systems extend these capabilities through tool orchestration, planning, and feedback-driven refinement [43, 9]. Programmatic approaches combine executable scene representations or simulations with neural rendering [22, 24, 7], although coding-based visual generation may sacrifice perceptual richness [55]. NeurCo empirically discovers model-specific control capabilities and selectively compiles requirements into textual instructions, visual conditions, or external operators without retraining the video generator.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Task Formulation

A user request x=(p,A,m₀) comprises a prompt p, optional visual assets A, and an initial conditioning mode m₀∈{T2V,I2V,R2V} for text-, first-frame-, and reference-to-video generation, respectively.

NeurCo parses x into semantic requirements ℝ(x)={rᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^K, where rᵢ=(cᵢ,ℓᵢ,eᵢ,θᵢ) records a predefined control type, difficulty level, source text span, and optional arguments (subject, count, order, or time). Controls span object properties and counts, spatial relations, events, cameras, appearance, physics, visual text, and reference conditions.

The model-agnostic intermediate representation (IR) z=Parse(x) retains the parsed requirements ℝ(x), original prompt p, visual assets A, and initial mode m₀.

A deployment d specifies the frozen checkpoint, inference configuration, and interface for each supported mode. Compilation consults the deployment-specific capability manual M_d and intervention catalog O_d, which defines text transformations, external operators, and their preconditions. The resulting plan Π is executed to generate video v:

Π=ℂ_d(z;M_d,O_d), v=Execute_d(Π).

(1)

The plan specifies prompts, visual conditions, external operations, and per-call modes, which may differ from m₀ (e.g., T2V to I2V after first-frame construction). The goal is deployment-compatible execution that preserves the original semantic requirements.

3.2 Capability Manual

A capability manual M_d records the empirical support of deployment d for predefined controls, with entries indexed by control type c, difficulty level ℓ, and conditioning mode m. For each tested entry, successful and scored trial counts s_d(c,ℓ,m) and n_d(c,ℓ,m) yield the empirical success rate

p̂_d(c,ℓ,m)=(s_d(c,ℓ,m))/(n_d(c,ℓ,m)), n_d(c,ℓ,m)>0.

(2)

The labels ok, weak, and bad indicate high, intermediate, and low empirical native success on the tested probes, respectively. Unknown denotes the absence of scored trials and is not evidence of either reliability or failure. The manual characterizes native generation under the tested prompts and inputs; interventions and their preconditions are defined separately in O_d. Support for individual controls does not guarantee their joint satisfaction in compositional requests.

4 Method

As shown in Figure 3, NeurCo constructs a capability manual for each deployment of a frozen video model and uses it to compile user requests into executable generation plans. The process comprises offline capability profiling, requirement-level compilation, and backend execution.

4.1 Offline Capability Profiling

We systematically probe the shared semantic-control vocabulary at different difficulty levels under the applicable T2V, I2V, and R2V modes. Each probe isolates a target requirement while varying the scene and subject context, and supplies the prompt and visual assets required by the mode. A video judge, supplemented by task-specific measurements where applicable, evaluates whether the generated video successfully satisfies the target requirement.

For each (c,ℓ,m), we retain successful and scored trial counts and compute the empirical success rate in Eq. (2). These measurements determine an ok, weak, or bad support status; entries without scored evidence are unknown. The assignment thresholds are given in the supplementary material. The manual records native generation performance, while the intervention catalog O_d specifies the transformations available to the compiler.

4.2 Capability-Guided Compilation

Given x=(p,A,m₀), NeurCo constructs the IR described in Sec. 3.1. The parser extracts explicitly stated requirements, normalizes their control types and difficulty levels, and links them to verbatim spans in the original prompt. The full description and user-provided assets are retained. For VComBench, task annotations supply this IR, isolating compilation and execution from parser errors.

For each requirement rᵢ, NeurCo retrieves the native support status σᵢ for (cᵢ,ℓᵢ,m₀). Let Fᵢ^λ contain the remedies for that requirement permitted by configuration λ whose deployment, interface, structural, and input-asset preconditions are satisfied. The decision is

aᵢ=\begincaseskeep,&σᵢ∈{ok,unknown}, intervene,&σᵢ∈{weak,bad}∧Fᵢ^λ≠∅, unresolved,&σᵢ∈{weak,bad}∧Fᵢ^λ=∅.\endcases

(3)

The intervention configuration λ determines which transformations and operators are available. The compiler assembles compatible interventions into an execution plan, while unresolved requirements retain their original wording. Native support is assessed in the initial mode m₀, but execution may switch modes when the destination interface and conditioning requirements are satisfied.

4.3 Backends and Execution

Targeted rewriting clarifies subject binding, counts, event order, camera behavior, spatial relations, or timing while preserving other stated requirements, including those sharing the edited text.

External operators provide alternative ways to express the selected controls. Reference images anchor appearance or attribute binding; first frames encode counts or visual text; layout images specify spatial placement; and proxy videos provide motion, timing, or camera guidance through compatible interfaces. Multi-shot requests can be handled within a single call when supported by the backend, or through shot concatenation when independent clips are permitted. Requests requiring a continuous shot are never split. The six operators are detailed in Appendix D.

Before execution, generated visual conditions are validated against their intended requirements. Invalid conditions are discarded, and the remaining text plan is retained. The executor then assembles the prompts, conditioning assets, and inference parameters required by the selected backend. When compilation leaves the executable inputs unchanged, the corresponding baseline output is reused if available. All video-generation checkpoints remain frozen throughout the process.

5 VComBench

VComBench evaluates whether multiple semantic requirements can be satisfied within the same generated video. It measures both individual requirement satisfaction and joint task success, allowing us to systematically assess whether compilation improves targeted requirements while preserving the remaining constraints.

5.1 Task Construction

VComBench contains 380 compositional tasks adapted from public video benchmarks covering general video quality, image-to-video generation, prompt enhancement, compositional generation, camera control, and physical commonsense [15, 16, 36, 37, 29, 1]. Each task specifies a prompt, optional visual assets, and annotated requirements with associated checks. The same task specifications are used across compiler variants.

Tasks span T2V, I2V, and R2V, providing text only, a first-frame image, and reference visual inputs, respectively. These modes describe the task’s input contract; execution may use a different conditioning mode after compilation. Figure 5 summarizes the task and requirement counts by input mode and illustrates representative semantic controls.

The tasks contain 1,617 scored requirements covering object properties and counts, spatial relations, actions and interactions, temporal order, camera behavior, appearance, physical effects, visual text, and reference conditions. We consolidate 50 raw annotation categories into 34 semantic-control dimensions shared with the capability manual. Input-validity checks are used for data validation and excluded from scoring, which measures requirements that the generated video must visibly realize.

Each task contains either three or six scored requirements: 221 tasks contain three, and 159 contain six. As described in Sec. 4.2, the main experiments use annotation-derived IRs to isolate compilation and execution from parser errors. Further construction and annotation details are provided in the supplementary material.

5.2 Scoring Protocol

A fixed video-judging pipeline evaluates each scored requirement, which passes only when all associated checks pass. Temporal, repetition, and multi-step camera requirements use denser frame sampling.

Let ℝ_q denote the scored requirements of task q, and y_q,r∈{0,1} indicate whether requirement r passes. Let 𝔼 denote the evaluated task–requirement pairs and ℚ_complete the tasks with complete judgments. Requirement satisfaction is defined as:

S_req=(1)/(|𝔼|)∑_(q,r)∈𝔼y_q,r.

(4)

Joint task success requires all scored requirements to pass:

Sₐₗₗ=(1)/(|ℚ_complete|)∑_q∈ℚ_complete1 [∑_r∈ℝ_qy_q,r=|ℝ_q|].

(5)

As illustrated in Figure 5, satisfying only two of three requirements yields partial requirement satisfaction but does not count as a successful task.

We additionally report a realism rate Sᵣₑₐₗ, defined as the fraction of evaluated videos judged photorealistic among the 366 tasks expected to produce photorealistic footage. The remaining 14 tasks explicitly request non-photorealistic styles and are excluded from this metric.

6 Experiments

6.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate frozen local deployments of MiniMax-H3 [32] and Wan [40], and a hosted Seedance 2.5 [2] model. Experiments cover the supported T2V, I2V, and R2V modes, with VACE used for Wan reference conditioning. For VComBench, we construct IRs from annotated task requirements to isolate compilation and execution from parsing errors. Three NeurCo configurations are used: targeted text rewriting (T), external operators without targeted rewriting (O), and their combination (T+O). We compare Native (original inputs), NeurCo (T), NeurCo (T+O), TIDE [54], and TIDE combined with each NeurCo configuration. Generation seeds are shared across methods where supported. TIDE implementation details are provided in Appendix G. External evaluation uses a VBench-2.0 [53] subset and the 150-task Sci-VBench testmini [49]. We report the unweighted mean over 17 valid dimensions for VBench-2.0, and PG, SCC, SC, VT, and their mean for Sci-VBench. Detailed VBench-2.0 scores are provided in Table 12 in the supplementary material.

6.2 Main Results on VComBench

Table 1 compares compilation with native generation and prompt enhancement. On native inputs, NeurCo (T+O) improves requirement satisfaction by 2.8 points on H3 and 5.5 on Wan, exceeding the 1.2 and 1.1 point gains from NeurCo (T). Wan also improves all-requirements success from 8.4% to 11.8%. On Seedance 2.5, NeurCo (T) raises requirement satisfaction from 68.5% to 69.7%, while NeurCo (T+O) reaches 68.2%. For requirement satisfaction, combined compilation performs better on H3 and Wan, while text-only compilation performs better on Seedance 2.5.

Wan improves both metrics, whereas H3’s higher requirement satisfaction coincides with lower all-requirements success (Sec. 6.3). NeurCo also complements prompt enhancement. Operator-only compilation improves TIDE’s requirement satisfaction by 0.5, 1.9, and 0.8 points on H3, Wan, and Seedance 2.5, respectively, and raises all-requirements success on all three. The combined variant achieves H3’s highest all-requirements success (34.5%), despite lower requirement satisfaction than TIDE, and improves both metrics over TIDE on Seedance 2.5. On Wan, it recovers much of the text-only loss but remains below TIDE. Additional rewriting does not consistently improve on operator-only compilation.

6.3 Mode and Quality Analysis

Table 2 analyzes native-input compilation by initial input mode. On H3, NeurCo (T+O) increases requirement satisfaction in all three modes, although R2V all-requirements success drops from 33.1% to 28.8%. On Wan, it gives larger requirement gains on T2V and R2V, while NeurCo (T) performs better on I2V. On Seedance 2.5, combined compilation raises R2V requirement satisfaction from 66.1% to 69.9% and all-requirements success from 20.7% to 28.9%, but I2V requirement satisfaction falls. The benefits therefore depend on both the backend and the input mode.

Figure 7 shows that NeurCo (T+O) improves fine-grained requirement satisfaction on H3 by 2.8 percentage points, satisfying 45 additional requirements. However, joint task success decreases by 2.9 points and realism by 6.3 points. The realism effect differs across backends: it remains stable on Wan (77.5% to 77.8%) and improves on Seedance 2.5 (68.3% to 71.0%). These results reveal backend-dependent trade-offs between semantic control, joint task success, and visual quality.

6.4 External Benchmark Results

On VBench-2.0 (Table 4), text-only compilation improves Wan’s native-input Mean17 from 0.5281 to 0.6275 (Table 13). Adding operators to TIDE improves H3 and Wan, whereas the combined strategy performs best on Seedance 2.5 (0.6963 vs. 0.6759 for TIDE). These results show that the most effective compilation strategy varies across backends.

Figure 7 shows that operator-only compilation improves composition (+0.055/+0.050) and motion order (+0.100 on both) on H3 and Wan. H3 also gains in dynamic spatial relations, while Wan improves camera motion. The improvements are concentrated in specific controls, with smaller regressions in other dimensions.

Sci-VBench tests whether the improvements extend beyond VComBench (Table 3). On native inputs, NeurCo (T+O) raises the mean from 2.668 to 2.724 on H3, from 2.561 to 2.595 on Wan, and from 2.992 to 3.025 on Seedance 2.5. After TIDE, operator-only compilation reaches 3.262 on H3 and 2.942 on Wan, while the combined variant reaches 3.233 and 2.923. On Seedance 2.5, the text-only and combined variants reach 3.268 and 3.255, respectively, compared with 3.181 for TIDE and 3.191 for the operator-only variant. The relative benefits of rewriting and operators therefore vary across backends.

6.5 Multi-Backend Routing

Table 5 reports routing over H3+Wan and H3+Wan+Seedance 2.5. The three-backend runs obtain higher VComBench requirement satisfaction under both raw and TIDE-enhanced inputs, reaching 69.7% and 74.3%, respectively. With TIDE, the Sci-VBench mean also rises from 3.128 to 3.214, while all-requirements success decreases from 33.8% to 33.2% and VBench-2.0 Mean17 decreases from 0.6749 to 0.6673. The gains are therefore not uniform across metrics. Evaluated task counts are reported in Table 10.

6.6 Case Study

Figure 8 illustrates two complementary conditioning strategies for paint mixing on Wan. The task requires three colored cups to pour matching paints into a bowl, followed by stirring until the colored streaks form a uniform mixture. Native and TIDE satisfy four of six requirements, both failing to reproduce paint intermixing and the final transition to a uniform color. NeurCo (T+O) constructs a first frame and switches from T2V to I2V to ground the scene, while TIDE + NeurCo (O) uses a proxy video through VACE to guide the mixing process. Both strategies satisfy all six requirements, capturing the temporal progression, whereas NeurCo (T) satisfies only three. Additional examples and failure cases are provided in Appendix E.

7 Conclusion

We presented NeurCo, which treats frozen video models as generative rendering backends and discovers their effective control capabilities through empirical profiling. Deployment-specific capability manuals guide the compilation of user intent into execution strategies that preserve reliable requirements and adapt challenging ones. Experiments on VComBench and two external benchmarks demonstrate improved semantic control across three backends, alongside trade-offs in joint task success and photorealism. Beyond individual renderers, these capability manuals provide a foundation for capability-aware tool selection and orchestration.

LLM Usage Statement

OpenAI Codex was used to assist with manuscript preparation, including drafting and revising the conclusion, adapting the existing LaTeX project to the CVPR template, formatting tables and figures, and resolving LaTeX compatibility issues.

Appendix A Additional Experimental Details

A.1 Backend Deployments and Generation Settings

We evaluate MiniMax-H3 and three Wan2.2 variants with frozen weights and BF16 precision. Table 6 summarizes their generation settings. For I2V, the first-frame aspect ratio is preserved: H3 uses a short side of 768 pixels, while Wan maintains approximately the pixel budget of 1280×720.

Conditioning.

H3 uses first-frame conditioning for I2V and image or video references for R2V. When both are present, reference images precede the proxy video, which is resampled to 24 fps. Wan uses VACE for reference-image and proxy-depth conditioning, with a control strength of 0.5 for both experts when a depth video is supplied. Depth-conditioned calls additionally use a photorealism instruction and negative terms suppressing cartoon-like rendering. Other Wan calls use the official default negative prompt.

Seedance 2.5.

We evaluate a fixed version of the hosted Seedance 2.5 model at 720p and 24 fps, with audio and watermarking disabled. We access the model through the official API. T2V and R2V use a 16:9 aspect ratio, while I2V follows the first frame. Requested durations are 5 or 10 seconds.

Sampling protocol.

VComBench uses nominal durations of 5 seconds, extended to 10 seconds for shot-count or timed-event requirements. Sci-VBench and VBench-2.0 use 5-second clips. A deterministic task-specific seed is shared across methods within each deployment. For text-only comparisons, conditioning inputs and generation settings are also held fixed. Multiple samples use distinct task–sample seeds, while clips belonging to the same concatenated task share a seed.

For VBench-2.0, native-input and raw-routing configurations use three videos per task, and TIDE-based configurations use one. Diversity evaluation uses 20 videos per prompt for all configurations. When compilation leaves the generation inputs unchanged, the corresponding baseline video is reused.

A.2 Models Used by Each Component

Table 7 summarizes the models specified for compilation, condition construction, and evaluation. For VComBench, we construct the IR directly from task annotations, isolating compilation and execution from requirement-parsing errors.

Compilation and condition construction.

Targeted rewriting and TIDE enhancement use the same language model with their respective instructions. This model also plans reference images, layouts, proxy animations, and shot decompositions, and validates the constructed visual conditions. Backend and operator selection follow the capability manual and operator eligibility rules without an additional model call. The TIDE instructions are provided in Appendix G.

Condition images.

The image generator is configured as ChatGPT Images 2.0 for single-backend experiments and GPT Image 1.5 for multi-backend experiments. Images are generated at 1536×1024 resolution. Layout first frames are obtained by editing rendered layout sketches. Comparisons between single- and multi-backend configurations therefore also reflect the difference in condition-image generators.

Evaluation settings.

Language-model temperature and top-p use provider defaults. Reasoning effort is set to medium when explicitly configured. VComBench evaluation requests specify the same judge model across configurations; route-dependent settings and agreement checks are reported in Sec. A.5. Sci-VBench scoring follows Sec. A.7, and VBench-2.0 uses the official evaluation suite.

A.3 Evaluated Samples

Some Seedance 2.5 requests in VComBench were rejected by the service’s content moderation. Table 8 reports completely judged tasks for each configuration. Table 9 gives the initial-mode counts used by the main mode analysis. Table 10 reports the evaluated task counts for the multi-backend routing experiments.

A.4 Evaluation Details

For VBench-2.0, native-input and raw-routing configurations use three generated videos per task, whereas TIDE-based configurations use one. Diversity uses 20 videos in all configurations. Mean17 is the unweighted mean over the 17 valid dimensions and is not an official benchmark aggregate. Multi-view consistency is excluded because it has no valid samples.

A.5 VComBench Judging Protocol

Frame sampling.

GPT-6.1 Sol evaluates each scored video once, without repeated scoring or voting. The judge receives uniformly sampled, timestamped frames, including the first and last frames, resized to a maximum side of 448 pixels. Tasks with nominal durations up to 5 seconds use 8 frames; longer tasks use 12. We use 24 frames when any scored requirement concerns repetition count, event timing, rebound count, event order, or a camera-move sequence. Original I2V first frames and R2V reference images are provided with their roles. Concatenated clips are evaluated as one video.

Requirement scoring.

Each requirement contains one to three atomic visual checks, generated during task construction and screened for quality. Quantitative targets, including distances, angles, and speeds, are recorded separately in task annotations. For each check, the judge returns yes, no, or unclear, with a brief explanation. The judge must reject checks not clearly satisfied and reserve unclear for cases that cannot be resolved from the sampled frames, such as events between frames.

A requirement passes only when all checks receive yes. Any no yields failure; otherwise, an unclear or missing answer makes the requirement unclear. Unclear requirements count as unmet. Across configurations, 2.3% of check answers were unclear. Input-validity checks are recorded separately and excluded from requirement satisfaction. For tasks requesting photorealistic footage, realism is assessed in a separate evaluation using four sampled frames. Videos without valid judgments after repeated request failures are excluded from metric denominators; affected configurations contain 8–12 videos.

Agreement checks.

Table 11 summarizes cross-route stability and preliminary human agreement. For configurations affected by route changes, method–baseline comparisons use baselines evaluated through the same route.

Human annotations were collected without access to automatic verdicts. Among requirements with definite labels in both sources, 255/286 agreed; the judge rejected 23 human-accepted requirements and accepted 8 human-rejected requirements. This earlier H3-only audit uses one annotation set, with no reported inter-annotator agreement. Its judge configuration was not retained, so it provides preliminary evidence rather than validation of the final protocol.

A.6 VBench-2.0 Subset

We select 175 text-to-video tasks from the 18 official dimensions, using 10 prompts per dimension except Diversity, which uses five. For a prompt list of length P, the k selected indices are ⌊iP/k⌋, i=0,…,k-1. All tasks use nominal 5-second clips; task identifiers are listed in the supplementary material. Video counts follow Sec. A.1.

We apply the official per-dimension scorers. Multi-view consistency yields no valid samples and is excluded, leaving 165 tasks across 17 scored dimensions. Mean17 is their unweighted mean, not an official aggregate. Scoring follows the official validity filters and excludes unavailable outputs, so effective sample counts vary across configurations.

A.7 Sci-VBench Scoring

We evaluate the 150-task testmini split using one nominal 5-second video per task. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B scores prompt grounding (PG), scientific and causal correctness (SCC), and spatiotemporal consistency (SC) using the benchmark’s task-specific 1–5 rubrics. It receives video frames at 2 fps, with temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.8. We use one scoring round instead of the default three, so small differences should be interpreted cautiously.

Perceptual quality is measured by VT, the mean of six normalized automatic metrics: subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic quality, and imaging quality. We rescale VT to 1–5 and report an equal-weight summary:

VT₁₋₋₅=1+4/6∑ⱼ₌₁⁶sⱼ, sⱼ∈[0,1],

(6)

AVG=(PG+SCC+SC+VT₁₋₋₅)/(4).

(7)

Reported scores are averaged over the 150 tasks. AVG is our summary statistic, not an official benchmark aggregate. Reused videos retain their existing evaluation scores.

A.8 Compute and Cost

Local generation uses NVIDIA H20 GPUs, with one GPU per H3 video and eight per Wan video. Table 13 reports the video-generation expenditure of the experiments in the main paper. Requests whose compiled inputs match a baseline reuse that baseline’s video and are not counted. Local counts therefore cover only generated videos, with VComBench scaled to its 380 scored tasks. Routing experiments are listed separately: a task routed to a backend inherits the video of a matching single-backend run when one exists, and only the remaining tasks are generated. GPU hours sum the recorded generation time of each video and exclude model loading, queueing, idle time, and failed retries; Seedance costs are recorded charges for successful requests only.

NeurCo adds compilation and condition-construction costs. Shot concatenation requires additional video generations, while visual conditioning can increase generation time. Language-model calls, image generation, proxy rendering, and evaluation were not fully timed or costed and are excluded from the table. The reported budget therefore does not measure total system cost or paired per-task overhead.

一句话：能力隐式地从训练中涌现，所以没人说得清它可靠执行哪些语义要求。

要点：

  • 问题定得准：生成式视频模型正成为强大的渲染器，但**缺少 HTML/CSS 引擎或 Blender 那种可预测的控制接口**；它们的能力**隐式地从训练中涌现**，于是难以判断「哪些事情它一定能可靠执行」
  • NeurCo（Neural Rendering Compiler）的做法是**自动探测冻结的视频模型**，为每个模型构造一份**专属的「能力手册」**，写明它能可靠满足哪些语义要求
  • 有了这份手册，调用方（上游程序/代码）就能像对编译器那样，只发它能兑现的指令——即把「生成式渲染器」变成可编程的

为什么值得看：这是「引擎出代理、模型出渲染」这条主线最关键的一块缺失：**接口契约**。此前几期都在解决「状态放哪」「记忆怎么留」，而这条路解决的是「我们怎么知道这个渲染器能干什么」。没有它，AI 渲染进管线就只能靠试。

中文摘要：生成式视频模型正在成为强大的渲染器，但它们缺少 HTML/CSS 引擎或 Blender 那样可预测的控制接口：能力是从训练中隐式涌现的，因此很难判断某个模型究竟能可靠执行哪些语义要求。Neural Rendering Compiler（NeurCo）因此提出自动探测冻结的视频模型，为每个模型构建一份专属的「能力手册」，说明它能可靠满足哪些语义要求。有了这份手册，上层程序就可以像调用编译器那样，只发出模型能兑现的指令，从而把「生成式渲染器」变成真正可编程的组件。对想把 AI 渲染接进生产管线的团队，这条补的是接口契约这一层。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

Neural Rendering Compiler: Generative Video Models as Programmable Renderers

Abstract

Generative video models are becoming powerful renderers, yet lack the predictable control interfaces of conventional systems such as HTML/CSS engines or Blender. Their capabilities emerge implicitly from training, making it difficult to determine what they can reliably execute. We present Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which automatically probes frozen video models to construct model-specific capability manuals describing which semantic requirements they can reliably satisfy. NeurCo represents user intent in a model-agnostic intermediate representation of objects, constraints, events, and cameras, then compiles it into model-specific execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while unreliable ones are selectively rewritten or compiled into alternative execution strategies. We introduce VComBench, a benchmark of 380 compositional, multi-requirement tasks spanning text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation. NeurCo improves requirement satisfaction from 46.8% to 52.3% on Wan and from 66.5% to 69.3% on Minimax H3, and achieves further gains when combined with prompt enhancers, including on Seedance 2.5. Our analysis reveals model-specific differences in control capabilities and trade-offs between controllability and photorealism, highlighting capability-guided compilation as a promising approach to programmable generative video rendering.

1 Introduction

Rendering is more than producing convincing visuals. It requires precise, composable control over how they are created. In conventional engines such as Blender, operations have well-defined semantics [3]. Moving a camera changes the viewpoint without altering scene geometry, while changing a material leaves an object’s motion intact. Such predictable effects allow complex scenes to be programmed. Generative video models instead synthesize rich scenes and motion directly from text or visual references [47, 44, 20, 38], but offer no comparable execution contract [14]. The effective control capabilities emerge implicitly from training and vary across models and conditioning modes [15, 53, 16]. Figure 1 illustrates this contrast between explicit and empirically discovered rendering controls. This raises a fundamental question: How can we program a generative renderer whose instruction set is unknown in advance?

Existing approaches improve the controllability of video generation from different directions. Prompt enhancers refine user instructions [17, 6], agentic pipelines [30, 25] decompose requests into plans or tool calls, and control-conditioned models introduce explicit camera or motion controls [14, 42]. However, they do not systematically characterize which requirements a given model can reliably execute or how control strategies should adapt to its capabilities. Consequently, they may unnecessarily rewrite requirements already satisfied by the model while failing to identify when alternative execution strategies are needed.

We approach this problem from a compiler perspective, treating generative video models as rendering backends [51, 21]. Conventional compilers target instruction sets with well-defined semantics, whereas generative renderers lack explicit execution specifications and exhibit uneven control capabilities [15, 37, 16]. Rather than imposing a universal interface, we systematically probe frozen models using a shared vocabulary of semantic primitives to identify which requirements they can reliably satisfy. The resulting model-specific capability manual guides the compilation of high-level user intent into appropriate execution strategies. Reliable requirements are preserved, while challenging ones are selectively rewritten or lowered into alternative controls [14, 12, 34]. Thus, while the primitive vocabulary is predefined, each renderer’s effective instruction set is discovered rather than assumed.

We introduce Neural Rendering Compiler (NeurCo), which treats frozen video models as black-box rendering backends. As illustrated in Figure 2, NeurCo systematically probes each model to construct a capability manual characterizing the reliability of semantic controls across conditioning modes. Given a user request, NeurCo identifies individual semantic requirements and consults the manual to determine appropriate execution strategies. Reliable requirements remain unchanged, while challenging ones are selectively rewritten or lowered into alternative controls, including reference images, first frames, and proxy videos. Unchanged inputs reuse native outputs, and the same compilation framework adapts to different rendering backends. We further introduce VComBench, comprising 380 challenging compositional tasks across text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video generation, evaluating multiple interacting requirements across conditioning modes. It measures both individual requirement satisfaction and whether all requirements are jointly satisfied, revealing potential interference between controls.

We evaluate NeurCo on three video model families: MiniMax-H3, Wan, and Seedance 2.5. On H3 and Wan, NeurCo achieves substantial improvements in requirement satisfaction, with larger gains on less capable backends. It also complements existing prompt enhancement methods, delivering further improvements on Seedance 2.5 across all three benchmarks. Rather than indiscriminately rewriting prompts, NeurCo selectively targets challenging requirements while preserving native generation when no intervention is needed. Our analysis further reveals that different execution strategies offer varying benefits across task types, while auxiliary controls can improve controllability at the cost of photorealism. Together, these findings highlight the value of capability-guided compilation and underscore the need for empirical specifications that characterize not only what generative renderers can reliably execute, but also the limitations and trade-offs that compilers must account for.

2 Related Work

2.1 Video Generation Evaluation

Video generation evaluation has shifted from distribution-level metrics such as FVD [39] toward capability diagnosis. FETV [28] categorizes prompts by content, attribute, and complexity; EvalCrafter [29] and VBench [15] assess visual quality, motion, temporal consistency, and prompt alignment, with VBench++ [16] adding image-to-video generation and VBench-2.0 [53] covering human fidelity, controllability, physics, and commonsense. Targeted benchmarks probe compositionality [37], temporal change [8], consecutive events [41], physical commonsense and laws [1, 27], scientific causality [49], and rule adherence and goal realization [31]. ETVA [13] checks fine-grained alignment, and PEBench [36] evaluates enhanced prompts.

2.2 Prompt Enhancement for Video Generation

Prompt enhancement improves video generation by adapting user descriptions. Existing methods employ preference learning and reward-guided rewriting [17, 6], retrieval-augmented optimization [10], and iterative feedback from generated videos [11, 18]. Recent approaches further explore cinematic planning and reasoning-based rewriting [56, 31], multi-agent refinement and semantic verification [30, 45], reusable optimization rules [54], and reference-guided prompt refinement [52]. Unlike these approaches, which primarily optimize prompt formulation, NeurCo uses empirically discovered, model-specific capabilities to selectively preserve, rewrite, or lower requirements into alternative execution strategies.

2.3 Structured and Programmatic Video Control

Structured video control uses layouts and interaction graphs to specify scenes and relationships [23, 26, 35], while image and reference conditioning improve appearance and temporal consistency [44, 50, 33, 19, 4]. Explicit camera, motion, and structural controls further enable fine-grained manipulation [42, 14, 48, 46, 5, 37]. Agentic systems extend these capabilities through tool orchestration, planning, and feedback-driven refinement [43, 9]. Programmatic approaches combine executable scene representations or simulations with neural rendering [22, 24, 7], although coding-based visual generation may sacrifice perceptual richness [55]. NeurCo empirically discovers model-specific control capabilities and selectively compiles requirements into textual instructions, visual conditions, or external operators without retraining the video generator.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Task Formulation

A user request x=(p,A,m₀) comprises a prompt p, optional visual assets A, and an initial conditioning mode m₀∈{T2V,I2V,R2V} for text-, first-frame-, and reference-to-video generation, respectively.

NeurCo parses x into semantic requirements ℝ(x)={rᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^K, where rᵢ=(cᵢ,ℓᵢ,eᵢ,θᵢ) records a predefined control type, difficulty level, source text span, and optional arguments (subject, count, order, or time). Controls span object properties and counts, spatial relations, events, cameras, appearance, physics, visual text, and reference conditions.

The model-agnostic intermediate representation (IR) z=Parse(x) retains the parsed requirements ℝ(x), original prompt p, visual assets A, and initial mode m₀.

A deployment d specifies the frozen checkpoint, inference configuration, and interface for each supported mode. Compilation consults the deployment-specific capability manual M_d and intervention catalog O_d, which defines text transformations, external operators, and their preconditions. The resulting plan Π is executed to generate video v:

Π=ℂ_d(z;M_d,O_d), v=Execute_d(Π).

(1)

The plan specifies prompts, visual conditions, external operations, and per-call modes, which may differ from m₀ (e.g., T2V to I2V after first-frame construction). The goal is deployment-compatible execution that preserves the original semantic requirements.

3.2 Capability Manual

A capability manual M_d records the empirical support of deployment d for predefined controls, with entries indexed by control type c, difficulty level ℓ, and conditioning mode m. For each tested entry, successful and scored trial counts s_d(c,ℓ,m) and n_d(c,ℓ,m) yield the empirical success rate

p̂_d(c,ℓ,m)=(s_d(c,ℓ,m))/(n_d(c,ℓ,m)), n_d(c,ℓ,m)>0.

(2)

The labels ok, weak, and bad indicate high, intermediate, and low empirical native success on the tested probes, respectively. Unknown denotes the absence of scored trials and is not evidence of either reliability or failure. The manual characterizes native generation under the tested prompts and inputs; interventions and their preconditions are defined separately in O_d. Support for individual controls does not guarantee their joint satisfaction in compositional requests.

4 Method

As shown in Figure 3, NeurCo constructs a capability manual for each deployment of a frozen video model and uses it to compile user requests into executable generation plans. The process comprises offline capability profiling, requirement-level compilation, and backend execution.

4.1 Offline Capability Profiling

We systematically probe the shared semantic-control vocabulary at different difficulty levels under the applicable T2V, I2V, and R2V modes. Each probe isolates a target requirement while varying the scene and subject context, and supplies the prompt and visual assets required by the mode. A video judge, supplemented by task-specific measurements where applicable, evaluates whether the generated video successfully satisfies the target requirement.

For each (c,ℓ,m), we retain successful and scored trial counts and compute the empirical success rate in Eq. (2). These measurements determine an ok, weak, or bad support status; entries without scored evidence are unknown. The assignment thresholds are given in the supplementary material. The manual records native generation performance, while the intervention catalog O_d specifies the transformations available to the compiler.

4.2 Capability-Guided Compilation

Given x=(p,A,m₀), NeurCo constructs the IR described in Sec. 3.1. The parser extracts explicitly stated requirements, normalizes their control types and difficulty levels, and links them to verbatim spans in the original prompt. The full description and user-provided assets are retained. For VComBench, task annotations supply this IR, isolating compilation and execution from parser errors.

For each requirement rᵢ, NeurCo retrieves the native support status σᵢ for (cᵢ,ℓᵢ,m₀). Let Fᵢ^λ contain the remedies for that requirement permitted by configuration λ whose deployment, interface, structural, and input-asset preconditions are satisfied. The decision is

aᵢ=\begincaseskeep,&σᵢ∈{ok,unknown}, intervene,&σᵢ∈{weak,bad}∧Fᵢ^λ≠∅, unresolved,&σᵢ∈{weak,bad}∧Fᵢ^λ=∅.\endcases

(3)

The intervention configuration λ determines which transformations and operators are available. The compiler assembles compatible interventions into an execution plan, while unresolved requirements retain their original wording. Native support is assessed in the initial mode m₀, but execution may switch modes when the destination interface and conditioning requirements are satisfied.

4.3 Backends and Execution

Targeted rewriting clarifies subject binding, counts, event order, camera behavior, spatial relations, or timing while preserving other stated requirements, including those sharing the edited text.

External operators provide alternative ways to express the selected controls. Reference images anchor appearance or attribute binding; first frames encode counts or visual text; layout images specify spatial placement; and proxy videos provide motion, timing, or camera guidance through compatible interfaces. Multi-shot requests can be handled within a single call when supported by the backend, or through shot concatenation when independent clips are permitted. Requests requiring a continuous shot are never split. The six operators are detailed in Appendix D.

Before execution, generated visual conditions are validated against their intended requirements. Invalid conditions are discarded, and the remaining text plan is retained. The executor then assembles the prompts, conditioning assets, and inference parameters required by the selected backend. When compilation leaves the executable inputs unchanged, the corresponding baseline output is reused if available. All video-generation checkpoints remain frozen throughout the process.

5 VComBench

VComBench evaluates whether multiple semantic requirements can be satisfied within the same generated video. It measures both individual requirement satisfaction and joint task success, allowing us to systematically assess whether compilation improves targeted requirements while preserving the remaining constraints.

5.1 Task Construction

VComBench contains 380 compositional tasks adapted from public video benchmarks covering general video quality, image-to-video generation, prompt enhancement, compositional generation, camera control, and physical commonsense [15, 16, 36, 37, 29, 1]. Each task specifies a prompt, optional visual assets, and annotated requirements with associated checks. The same task specifications are used across compiler variants.

Tasks span T2V, I2V, and R2V, providing text only, a first-frame image, and reference visual inputs, respectively. These modes describe the task’s input contract; execution may use a different conditioning mode after compilation. Figure 5 summarizes the task and requirement counts by input mode and illustrates representative semantic controls.

The tasks contain 1,617 scored requirements covering object properties and counts, spatial relations, actions and interactions, temporal order, camera behavior, appearance, physical effects, visual text, and reference conditions. We consolidate 50 raw annotation categories into 34 semantic-control dimensions shared with the capability manual. Input-validity checks are used for data validation and excluded from scoring, which measures requirements that the generated video must visibly realize.

Each task contains either three or six scored requirements: 221 tasks contain three, and 159 contain six. As described in Sec. 4.2, the main experiments use annotation-derived IRs to isolate compilation and execution from parser errors. Further construction and annotation details are provided in the supplementary material.

5.2 Scoring Protocol

A fixed video-judging pipeline evaluates each scored requirement, which passes only when all associated checks pass. Temporal, repetition, and multi-step camera requirements use denser frame sampling.

Let ℝ_q denote the scored requirements of task q, and y_q,r∈{0,1} indicate whether requirement r passes. Let 𝔼 denote the evaluated task–requirement pairs and ℚ_complete the tasks with complete judgments. Requirement satisfaction is defined as:

S_req=(1)/(|𝔼|)∑_(q,r)∈𝔼y_q,r.

(4)

Joint task success requires all scored requirements to pass:

Sₐₗₗ=(1)/(|ℚ_complete|)∑_q∈ℚ_complete1 [∑_r∈ℝ_qy_q,r=|ℝ_q|].

(5)

As illustrated in Figure 5, satisfying only two of three requirements yields partial requirement satisfaction but does not count as a successful task.

We additionally report a realism rate Sᵣₑₐₗ, defined as the fraction of evaluated videos judged photorealistic among the 366 tasks expected to produce photorealistic footage. The remaining 14 tasks explicitly request non-photorealistic styles and are excluded from this metric.

6 Experiments

6.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate frozen local deployments of MiniMax-H3 [32] and Wan [40], and a hosted Seedance 2.5 [2] model. Experiments cover the supported T2V, I2V, and R2V modes, with VACE used for Wan reference conditioning. For VComBench, we construct IRs from annotated task requirements to isolate compilation and execution from parsing errors. Three NeurCo configurations are used: targeted text rewriting (T), external operators without targeted rewriting (O), and their combination (T+O). We compare Native (original inputs), NeurCo (T), NeurCo (T+O), TIDE [54], and TIDE combined with each NeurCo configuration. Generation seeds are shared across methods where supported. TIDE implementation details are provided in Appendix G. External evaluation uses a VBench-2.0 [53] subset and the 150-task Sci-VBench testmini [49]. We report the unweighted mean over 17 valid dimensions for VBench-2.0, and PG, SCC, SC, VT, and their mean for Sci-VBench. Detailed VBench-2.0 scores are provided in Table 12 in the supplementary material.

6.2 Main Results on VComBench

Table 1 compares compilation with native generation and prompt enhancement. On native inputs, NeurCo (T+O) improves requirement satisfaction by 2.8 points on H3 and 5.5 on Wan, exceeding the 1.2 and 1.1 point gains from NeurCo (T). Wan also improves all-requirements success from 8.4% to 11.8%. On Seedance 2.5, NeurCo (T) raises requirement satisfaction from 68.5% to 69.7%, while NeurCo (T+O) reaches 68.2%. For requirement satisfaction, combined compilation performs better on H3 and Wan, while text-only compilation performs better on Seedance 2.5.

Wan improves both metrics, whereas H3’s higher requirement satisfaction coincides with lower all-requirements success (Sec. 6.3). NeurCo also complements prompt enhancement. Operator-only compilation improves TIDE’s requirement satisfaction by 0.5, 1.9, and 0.8 points on H3, Wan, and Seedance 2.5, respectively, and raises all-requirements success on all three. The combined variant achieves H3’s highest all-requirements success (34.5%), despite lower requirement satisfaction than TIDE, and improves both metrics over TIDE on Seedance 2.5. On Wan, it recovers much of the text-only loss but remains below TIDE. Additional rewriting does not consistently improve on operator-only compilation.

6.3 Mode and Quality Analysis

Table 2 analyzes native-input compilation by initial input mode. On H3, NeurCo (T+O) increases requirement satisfaction in all three modes, although R2V all-requirements success drops from 33.1% to 28.8%. On Wan, it gives larger requirement gains on T2V and R2V, while NeurCo (T) performs better on I2V. On Seedance 2.5, combined compilation raises R2V requirement satisfaction from 66.1% to 69.9% and all-requirements success from 20.7% to 28.9%, but I2V requirement satisfaction falls. The benefits therefore depend on both the backend and the input mode.

Figure 7 shows that NeurCo (T+O) improves fine-grained requirement satisfaction on H3 by 2.8 percentage points, satisfying 45 additional requirements. However, joint task success decreases by 2.9 points and realism by 6.3 points. The realism effect differs across backends: it remains stable on Wan (77.5% to 77.8%) and improves on Seedance 2.5 (68.3% to 71.0%). These results reveal backend-dependent trade-offs between semantic control, joint task success, and visual quality.

6.4 External Benchmark Results

On VBench-2.0 (Table 4), text-only compilation improves Wan’s native-input Mean17 from 0.5281 to 0.6275 (Table 13). Adding operators to TIDE improves H3 and Wan, whereas the combined strategy performs best on Seedance 2.5 (0.6963 vs. 0.6759 for TIDE). These results show that the most effective compilation strategy varies across backends.

Figure 7 shows that operator-only compilation improves composition (+0.055/+0.050) and motion order (+0.100 on both) on H3 and Wan. H3 also gains in dynamic spatial relations, while Wan improves camera motion. The improvements are concentrated in specific controls, with smaller regressions in other dimensions.

Sci-VBench tests whether the improvements extend beyond VComBench (Table 3). On native inputs, NeurCo (T+O) raises the mean from 2.668 to 2.724 on H3, from 2.561 to 2.595 on Wan, and from 2.992 to 3.025 on Seedance 2.5. After TIDE, operator-only compilation reaches 3.262 on H3 and 2.942 on Wan, while the combined variant reaches 3.233 and 2.923. On Seedance 2.5, the text-only and combined variants reach 3.268 and 3.255, respectively, compared with 3.181 for TIDE and 3.191 for the operator-only variant. The relative benefits of rewriting and operators therefore vary across backends.

6.5 Multi-Backend Routing

Table 5 reports routing over H3+Wan and H3+Wan+Seedance 2.5. The three-backend runs obtain higher VComBench requirement satisfaction under both raw and TIDE-enhanced inputs, reaching 69.7% and 74.3%, respectively. With TIDE, the Sci-VBench mean also rises from 3.128 to 3.214, while all-requirements success decreases from 33.8% to 33.2% and VBench-2.0 Mean17 decreases from 0.6749 to 0.6673. The gains are therefore not uniform across metrics. Evaluated task counts are reported in Table 10.

6.6 Case Study

Figure 8 illustrates two complementary conditioning strategies for paint mixing on Wan. The task requires three colored cups to pour matching paints into a bowl, followed by stirring until the colored streaks form a uniform mixture. Native and TIDE satisfy four of six requirements, both failing to reproduce paint intermixing and the final transition to a uniform color. NeurCo (T+O) constructs a first frame and switches from T2V to I2V to ground the scene, while TIDE + NeurCo (O) uses a proxy video through VACE to guide the mixing process. Both strategies satisfy all six requirements, capturing the temporal progression, whereas NeurCo (T) satisfies only three. Additional examples and failure cases are provided in Appendix E.

7 Conclusion

We presented NeurCo, which treats frozen video models as generative rendering backends and discovers their effective control capabilities through empirical profiling. Deployment-specific capability manuals guide the compilation of user intent into execution strategies that preserve reliable requirements and adapt challenging ones. Experiments on VComBench and two external benchmarks demonstrate improved semantic control across three backends, alongside trade-offs in joint task success and photorealism. Beyond individual renderers, these capability manuals provide a foundation for capability-aware tool selection and orchestration.

LLM Usage Statement

OpenAI Codex was used to assist with manuscript preparation, including drafting and revising the conclusion, adapting the existing LaTeX project to the CVPR template, formatting tables and figures, and resolving LaTeX compatibility issues.
