Appendix A Additional Experimental Details

A.1 Backend Deployments and Generation Settings

We evaluate MiniMax-H3 and three Wan2.2 variants with frozen weights and BF16 precision. Table 6 summarizes their generation settings. For I2V, the first-frame aspect ratio is preserved: H3 uses a short side of 768 pixels, while Wan maintains approximately the pixel budget of 1280×720.

Conditioning.

H3 uses first-frame conditioning for I2V and image or video references for R2V. When both are present, reference images precede the proxy video, which is resampled to 24 fps. Wan uses VACE for reference-image and proxy-depth conditioning, with a control strength of 0.5 for both experts when a depth video is supplied. Depth-conditioned calls additionally use a photorealism instruction and negative terms suppressing cartoon-like rendering. Other Wan calls use the official default negative prompt.

Seedance 2.5.

We evaluate a fixed version of the hosted Seedance 2.5 model at 720p and 24 fps, with audio and watermarking disabled. We access the model through the official API. T2V and R2V use a 16:9 aspect ratio, while I2V follows the first frame. Requested durations are 5 or 10 seconds.

Sampling protocol.

VComBench uses nominal durations of 5 seconds, extended to 10 seconds for shot-count or timed-event requirements. Sci-VBench and VBench-2.0 use 5-second clips. A deterministic task-specific seed is shared across methods within each deployment. For text-only comparisons, conditioning inputs and generation settings are also held fixed. Multiple samples use distinct task–sample seeds, while clips belonging to the same concatenated task share a seed.

For VBench-2.0, native-input and raw-routing configurations use three videos per task, and TIDE-based configurations use one. Diversity evaluation uses 20 videos per prompt for all configurations. When compilation leaves the generation inputs unchanged, the corresponding baseline video is reused.

A.2 Models Used by Each Component

Table 7 summarizes the models specified for compilation, condition construction, and evaluation. For VComBench, we construct the IR directly from task annotations, isolating compilation and execution from requirement-parsing errors.

Compilation and condition construction.

Targeted rewriting and TIDE enhancement use the same language model with their respective instructions. This model also plans reference images, layouts, proxy animations, and shot decompositions, and validates the constructed visual conditions. Backend and operator selection follow the capability manual and operator eligibility rules without an additional model call. The TIDE instructions are provided in Appendix G.

Condition images.

The image generator is configured as ChatGPT Images 2.0 for single-backend experiments and GPT Image 1.5 for multi-backend experiments. Images are generated at 1536×1024 resolution. Layout first frames are obtained by editing rendered layout sketches. Comparisons between single- and multi-backend configurations therefore also reflect the difference in condition-image generators.

Evaluation settings.

Language-model temperature and top-p use provider defaults. Reasoning effort is set to medium when explicitly configured. VComBench evaluation requests specify the same judge model across configurations; route-dependent settings and agreement checks are reported in Sec. A.5. Sci-VBench scoring follows Sec. A.7, and VBench-2.0 uses the official evaluation suite.

A.3 Evaluated Samples

Some Seedance 2.5 requests in VComBench were rejected by the service’s content moderation. Table 8 reports completely judged tasks for each configuration. Table 9 gives the initial-mode counts used by the main mode analysis. Table 10 reports the evaluated task counts for the multi-backend routing experiments.

A.4 Evaluation Details

For VBench-2.0, native-input and raw-routing configurations use three generated videos per task, whereas TIDE-based configurations use one. Diversity uses 20 videos in all configurations. Mean17 is the unweighted mean over the 17 valid dimensions and is not an official benchmark aggregate. Multi-view consistency is excluded because it has no valid samples.

A.5 VComBench Judging Protocol

Frame sampling.

GPT-6.1 Sol evaluates each scored video once, without repeated scoring or voting. The judge receives uniformly sampled, timestamped frames, including the first and last frames, resized to a maximum side of 448 pixels. Tasks with nominal durations up to 5 seconds use 8 frames; longer tasks use 12. We use 24 frames when any scored requirement concerns repetition count, event timing, rebound count, event order, or a camera-move sequence. Original I2V first frames and R2V reference images are provided with their roles. Concatenated clips are evaluated as one video.

Requirement scoring.

Each requirement contains one to three atomic visual checks, generated during task construction and screened for quality. Quantitative targets, including distances, angles, and speeds, are recorded separately in task annotations. For each check, the judge returns yes, no, or unclear, with a brief explanation. The judge must reject checks not clearly satisfied and reserve unclear for cases that cannot be resolved from the sampled frames, such as events between frames.

A requirement passes only when all checks receive yes. Any no yields failure; otherwise, an unclear or missing answer makes the requirement unclear. Unclear requirements count as unmet. Across configurations, 2.3% of check answers were unclear. Input-validity checks are recorded separately and excluded from requirement satisfaction. For tasks requesting photorealistic footage, realism is assessed in a separate evaluation using four sampled frames. Videos without valid judgments after repeated request failures are excluded from metric denominators; affected configurations contain 8–12 videos.

Agreement checks.

Table 11 summarizes cross-route stability and preliminary human agreement. For configurations affected by route changes, method–baseline comparisons use baselines evaluated through the same route.

Human annotations were collected without access to automatic verdicts. Among requirements with definite labels in both sources, 255/286 agreed; the judge rejected 23 human-accepted requirements and accepted 8 human-rejected requirements. This earlier H3-only audit uses one annotation set, with no reported inter-annotator agreement. Its judge configuration was not retained, so it provides preliminary evidence rather than validation of the final protocol.

A.6 VBench-2.0 Subset

We select 175 text-to-video tasks from the 18 official dimensions, using 10 prompts per dimension except Diversity, which uses five. For a prompt list of length P, the k selected indices are ⌊iP/k⌋, i=0,…,k-1. All tasks use nominal 5-second clips; task identifiers are listed in the supplementary material. Video counts follow Sec. A.1.

We apply the official per-dimension scorers. Multi-view consistency yields no valid samples and is excluded, leaving 165 tasks across 17 scored dimensions. Mean17 is their unweighted mean, not an official aggregate. Scoring follows the official validity filters and excludes unavailable outputs, so effective sample counts vary across configurations.

A.7 Sci-VBench Scoring

We evaluate the 150-task testmini split using one nominal 5-second video per task. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B scores prompt grounding (PG), scientific and causal correctness (SCC), and spatiotemporal consistency (SC) using the benchmark’s task-specific 1–5 rubrics. It receives video frames at 2 fps, with temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.8. We use one scoring round instead of the default three, so small differences should be interpreted cautiously.

Perceptual quality is measured by VT, the mean of six normalized automatic metrics: subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic quality, and imaging quality. We rescale VT to 1–5 and report an equal-weight summary:

VT₁₋₋₅=1+4/6∑ⱼ₌₁⁶sⱼ, sⱼ∈[0,1],

(6)

AVG=(PG+SCC+SC+VT₁₋₋₅)/(4).

(7)

Reported scores are averaged over the 150 tasks. AVG is our summary statistic, not an official benchmark aggregate. Reused videos retain their existing evaluation scores.

A.8 Compute and Cost

Local generation uses NVIDIA H20 GPUs, with one GPU per H3 video and eight per Wan video. Table 13 reports the video-generation expenditure of the experiments in the main paper. Requests whose compiled inputs match a baseline reuse that baseline’s video and are not counted. Local counts therefore cover only generated videos, with VComBench scaled to its 380 scored tasks. Routing experiments are listed separately: a task routed to a backend inherits the video of a matching single-backend run when one exists, and only the remaining tasks are generated. GPU hours sum the recorded generation time of each video and exclude model loading, queueing, idle time, and failed retries; Seedance costs are recorded charges for successful requests only.

NeurCo adds compilation and condition-construction costs. Shot concatenation requires additional video generations, while visual conditioning can increase generation time. Language-model calls, image generation, proxy rendering, and evaluation were not fully timed or costed and are excluded from the table. The reported budget therefore does not measure total system cost or paired per-task overhead.

item.title: 不同材质该怎么动，视频世界模型一直没搞清：WorldInteract 把「材质行为」与「接触响应」拆开算 ｜ WorldInteract: Controllable Streaming Video Generation for Multi-Material Interactions
item.description:
一句话：材质相关动力学在可控视频生成里长期欠缺，导致多材质场景的控制不可靠。

要点：

  • 缺口：视频世界模型要构建可交互的物理世界，必须刻画**不同材质如何运动与相互作用**，但**材质相关的动力学在可控视频生成中一直欠缺**，使不同材质场景下的控制不可靠
  • WorldInteract 是流式视频生成框架，把**跨材质交互**分解为两步：**与材质相关的行为生成**，以及**接触响应的计算**
  • 外部输入（用户控制）作用在这个分解结构上，而不是直接喂给一个端到端模型

为什么值得看：「水、布、木、金属混在一起」是游戏里最常见的场景，也是最难生成对的。把材质行为与接触响应分开，等于让「什么在动」和「撞上之后怎么变」各自可调——这是可控性的来源。

中文摘要：视频世界模型的目标是构建可交互的物理世界，这就要求模型刻画不同材质如何运动、以及它们之间如何相互作用；然而在可控视频生成领域，与材质相关的动力学一直是欠探索的部分，导致包含多种材质的场景难以被可靠控制。WorldInteract 因此提出一个流式视频生成框架，把跨材质的交互分解成两件事：一是与材质相关的行为生成，二是接触响应的计算，外部控制输入作用于这个分解结构之上。对需要生成水、布料、金属等混合场景的管线，这种分解让「什么在动」与「撞上之后怎么变」分别可调。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

WorldInteract: Controllable Streaming Video Generation for Multi-Material Interactions

Abstract

Video world models aim to create interactive physical worlds that capture how diverse materials move and interact. Yet material-dependent dynamics remain underexplored in controllable video generation, limiting reliable control in scenes with different materials. We present WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that decomposes cross-material interaction into material-dependent behavior generation and contact response computation. External pushes and contact impulses are expressed through a shared velocity-increment interface, allowing material behaviors learned from interaction-free videos to be reused in interacting scenes. A physics controller predicts contacts and computes velocity increments from estimated masses and restitution coefficients, while a causal generator executes these increments using learned material behaviors. This separation enables cross-material interaction without supervised contact videos spanning diverse material pairings and contact configurations. We train the generator on 30k simulated interaction-free videos spanning 22 material classes and introduce Material-Aware RL, using verifiable physical rewards to refine material behavior and control execution. WorldInteract substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods on Physics-IQ and delivers more reliable push control on real-world images.

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models aim to respond to user actions with physically plausible outcomes, yet the same push can roll a ball, slide a box, or scatter a pile of sand. Mass and friction affect how far an object travels after a push; mass and restitution govern how contact changes the motion of both objects. Reliable control therefore requires modeling both material behavior, which describes how an object moves under an applied velocity change, and contact response, which determines how momentum is exchanged when objects collide. Their combination governs cross-material interactions. Ignoring either component makes control unreliable when materials or contact partners change.

Recent work establishes important foundations for physical control. Force Prompting [10] and PhysCtrl [34] learn force control from simulated data, while Goal Force [11] extends video generation to goals involving object interactions. StreamForce [35] and PhysStream [7] support updated controls during streaming generation. However, systematic modeling of material behavior and cross-material interaction remains underexplored. Material properties determine how much motion occurs, how long it persists, and how it propagates through contact. These dependencies must be captured for controls to remain physically consistent across different materials.

Learning these behaviors directly from contact videos creates a coverage problem. Adding a material introduces new pairings with existing materials, even if its individual behavior is already represented. Each pairing can also appear under different contact configurations. Supervision must cover these combinations as well as individual material behaviors, making it costly to extend control to new materials.

We present WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that separates material behavior learning from contact response computation. Our key observation is that external pushes and contact impulses both change object velocity. A shared velocity-increment interface therefore allows material behaviors learned from interaction-free videos to be reused in interacting scenes. At inference, a physics controller predicts contacts and computes velocity increments from estimated masses and restitution coefficients, while a causal generator executes these increments using learned material behaviors. The controller determines the momentum exchange; the generator produces the resulting behavior. This decomposition enables interaction without supervised contact videos spanning material pairings and contact configurations.

We construct 30k simulated interaction-free videos, which contain no object–object contact, spanning 22 material classes. Scene memory maintains spatial state and object identity as generation proceeds under updated controls. Supervised video reconstruction alone does not directly enforce relative material behaviors or the timing of control events. We introduce Material-Aware RL to refine material behavior and control execution through verifiable physical rewards on generated rollouts. These rollouts include contact scenes produced with the physics controller, extending training beyond the interaction-free supervision. Experiments demonstrate clear advantages over state-of-the-art methods, with stronger physical consistency on Physics-IQ and higher push success on real-world images.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A compositional framework for cross-material interaction. We couple a streaming video generator for material-dependent behavior with a physics controller for contact response computation. Their shared velocity-increment interface enables cross-material interaction to be composed at inference.

  • •

    Material-Aware RL. We improve velocity-increment execution with verifiable rewards that assess material behavior and cross-material interaction in generated rollouts.

  • •

    An interaction-free multi-material dataset. We provide 30k simulated videos across 22 material classes to learn material behavior from applied pushes, avoiding exhaustive supervision over material pairings and contact configurations.

    • 2 Related Work

    Controllable video generation.

    Motion-conditioned video models guide objects through spatial controls. DragAnything [36], Tora [40], and FlashMotion [19] generate motion along specified trajectories, while DragStream [41] and MotionStream [29] allow motion guidance to change during streaming generation. Such controls specify desired motion, but do not by themselves determine how material properties and contact alter that motion. WorldInteract uses velocity increments as physical inputs, leaving material behavior to the generator and contact response computation to the physics controller.

    Physics-grounded video generation.

    Simulation provides explicit physical structure for visual synthesis. PhysGen [23], PhysGen3D [5], PhysMotion [31], and PSIVG [9] use simulated dynamics to guide generation. RealWonder [24] combines single-image 3D reconstruction, physics simulation, and a distilled generator for real-time physical control. Another line learns physical control from simulated videos: Force Prompting [10] and PhysCtrl [34] learn force-conditioned motion, while Goal Force [11] targets physics-conditioned goals involving object interactions. StreamForce [35] supports updated forces during streaming generation, and PhysStream [7] introduces structured scene memory for velocity-increment control. WorldInteract differs by separating material-dependent behavior generation from contact response computation. Learning the former from interaction-free videos and computing the latter online reduces the need for supervision over material pairings and contact configurations.

    Streaming video generation.

    Autoregressive video models support streaming synthesis through incremental generation and history conditioning [16, 12, 6, 30]. Causal distillation and training on generated histories improve inference speed and rollout stability [39, 14, 42]. Further work addresses long-horizon consistency and context management [22, 37, 18]. WorldInteract focuses on material-dependent behavior and cross-material interaction, using velocity increments to connect a physics controller with the streaming generator.

    3 Method

    As shown in Fig.2, WorldInteract assigns material-dependent behavior generation to a video generator and contact response computation to a physics controller. The controller expresses external pushes and predicted contact impulses through a shared velocity-increment interface. At inference, it computes these increments from object properties estimated by a vision-language model (VLM), while the generator, trained on how materials move after a velocity change, executes them. This division allows supervised training to cover individual material behaviors without enumerating material pairings and contact configurations.

    Training overview.

    Training has three stages. Stage 1 learns material behavior from interaction-free videos (Sec.3.1). Stage 2 introduces causal generation with scene memory and a physics map (Sec.3.2). Stage 3, Material-Aware RL, improves control execution on generated rollouts (Sec.3.3). The first two stages use supervised flow matching; the third uses reward-based preference optimization with supervised replay. At inference, the controller computes contact responses and the generator executes them (Sec.3.4). Full training objectives are provided in the Appendix.

    3.1 Material Behavior Learning

    This stage learns material-dependent behavior conditioned on user interactions. We first convert each interaction into a velocity increment, providing a shared interface for external pushes and contact impulses. The generator then learns from interaction-free videos how different materials behave under these increments.

    Interaction-free data.

    We construct 30k simulated interaction-free videos spanning diverse material classes. Figure 3 shows examples of rigid and elastic solids, fluids, and sand. Here, interaction-free excludes object–object contact; contact with the ground, friction, and rebounds remain in the videos.

    Velocity-increment interface.

    Let (t,o,J) denote a user interaction, where t is the frame at which a push is applied, o identifies the target object, and J∈ℝ³ is the applied impulse. We define the resulting velocity increment as Δv=J/mₒ, where mₒ is the object’s mass. Training uses the simulator’s true mass; at inference, the controller uses the VLM estimate m̂ₒ (Sec.3.4). The shared velocity-increment interface represents both external pushes and contact impulses, allowing material behaviors learned from pushes to be reused after contact.

    Behavior supervision.

    We encode user interactions as the push control cᵘ, whose three channels represent the x-, y-, and z-components of Δv. Encoding details are provided in the Appendix.

    Starting from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [32], we add a zero-initialized patch embedding Pᵤ for the push control and fine-tune the diffusion transformer (DiT) on 49-frame clips with full attention. Let 𝔼 denote the VAE encoder, z₀ the clean first-frame latent, z the remaining clean video latents, and y the backbone’s text conditioning. We sample τ∼U(0,1) and Gaussian noise ε∼ℕ(0,I), forming z^τ=(1-τ)z+τε. We fuse the noisy video and push control into input tokens:

    h^τ=Pₚᵣₑ(z^τ)+Pᵤ(𝔼(cᵘ)),

    		(1)

    where Pₚᵣₑ is the pretrained video patch embedding. The DiT takes h^τ, conditioned on τ, z₀, and y, and predicts the latent-space vector field v̂_θ^τ(h^τ,τ,z₀,y) used to denoise the video. We train the DiT, Pᵤ, Pₚᵣₑ, and the output head with the rectified-flow matching loss [21]:

    F_θ(z)=𝔼_τ,ε∥v̂_θ^τ(h^τ,τ,z₀,y)-(ε-z)∥₂².

    		(2)

    The VAE, the text encoder, and the text cross-attention keys and values stay frozen.

    3.2 Causal State Propagation

    This stage learns to preserve material-dependent behavior while accepting new interactions during streaming generation. Scene memory records the evolving scene, while a physics map specifies velocity increments at recent object locations.

    Causal generator.

    Starting from the Stage-1 checkpoint, we replace full attention with block-causal attention [42]. The causal VAE represents the first frame as z₀ and each subsequent four-frame chunk as z_ℓ. The DiT denoises one chunk at a time, attending to earlier latent chunks through a key–value cache.

    Scene memory.

    We represent scene state with two maps: cᵖᵒˢ records 3D positions derived from Depth-Anything-3 [20], and cᵗʳᵏ assigns each object a persistent identity using SAM2 [28]. Both maps are updated from each decoded chunk, providing the generator with object locations and identities for the next chunk.

    Physics map.

    The three-channel map cᵖ encodes velocity increments on objects’ recent masks, allowing control to follow objects as they move. At inference, it carries velocity increments computed by the physics controller for predicted contacts. To train this interface without contact videos, we route a subset of mid-video pushes, including all re-pushes, through cᵖ. The branch thus learns to execute the same velocity increments used for contact response.

    Causal supervision.

    As shown in Fig.2, we VAE-encode the condition maps and add their patch embeddings to the noisy video tokens:

    h_ℓ^τ=Pₚᵣₑ(z_ℓ^τ)+∑_m∈MPₘ(𝔼(cᵐ_ℓ-1)),

    		(3)

    where M={u,pos,trk,p}. The one-chunk shift ensures that spatial conditions use only earlier frames. The DiT takes h_ℓ^τ, τ, y, and preceding latents to predict the vector field for denoising chunk ℓ. We train with teacher forcing, using clean ground-truth history and the flow-matching loss in Eq.2. We train the DiT and the three new, zero-initialized branches Pₚₒₛ,Pₜᵣₖ,Pₚ, while the Stage-1 layers Pᵤ, Pₚᵣₑ, and the output head stay frozen.

    3.3 Material-Aware RL

    Flow matching does not directly enforce physical relations such as stronger pushes producing greater displacement. Material-Aware RL uses verifiable rewards on generated rollouts to refine material behavior and velocity-increment execution.

    Training inputs.

    We use simulated pairs that vary only in material or push magnitude, real-world image pairs with different push magnitudes, and simulated initial scenes with objects on a collision course. For each input, we sample K=4 rollouts. In contact scenes, the controller supplies velocity increments for predicted contacts, providing interaction experience without supervised contact videos.

    Physical rewards.

    SAM2 masks, CoTracker3 [15] tracks, and depth maps provide four checks: displacement accuracy (r_disp), agreement with requested velocity increments (r_Δv), relative behavior across paired inputs (rᵣₑₗ), and event timing (r_sync). Simulated interaction-free inputs provide target displacements. For real-world images and contact scenes, displacement is scored only for objects receiving no increment, rewarding unaffected neighbors that stay still. Contact execution is evaluated against the controller’s increments, so the rewards train the generator to follow a contact response while the controller remains responsible for computing it.

    Preference optimization.

    We select the highest- and lowest-reward rollouts, xʷ and xˡ, among candidates with the same predicted contacts. Diffusion-DPO [33, 27], adapted to flow matching, increases the preferred rollout’s relative likelihood using a frozen copy of the final Stage-2 model as reference. We train rank-64 LoRA adapters on the DiT’s linear layers and fully fine-tune the four condition branches. We also replay flow-matching supervision on simulated videos to limit visual drift.

    Acceleration.

    We distill the Stage-3 model into a four-step causal student with DMD [38, 39]. Initializing from the causal teacher avoids the ODE-regression stage needed when distilling a bidirectional teacher [42]. The distilled model supports interactive streaming generation at 8 fps on a single H100. VLM queries are cached per object (Sec.3.4) and do not affect per-chunk speed.

    3.4 Inference

    As shown in Fig.2, inference alternates between the physics controller, which estimates scene state and computes contact responses, and the video generator, which produces the next chunk. All state estimates use the initial image or previously generated frames.

    Physics controller.

    For each object k, the controller queries the VLM to estimate mass m̂ₖ and restitution coefficient êₖ from its image crop and approximate metric size. These properties are queried when the object enters a contact and cached for later interactions.

    Depth and object tracks provide each object’s 3D position, velocity vₖ, and acceleration. After incorporating user pushes, the controller extrapolates these states over the next chunk and predicts contacts where projected masks and depth intervals overlap. Only approaching contacts (vₙ>0, defined below) trigger impulses; resting contacts are left to the generator’s learned behavior.

    For contacting objects i and j, let n point from j to i along their centroid line, and let vₙ=(vⱼ-vᵢ)·n be their closing speed. With combined restitution ê=êᵢêⱼ, a frictionless central collision model [8] gives

    Δvᵢ=-(1+ê)\tfracm̂ⱼm̂ᵢ+m̂ⱼ vₙn,(4)
    Δvⱼ=-(1+ê)\tfracm̂ᵢm̂ᵢ+m̂ⱼ vₙn.

    After each predicted contact, the controller updates both objects’ extrapolated velocities and re-predicts later contacts, propagating velocity changes along contact chains. It writes the contact increments to cᵖ using recent masks and the one-chunk shift defined above. Contact thresholds, map timing, and simultaneous-contact handling are specified in the Appendix.

    Video generator.

    The DiT denoises the next chunk using the user push control, updated scene memory, and physics map. The decoded frames become the history for the next update.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate our approach along three axes: its physical accuracy compared with methods that learn forces or collisions directly (Sec.4.2), its physics awareness (Sec.4.3), and the contribution of each component (Sec.4.4).

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Implementation details.

    We train at 480×832 resolution with the three stages of Sec.3; hyperparameters are in the Appendix. Depth, segmentation, and point tracks come from Depth-Anything-3 [20], SAM2 [28], and CoTracker3 [15], and the controller queries Qwen2.5-VL-3B [1] for object properties. More details are provided in Appendix.

    Benchmarks.

    Physics-IQ[26] compares generated videos with real recordings of physical events. We use its solid-mechanics subset, the rigid-body scenarios our controls address (e.g., collisions, rolling, sliding, toppling). All methods use the same subset and conditioning frame. Since Physics-IQ has few material contrasts, we also build a real-image test set of 200 images in groups that share the scene and push and differ only in the material of the pushed object (e.g., rubber vs. steel), so a method cannot succeed by producing the same behavior for every material.

    Baselines.

    We compare against Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [32], which receives each push as text appended to the prompt; Force Prompting [10], a bidirectional model conditioned on a first-frame force; Goal Force [11], trained on synthetic ball and domino collisions and evaluated in its direct-force mode; and StreamForce [35], a causal generator conditioned on time-varying forces. For pushes issued during streaming, we also compare qualitatively with RealWonder [24], which simulates reconstructed 3D scenes, and FlashMotion [19], which follows trajectories.

    Metrics.

    On Physics-IQ, we report the Physics-IQ score (P-IQ), which aggregates the benchmark’s metrics normalized so that two real recordings of the same event score 100, under the verified and original protocols, together with its spatiotemporal (ST), spatial (S), and weighted spatial (WS) IoU components, averaged over 5 seeds. Since real images lack ground-truth videos, we follow the VLM-based protocol of VideoPhy [2, 34] and query GPT-4o for semantic adherence (SA) and physical commonsense (PC) on a 1–5 Likert scale. Push success (the share of pushes that set the object in motion) measures responsiveness, and the median direction error measures whether it moves the right way.

    4.2 Comparison with Baselines

    Quantitative Comparison.

    On Physics-IQ, WorldInteract achieves the highest score under both protocols (Tab.1), 15 points above the strongest baseline, Goal Force, even though Goal Force uses a much larger backbone. The IoU components explain the gain. On spatial IoU, which checks only where motion happens, Goal Force is close to our model. On spatiotemporal IoU, which also checks when it happens, our model scores more than twice as high as any baseline. Both models move objects to similar places, but ours moves them at the right time.

    On real-world images (Tab.2), our model raises push success from 67% (StreamForce, the strongest baseline) to 90%, reduces the median direction error from 10.1∘ to 5.2∘, and obtains the highest SA and PC. The baselines instead trade these criteria off: Wan2.2 attains a high SA but moves the object in only 30% of pushes, whereas Force Prompting achieves a high PC at the cost of the lowest SA.

    Qualitative comparison.

    Figure 4 shows that the baselines fail in three characteristic ways. First, Force Prompting and StreamForce often barely move the pushed object, so the described contact never happens (e.g., the tissue box does not reach the pillow). Second, Goal Force moves objects but violates rigid-body behavior: the rock breaks into fragments, tissues spill out of the tissue box, and the snow heap bursts into a spray. Third, Wan2.2 adds content instead of simulating the push, for instance a hand that enters the food-container scene, which explains its high SA but low PC. Our model keeps each pushed object intact and resolves the contact the prompt describes: the rock stops against the heavy boulder, the tissue box slides into the pillow, and the first food container pushes the second. In streaming rollouts (Fig.5), RealWonder distorts pushed objects, FlashMotion leaves them static, and StreamForce loses scene detail, whereas WorldInteract resolves the glass–can contact.

    4.3 Physics Awareness

    Figure 6 varies one physical factor at a time while holding the others fixed. External interaction intensity: the rock barely moves under the 1× push, travels farther under 3×, and reaches the cushion under 7×. External interaction direction: changing the push direction steers the cue ball toward different billiard balls, transferring motion upon contact. Material: under the same push, the steel box barely moves, the leather box travels a short distance, and the cardboard box reaches the large box, consistent with their estimated masses. Shape: the basketball rolls into the pouf and rebounds, the can reaches it more slowly, and the container slides and stops short, showing distinct rolling and sliding behaviors. The Appendix provides baseline comparisons.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    Component ablations.

    Each component contributes to the final model (Tab.3). Causal state propagation matters most: without Stages 2 and 3, P-IQ falls from 63.0 to 52.4 and push success from 90% to 82%, highlighting the importance of tracking objects as the scene evolves. Material-Aware RL adds a further 2.0 P-IQ points on top of supervised training. The physics controller leaves push success unchanged but adds 4.0 P-IQ points, indicating that explicit contact computation drives the gain in physical accuracy.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that combines material-dependent behavior generation with contact response computation through a shared velocity-increment interface. Interaction-free videos teach reusable material behavior, causal training with scene memory maintains spatial state and object identity, and Material-Aware RL improves the execution of physical controls on generated rollouts. A physics controller composes contact responses from object properties estimated by a VLM, allowing supervised data to focus on individual materials without enumerating every material pairing and contact configuration. The existing evaluations on Physics-IQ and real images support the effectiveness of this decomposition for physical accuracy and control adherence. The current controller uses approximate geometry and a frictionless central collision model; extending the same interface to richer contact models is a direction for future work.

    LLM Usage Statement

    LLMs played a supporting role, helping with selected implementation and experimental coding tasks, debugging, feedback on experimental plans, and literature searches. The authors take responsibility for the final manuscript and reported results.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    This appendix complements the main paper. AppendixA describes the interaction-free dataset. AppendixB details the implementation and training settings, while AppendicesC and D explain causal generation and the supervised objectives. AppendixE presents Material-Aware RL, AppendixF describes the physics controller, and AppendixG provides additional qualitative results.

    Appendix A Interaction-free Dataset

    Each clip shows one simulated object pushed horizontally on a textured floor under an HDRI environment map, rendered with Blender Cycles [4] at 480×832 and 16 fps. Training uses 49 frames per clip. Other objects in the scene either stay still or move in their own separate simulation, so no object–object contact occurs. Contact with the floor, friction, and rebounds remain. The 30k clips span 22 material classes across rigid and elastic solids, sand, and fluids (Tabs.S1 and S2).

    Pushes.

    A rigid or elastic push applies a horizontal force for 0.1 s; its impulse J is the force times this duration, and the simulator’s true mass gives the velocity increment Δv=J/mₒ. In clips with several pushes, the later pushes act during motion, including re-pushes of the already moving object.

    Paired groups.

    The rigid and elastic categories also contain clips rendered in paired groups that share the scene. Force ladders repeat a scene at 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0× the push force, and material pairs change the pushed object’s material, making it 2–2.5× heavier or 0.4–0.5× lighter. These groups supply the simulated pairs for Material-Aware RL (AppendixE). Hard negatives, in which the pushed object passes close to other objects without touching them, are also included.

    Appendix B Implementation Details

    Velocity-increment encoding.

    A push (t,o,J) applies a camera-frame impulse J to object o at frame t. During training, the corresponding velocity increment uses the simulator’s true mass; the generator does not receive mass as an input. Velocities are expressed in metric units in the camera frame, using simulator units during training and metric depth from Depth-Anything-3 [20] at inference, so V_\max has the same physical meaning in both. Each component is clipped to [-V_\max,V_\max]. The push control cᵘ={cᵘₜ}ₜ is a sequence of three-channel maps. At the event frame t, cᵘₜ=(Δv/V_\max+1)/2∈[0,1]³ on object o’s first-frame segmentation mask, where 1 is the all-ones vector; all other pixels and frames equal 0.5, encoding a zero increment. The first-frame mask identifies the target without revealing its future position [7].

    Training configuration.

    TableS3 lists the trained and frozen modules, learning rates, and optimizer settings of each stage. Stage 1 fine-tunes Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [32] with full attention on 49-frame clips at 480×832. Stage 2 starts from the Stage-1 checkpoint, and Stage 3 uses the final Stage-2 model as its frozen reference. The four-step student is distilled from the Stage-3 model with DMD, using a critic trained alongside it.

    Appendix C Causal Generation

    Causal generator.

    The causal VAE 𝔼 maps a video to latents z_0:L, where z₀ encodes the first frame x₀ and each subsequent z_ℓ a chunk of four frames. With block-causal attention and a key–value cache, the DiT factorizes the video distribution as

    p_θ(z_1:L|z₀,y)=∏_ℓ=1^Lp_θ(z_ℓ|z_<ℓ, y, c_<ℓ),

    		(S1)

    where y is the text conditioning and c_<ℓ denotes condition maps computed from earlier chunks only.

    Condition maps.

    The scene memory consists of a positional map cᵖᵒˢ, back-projected from Depth-Anything-3 [20] depth and normalized by the first-frame scene bounds so that positions remain comparable across chunks, and a tracking map cᵗʳᵏ in which SAM2 [28] assigns each object a fixed color. Both are re-estimated from every decoded chunk. All condition maps are rasterized per frame, VAE-encoded per chunk, shifted forward by one chunk, and added to the noisy video tokens through zero-initialized patch embeddings:

    h_ℓ^τ=Pₚᵣₑ(z^τ_ℓ)+∑_m∈MPₘ(𝔼(cᵐ_ℓ-1)),

    		(S2)

    where M={u,pos,trk,p}. The shift ensures that the conditions for chunk ℓ come only from chunk ℓ-1, so no information from chunk ℓ leaks into its own conditioning. Because the VAE compresses four frames into one latent, the timing of an event within a chunk reaches the generator only to the extent that the encoding preserves it.

    Physics map.

    The physics map cᵖ is encoded like cᵘ but can carry increments for several objects and is painted on each object’s recent mask, so the generator can identify the target after it has moved. Because of the one-chunk shift, an increment that should act at frame t of chunk ℓ+1 is painted into the map of chunk ℓ, at the same position within the chunk, on the object’s mask at frame t-4. This mask comes from an already generated chunk and matches the accompanying tracking map cᵗʳᵏ_ℓ, so it does not reveal where the object lies in the chunk being generated. The same rule is used in training and at inference. At inference, cᵖ carries the increments computed by the physics controller for predicted contacts. Material therefore enters at two points: in the generator’s learned behavior (friction, rolling resistance, rebounds from the ground) and in the controller, where mass and restitution determine the exchange at contact (Eq.S7).

    Physics-map supervision.

    Since the interaction-free videos contain no object–object contact, we supervise Pₚ with ordinary pushes. For a random subset of mid-video pushes, including all re-pushes, the increment is written to cᵖ instead of cᵘ, painted by the rule above on the object’s ground-truth mask one chunk before the push. This is the same operation the controller performs at a contact, and because these pushes vary in timing, magnitude, and direction, the branch learns to execute increments of contacts it has never seen.

    Condition perturbations.

    To narrow the gap between simulator-rendered conditions and those estimated at inference, Stage 2 jitters the timing, magnitude, and direction of increments and perturbs depth and tracking masks. We never drop cᵖ while the video shows the corresponding velocity change, since that would teach the generator to change velocities without a cause.

    Appendix D Supervised Objectives

    Flow matching.

    Stages 1 and 2 use rectified-flow matching [21], following PhysStream [7] with the additional physics branch in Stage 2. Let z₀ encode the initial image x₀, z denote the remaining clean video latents, and y the backbone’s text conditioning. With τ∼U(0,1), ε∼ℕ(0,I), and z^τ=(1-τ)z+τε, Stage 1 fuses the noisy video and push control into input tokens h^τ=Pₚᵣₑ(z^τ)+Pᵤ(𝔼(cᵘ)) and minimizes

    F_θ(z)=𝔼_τ,ε∥v̂_θ^τ(h^τ,τ,z₀,y)-(ε-z)∥₂²,

    		(S3)

    where v̂_θ^τ predicts the latent-space vector field, not an object’s physical velocity. The clean latent of x₀ occupies the first slot with its condition slot set to zero, and the loss is evaluated on the remaining latents.

    Teacher forcing.

    Stage 2 switches to block-causal attention with one latent per block [42] and trains with teacher forcing: each latent is denoised given the clean ground-truth latents that precede it, with the conditions of the preceding chunk fused into h^τ_ℓ by Eq.S2,

    v̂_ℓ=v̂_θ^τ(h^τ_ℓ,τ, zᵍᵗ_<ℓ, y),

    		(S4)

    and Eq.S3 averaged over the clip.

    Appendix E Material-Aware RL

    Motivation.

    Flow matching scores each clip in isolation and weighs all pixels equally, so small physical errors, such as a drifting neighbor or a velocity change one frame early, cost little, and relations such as a harder push traveling farther are never compared. Stage 3 therefore samples rollouts from the current model, including rollouts with controller-generated contacts, scores them with verifiable checkers, and increases the relative likelihood of rollouts that satisfy them. During Stage 3, the controller uses simulator properties for simulated inputs and VLM estimates precomputed offline for real images, so no VLM runs inside the training loop.

    Training inputs.

    Inputs are (i) simulated pairs (x₀⁺,x₀⁻) from the force ladders and material pairs (AppendixA), differing only in push magnitude or in the pushed object’s material, where x₀⁺ travels farther in simulation; (ii) real-image pairs, where x₀⁺ receives the stronger push; and (iii) contact scenes, simulated first frames with objects on a collision course, whose contacts occur only in the model’s own rollouts.

    Verifiable rewards.

    Rewards are computed from SAM2 masks, CoTracker3 [15] point tracks, and depth maps. For object k∈O, let uₖ⁻ and uₖ be its image velocity in the chunks before and after an increment Δvₖ (from cᵘ or cᵖ), ūₖ=u⁻ₖ+ΠΔvₖ its expected velocity, with Π the depth-based projection to the image, and dₖ and d^⋆ₖ its generated and target displacements, normalized by its first-frame bounding-box diagonal. On simulated interaction-free inputs, d^⋆ₖ comes from the simulator. On real images and contact scenes, it is defined only for objects that receive no increment, where d^⋆ₖ=0 rewards neighbors that stay still. Objects involved in a contact are scored only by r_Δv and r_sync against the controller’s increments. Scoring them against the simulator, whose contact model includes friction and spin, would penalize the generator for executing the controller faithfully; Stage 3 thus teaches the generator to execute contact increments, while the controller remains solely responsible for deciding them. For a pair, let x⁺ₐ and x⁻_b, a,b∈{1,…,K}, be the rollouts of the two inputs and d(·) the target’s displacement. Let tₘ be the frame at which an increment is scheduled and tᵥ the frame at which the object’s tracked velocity changes most, found by change-point detection on its speed. The checkers are

    r_disp=\tfrac1|O|∑_k∈O\exp (-|dₖ-d^⋆ₖ|/ρ),(S5)
    r_Δv=\tfrac1|O_Δ|∑_k∈O_Δ\exp (-\tfrac∥uₖ-ūₖ∥\max(η∥ūₖ∥, v_\min)),
    rᵣₑₗ(x⁺ₐ)=\tfrac1K∑_bσ((d(x⁺ₐ)-d(x⁻_b))/κ),
    r_sync=\tfrac1|I|∑_(k,tₘ)∈I\exp (-|tᵥ-tₘ|/ω),

    where O_Δ is the set of objects that receive an increment, I the set of scheduled increments, σ the logistic function, and ρ,η,v_\min,κ,ω temperatures; rᵣₑₗ(x⁻_b) is defined symmetrically with the sign reversed. A rollout’s reward is the weighted mean r=∑_cw_cr_c/∑_cw_c over the checkers available for its input (rᵣₑₗ only for pairs, r_disp only for objects with a defined d^⋆ₖ).

    Preference optimization.

    For each input, we draw K=4 rollouts with the 50-step sampler and different seeds. Among rollouts with the same predicted contacts, so that the comparison is not confounded by the controller, we take the highest- and lowest-reward ones as winner xʷ and loser xˡ, with latents zʷ and zˡ, and discard the input if their reward gap is below 0.1. We apply Diffusion-DPO [33, 27], adapted to flow matching, with a frozen copy of the final Stage-2 model, v̂_ref^τ, as reference. Both rollouts are re-noised and denoised under teacher forcing (Eq.S4) with their own preceding latents and condition maps. With shared (τ,ε) and δ_θ(z)=∥v̂_θ^τ(h^τ,τ)-(ε-z)∥²-∥v̂_ref^τ(h^τ,τ)-(ε-z)∥², with conditioning omitted for brevity,

    L_RL=-𝔼 \logσ(-β [δ_θ(zʷ)-δ_θ(zˡ)])+λ F_θ(zˢⁱᵐ),

    		(S6)

    where the second term replays flow matching on simulated clips zˢⁱᵐ to limit visual drift; we use β=500. We train rank-64 LoRA adapters on the DiT’s linear layers and fully fine-tune the four condition branches.

    Acceleration.

    We distill the Stage-3 model into a four-step causal student with DMD [38, 39]. Initializing from the block-causal teacher avoids the ODE-regression stage required when distilling a bidirectional teacher [39, 42].

    Appendix F Inference

    Before each chunk, the physics controller updates scene memory from committed frames, predicts upcoming contacts, and schedules the resulting increments; the generator then executes them and commits the chunk (AlgorithmS1).

    Contact prediction.

    From the depth and tracks of committed chunks, the controller fits each object’s camera-space centroid pₖ, velocity vₖ, and acceleration over the last chunk, adds any user increment already received for the next chunk, and extrapolates over that chunk, translating each object’s last mask by its projected displacement. A contact between objects i and j is predicted at the first frame t_c at which their translated silhouettes overlap and their depth intervals, estimated from the visible depth and each object’s metric extent, overlap within a margin ε_z. The contact normal follows the line between centroids, n=(pᵢ-pⱼ)/∥pᵢ-pⱼ∥, pointing from j to i; this is exact for spheres and approximate for other shapes. The closing speed vₙ=(vⱼ-vᵢ)·n is positive when the objects approach each other. Only approaching contacts (vₙ>0) trigger impulses, and a pair that has received an impulse is excluded until its masks separate, which prevents repeated impulses while the objects remain in contact. Resting contacts are left to the generator’s learned behavior.

    Object properties.

    The first time an object enters a contact, the VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-3B [1]) receives a crop of the object and its approximate metric extent from the depth map, and returns a mass estimate m̂ₖ and a restitution class mapped to êₖ∈{0.8,0.5,0.2}. Answers are cached per object for later interactions.

    Contact response.

    With combined restitution ê=êᵢêⱼ, as in common rigid-body engines [8], a frictionless central collision gives

    Δvᵢ=-(1+ê)\tfracm̂ⱼm̂ᵢ+m̂ⱼ vₙn,(S7)
    Δvⱼ=-(1+ê)\tfracm̂ᵢm̂ᵢ+m̂ⱼ vₙn,

    clipped to [-V_\max,V_\max]³. Before clipping, the objects separate along n with relative normal speed ê vₙ and total momentum is conserved. Since increments take effect one chunk after they are painted, a contact predicted at frame t_c of chunk ℓ+1 is written into the map of chunk ℓ on both objects’ masks at frame t_c-4; contacts must therefore be predicted rather than detected. Contacts within a chunk are resolved in temporal order, and after each one the updated velocities are used to re-predict later contacts, so collision chains can propagate within a chunk. Simultaneous contacts on the same object have their increments summed, approximating coupled multi-body resolution.

    Appendix G Additional Qualitative Results

    This section extends the qualitative studies of the main paper: Fig.S1 complements Fig. 4, Figs.S2 and S3 complement Fig. 5, and Fig.S4 adds baselines to Fig. 6. All methods, namely Wan2.2 [32], Force Prompting [10], Goal Force [11], StreamForce [35], and, for streaming, RealWonder [24] and FlashMotion [19], receive the same image, prompt, and pushes.

    Push-driven interactions.

    FigureS1 shows six scenes in which a pushed object strikes a second object, in most cases of a different material: a steel bottle and a knitted pouf, two wooden blocks, a brick and a bean bag, a stone and a foam block, a wooden cube and a plastic toy bin, and a wooden box and a cushion. The failure modes identified in the main paper recur across all six scenes. Wan2.2 adds content instead of executing the push: a hand, a foot, or a pair of legs enters the frame in three scenes, the pouf swells until it fills the view, and the wooden box tumbles and breaks apart. Force Prompting leaves the pushed object nearly in place, and StreamForce moves it only slightly, so in both cases the contact described by the prompt never occurs. Goal Force produces motion but violates rigid-body behavior: the brick splits in two, the foam block and the wooden cube deform, the wooden box collapses into a wedge, and the pouf dissolves into colored artifacts. Our model moves each pushed object along the push until it reaches the target and keeps both objects intact through the contact.

    Streaming interactions.

    FiguresS2 and S3 show six streaming rollouts with four to five pushes each. Pushes are issued while generation is in progress, often to an object that has already moved, and a single rollout can involve several objects of different materials, e.g., an apple, a cast-iron pot, a copper saucepan, and a heap of flour on the same counter. The three baselines fail in distinct ways. RealWonder simulates reconstructed 3D geometry, so reconstruction errors become visible as soon as an object moves: the tissue box folds into an open tray, the mug shatters into flat discs and disappears, the sled turns into a green boat, the apple splits, and the winter table fills with objects that were never in the input, such as a toy plane and glowing rings. FlashMotion keeps every scene essentially static. StreamForce moves some objects but accumulates error over the rollout, with haze, loss of contrast and texture, and ghosted objects by the final frames. Our model executes each push at the object’s current position, produces both rigid sliding and the spreading of granular flour and snow, and preserves the appearance of the scene for the full rollout.

    Physics awareness.

    FigureS4 varies one factor at a time. Force Prompting and StreamForce largely ignore it: the rock travels the same short distance at every intensity, the cue ball and the shaped objects barely move, and StreamForce moves all three boxes equally far. Goal Force reacts but not in proportion, carrying the rock to the cushion even at 1×, sending the cue ball past or short of the target balls, toppling the pouf, and driving every box into the large box regardless of material. Only our model yields graded outcomes: travel grows with intensity, the cue ball reaches the red, yellow, and blue balls in turn, the basketball rebounds while the can arrives slowly and the container stops short, and the steel, leather, and cardboard boxes travel in order of their estimated masses.

一句话：材质相关动力学在可控视频生成里长期欠缺，导致多材质场景的控制不可靠。

要点：

  • 缺口：视频世界模型要构建可交互的物理世界，必须刻画**不同材质如何运动与相互作用**，但**材质相关的动力学在可控视频生成中一直欠缺**，使不同材质场景下的控制不可靠
  • WorldInteract 是流式视频生成框架，把**跨材质交互**分解为两步：**与材质相关的行为生成**，以及**接触响应的计算**
  • 外部输入（用户控制）作用在这个分解结构上，而不是直接喂给一个端到端模型

为什么值得看：「水、布、木、金属混在一起」是游戏里最常见的场景，也是最难生成对的。把材质行为与接触响应分开，等于让「什么在动」和「撞上之后怎么变」各自可调——这是可控性的来源。

中文摘要：视频世界模型的目标是构建可交互的物理世界，这就要求模型刻画不同材质如何运动、以及它们之间如何相互作用；然而在可控视频生成领域，与材质相关的动力学一直是欠探索的部分，导致包含多种材质的场景难以被可靠控制。WorldInteract 因此提出一个流式视频生成框架，把跨材质的交互分解成两件事：一是与材质相关的行为生成，二是接触响应的计算，外部控制输入作用于这个分解结构之上。对需要生成水、布料、金属等混合场景的管线，这种分解让「什么在动」与「撞上之后怎么变」分别可调。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

WorldInteract: Controllable Streaming Video Generation for Multi-Material Interactions

Abstract

Video world models aim to create interactive physical worlds that capture how diverse materials move and interact. Yet material-dependent dynamics remain underexplored in controllable video generation, limiting reliable control in scenes with different materials. We present WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that decomposes cross-material interaction into material-dependent behavior generation and contact response computation. External pushes and contact impulses are expressed through a shared velocity-increment interface, allowing material behaviors learned from interaction-free videos to be reused in interacting scenes. A physics controller predicts contacts and computes velocity increments from estimated masses and restitution coefficients, while a causal generator executes these increments using learned material behaviors. This separation enables cross-material interaction without supervised contact videos spanning diverse material pairings and contact configurations. We train the generator on 30k simulated interaction-free videos spanning 22 material classes and introduce Material-Aware RL, using verifiable physical rewards to refine material behavior and control execution. WorldInteract substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods on Physics-IQ and delivers more reliable push control on real-world images.

1 Introduction

Interactive video world models aim to respond to user actions with physically plausible outcomes, yet the same push can roll a ball, slide a box, or scatter a pile of sand. Mass and friction affect how far an object travels after a push; mass and restitution govern how contact changes the motion of both objects. Reliable control therefore requires modeling both material behavior, which describes how an object moves under an applied velocity change, and contact response, which determines how momentum is exchanged when objects collide. Their combination governs cross-material interactions. Ignoring either component makes control unreliable when materials or contact partners change.

Recent work establishes important foundations for physical control. Force Prompting [10] and PhysCtrl [34] learn force control from simulated data, while Goal Force [11] extends video generation to goals involving object interactions. StreamForce [35] and PhysStream [7] support updated controls during streaming generation. However, systematic modeling of material behavior and cross-material interaction remains underexplored. Material properties determine how much motion occurs, how long it persists, and how it propagates through contact. These dependencies must be captured for controls to remain physically consistent across different materials.

Learning these behaviors directly from contact videos creates a coverage problem. Adding a material introduces new pairings with existing materials, even if its individual behavior is already represented. Each pairing can also appear under different contact configurations. Supervision must cover these combinations as well as individual material behaviors, making it costly to extend control to new materials.

We present WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that separates material behavior learning from contact response computation. Our key observation is that external pushes and contact impulses both change object velocity. A shared velocity-increment interface therefore allows material behaviors learned from interaction-free videos to be reused in interacting scenes. At inference, a physics controller predicts contacts and computes velocity increments from estimated masses and restitution coefficients, while a causal generator executes these increments using learned material behaviors. The controller determines the momentum exchange; the generator produces the resulting behavior. This decomposition enables interaction without supervised contact videos spanning material pairings and contact configurations.

We construct 30k simulated interaction-free videos, which contain no object–object contact, spanning 22 material classes. Scene memory maintains spatial state and object identity as generation proceeds under updated controls. Supervised video reconstruction alone does not directly enforce relative material behaviors or the timing of control events. We introduce Material-Aware RL to refine material behavior and control execution through verifiable physical rewards on generated rollouts. These rollouts include contact scenes produced with the physics controller, extending training beyond the interaction-free supervision. Experiments demonstrate clear advantages over state-of-the-art methods, with stronger physical consistency on Physics-IQ and higher push success on real-world images.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A compositional framework for cross-material interaction. We couple a streaming video generator for material-dependent behavior with a physics controller for contact response computation. Their shared velocity-increment interface enables cross-material interaction to be composed at inference.

  • •

    Material-Aware RL. We improve velocity-increment execution with verifiable rewards that assess material behavior and cross-material interaction in generated rollouts.

  • •

    An interaction-free multi-material dataset. We provide 30k simulated videos across 22 material classes to learn material behavior from applied pushes, avoiding exhaustive supervision over material pairings and contact configurations.

    • 2 Related Work

    Controllable video generation.

    Motion-conditioned video models guide objects through spatial controls. DragAnything [36], Tora [40], and FlashMotion [19] generate motion along specified trajectories, while DragStream [41] and MotionStream [29] allow motion guidance to change during streaming generation. Such controls specify desired motion, but do not by themselves determine how material properties and contact alter that motion. WorldInteract uses velocity increments as physical inputs, leaving material behavior to the generator and contact response computation to the physics controller.

    Physics-grounded video generation.

    Simulation provides explicit physical structure for visual synthesis. PhysGen [23], PhysGen3D [5], PhysMotion [31], and PSIVG [9] use simulated dynamics to guide generation. RealWonder [24] combines single-image 3D reconstruction, physics simulation, and a distilled generator for real-time physical control. Another line learns physical control from simulated videos: Force Prompting [10] and PhysCtrl [34] learn force-conditioned motion, while Goal Force [11] targets physics-conditioned goals involving object interactions. StreamForce [35] supports updated forces during streaming generation, and PhysStream [7] introduces structured scene memory for velocity-increment control. WorldInteract differs by separating material-dependent behavior generation from contact response computation. Learning the former from interaction-free videos and computing the latter online reduces the need for supervision over material pairings and contact configurations.

    Streaming video generation.

    Autoregressive video models support streaming synthesis through incremental generation and history conditioning [16, 12, 6, 30]. Causal distillation and training on generated histories improve inference speed and rollout stability [39, 14, 42]. Further work addresses long-horizon consistency and context management [22, 37, 18]. WorldInteract focuses on material-dependent behavior and cross-material interaction, using velocity increments to connect a physics controller with the streaming generator.

    3 Method

    As shown in Fig.2, WorldInteract assigns material-dependent behavior generation to a video generator and contact response computation to a physics controller. The controller expresses external pushes and predicted contact impulses through a shared velocity-increment interface. At inference, it computes these increments from object properties estimated by a vision-language model (VLM), while the generator, trained on how materials move after a velocity change, executes them. This division allows supervised training to cover individual material behaviors without enumerating material pairings and contact configurations.

    Training overview.

    Training has three stages. Stage 1 learns material behavior from interaction-free videos (Sec.3.1). Stage 2 introduces causal generation with scene memory and a physics map (Sec.3.2). Stage 3, Material-Aware RL, improves control execution on generated rollouts (Sec.3.3). The first two stages use supervised flow matching; the third uses reward-based preference optimization with supervised replay. At inference, the controller computes contact responses and the generator executes them (Sec.3.4). Full training objectives are provided in the Appendix.

    3.1 Material Behavior Learning

    This stage learns material-dependent behavior conditioned on user interactions. We first convert each interaction into a velocity increment, providing a shared interface for external pushes and contact impulses. The generator then learns from interaction-free videos how different materials behave under these increments.

    Interaction-free data.

    We construct 30k simulated interaction-free videos spanning diverse material classes. Figure 3 shows examples of rigid and elastic solids, fluids, and sand. Here, interaction-free excludes object–object contact; contact with the ground, friction, and rebounds remain in the videos.

    Velocity-increment interface.

    Let (t,o,J) denote a user interaction, where t is the frame at which a push is applied, o identifies the target object, and J∈ℝ³ is the applied impulse. We define the resulting velocity increment as Δv=J/mₒ, where mₒ is the object’s mass. Training uses the simulator’s true mass; at inference, the controller uses the VLM estimate m̂ₒ (Sec.3.4). The shared velocity-increment interface represents both external pushes and contact impulses, allowing material behaviors learned from pushes to be reused after contact.

    Behavior supervision.

    We encode user interactions as the push control cᵘ, whose three channels represent the x-, y-, and z-components of Δv. Encoding details are provided in the Appendix.

    Starting from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [32], we add a zero-initialized patch embedding Pᵤ for the push control and fine-tune the diffusion transformer (DiT) on 49-frame clips with full attention. Let 𝔼 denote the VAE encoder, z₀ the clean first-frame latent, z the remaining clean video latents, and y the backbone’s text conditioning. We sample τ∼U(0,1) and Gaussian noise ε∼ℕ(0,I), forming z^τ=(1-τ)z+τε. We fuse the noisy video and push control into input tokens:

    h^τ=Pₚᵣₑ(z^τ)+Pᵤ(𝔼(cᵘ)),

    		(1)

    where Pₚᵣₑ is the pretrained video patch embedding. The DiT takes h^τ, conditioned on τ, z₀, and y, and predicts the latent-space vector field v̂_θ^τ(h^τ,τ,z₀,y) used to denoise the video. We train the DiT, Pᵤ, Pₚᵣₑ, and the output head with the rectified-flow matching loss [21]:

    F_θ(z)=𝔼_τ,ε∥v̂_θ^τ(h^τ,τ,z₀,y)-(ε-z)∥₂².

    		(2)

    The VAE, the text encoder, and the text cross-attention keys and values stay frozen.

    3.2 Causal State Propagation

    This stage learns to preserve material-dependent behavior while accepting new interactions during streaming generation. Scene memory records the evolving scene, while a physics map specifies velocity increments at recent object locations.

    Causal generator.

    Starting from the Stage-1 checkpoint, we replace full attention with block-causal attention [42]. The causal VAE represents the first frame as z₀ and each subsequent four-frame chunk as z_ℓ. The DiT denoises one chunk at a time, attending to earlier latent chunks through a key–value cache.

    Scene memory.

    We represent scene state with two maps: cᵖᵒˢ records 3D positions derived from Depth-Anything-3 [20], and cᵗʳᵏ assigns each object a persistent identity using SAM2 [28]. Both maps are updated from each decoded chunk, providing the generator with object locations and identities for the next chunk.

    Physics map.

    The three-channel map cᵖ encodes velocity increments on objects’ recent masks, allowing control to follow objects as they move. At inference, it carries velocity increments computed by the physics controller for predicted contacts. To train this interface without contact videos, we route a subset of mid-video pushes, including all re-pushes, through cᵖ. The branch thus learns to execute the same velocity increments used for contact response.

    Causal supervision.

    As shown in Fig.2, we VAE-encode the condition maps and add their patch embeddings to the noisy video tokens:

    h_ℓ^τ=Pₚᵣₑ(z_ℓ^τ)+∑_m∈MPₘ(𝔼(cᵐ_ℓ-1)),

    		(3)

    where M={u,pos,trk,p}. The one-chunk shift ensures that spatial conditions use only earlier frames. The DiT takes h_ℓ^τ, τ, y, and preceding latents to predict the vector field for denoising chunk ℓ. We train with teacher forcing, using clean ground-truth history and the flow-matching loss in Eq.2. We train the DiT and the three new, zero-initialized branches Pₚₒₛ,Pₜᵣₖ,Pₚ, while the Stage-1 layers Pᵤ, Pₚᵣₑ, and the output head stay frozen.

    3.3 Material-Aware RL

    Flow matching does not directly enforce physical relations such as stronger pushes producing greater displacement. Material-Aware RL uses verifiable rewards on generated rollouts to refine material behavior and velocity-increment execution.

    Training inputs.

    We use simulated pairs that vary only in material or push magnitude, real-world image pairs with different push magnitudes, and simulated initial scenes with objects on a collision course. For each input, we sample K=4 rollouts. In contact scenes, the controller supplies velocity increments for predicted contacts, providing interaction experience without supervised contact videos.

    Physical rewards.

    SAM2 masks, CoTracker3 [15] tracks, and depth maps provide four checks: displacement accuracy (r_disp), agreement with requested velocity increments (r_Δv), relative behavior across paired inputs (rᵣₑₗ), and event timing (r_sync). Simulated interaction-free inputs provide target displacements. For real-world images and contact scenes, displacement is scored only for objects receiving no increment, rewarding unaffected neighbors that stay still. Contact execution is evaluated against the controller’s increments, so the rewards train the generator to follow a contact response while the controller remains responsible for computing it.

    Preference optimization.

    We select the highest- and lowest-reward rollouts, xʷ and xˡ, among candidates with the same predicted contacts. Diffusion-DPO [33, 27], adapted to flow matching, increases the preferred rollout’s relative likelihood using a frozen copy of the final Stage-2 model as reference. We train rank-64 LoRA adapters on the DiT’s linear layers and fully fine-tune the four condition branches. We also replay flow-matching supervision on simulated videos to limit visual drift.

    Acceleration.

    We distill the Stage-3 model into a four-step causal student with DMD [38, 39]. Initializing from the causal teacher avoids the ODE-regression stage needed when distilling a bidirectional teacher [42]. The distilled model supports interactive streaming generation at 8 fps on a single H100. VLM queries are cached per object (Sec.3.4) and do not affect per-chunk speed.

    3.4 Inference

    As shown in Fig.2, inference alternates between the physics controller, which estimates scene state and computes contact responses, and the video generator, which produces the next chunk. All state estimates use the initial image or previously generated frames.

    Physics controller.

    For each object k, the controller queries the VLM to estimate mass m̂ₖ and restitution coefficient êₖ from its image crop and approximate metric size. These properties are queried when the object enters a contact and cached for later interactions.

    Depth and object tracks provide each object’s 3D position, velocity vₖ, and acceleration. After incorporating user pushes, the controller extrapolates these states over the next chunk and predicts contacts where projected masks and depth intervals overlap. Only approaching contacts (vₙ>0, defined below) trigger impulses; resting contacts are left to the generator’s learned behavior.

    For contacting objects i and j, let n point from j to i along their centroid line, and let vₙ=(vⱼ-vᵢ)·n be their closing speed. With combined restitution ê=êᵢêⱼ, a frictionless central collision model [8] gives

    Δvᵢ=-(1+ê)\tfracm̂ⱼm̂ᵢ+m̂ⱼ vₙn,(4)
    Δvⱼ=-(1+ê)\tfracm̂ᵢm̂ᵢ+m̂ⱼ vₙn.

    After each predicted contact, the controller updates both objects’ extrapolated velocities and re-predicts later contacts, propagating velocity changes along contact chains. It writes the contact increments to cᵖ using recent masks and the one-chunk shift defined above. Contact thresholds, map timing, and simultaneous-contact handling are specified in the Appendix.

    Video generator.

    The DiT denoises the next chunk using the user push control, updated scene memory, and physics map. The decoded frames become the history for the next update.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate our approach along three axes: its physical accuracy compared with methods that learn forces or collisions directly (Sec.4.2), its physics awareness (Sec.4.3), and the contribution of each component (Sec.4.4).

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Implementation details.

    We train at 480×832 resolution with the three stages of Sec.3; hyperparameters are in the Appendix. Depth, segmentation, and point tracks come from Depth-Anything-3 [20], SAM2 [28], and CoTracker3 [15], and the controller queries Qwen2.5-VL-3B [1] for object properties. More details are provided in Appendix.

    Benchmarks.

    Physics-IQ[26] compares generated videos with real recordings of physical events. We use its solid-mechanics subset, the rigid-body scenarios our controls address (e.g., collisions, rolling, sliding, toppling). All methods use the same subset and conditioning frame. Since Physics-IQ has few material contrasts, we also build a real-image test set of 200 images in groups that share the scene and push and differ only in the material of the pushed object (e.g., rubber vs. steel), so a method cannot succeed by producing the same behavior for every material.

    Baselines.

    We compare against Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [32], which receives each push as text appended to the prompt; Force Prompting [10], a bidirectional model conditioned on a first-frame force; Goal Force [11], trained on synthetic ball and domino collisions and evaluated in its direct-force mode; and StreamForce [35], a causal generator conditioned on time-varying forces. For pushes issued during streaming, we also compare qualitatively with RealWonder [24], which simulates reconstructed 3D scenes, and FlashMotion [19], which follows trajectories.

    Metrics.

    On Physics-IQ, we report the Physics-IQ score (P-IQ), which aggregates the benchmark’s metrics normalized so that two real recordings of the same event score 100, under the verified and original protocols, together with its spatiotemporal (ST), spatial (S), and weighted spatial (WS) IoU components, averaged over 5 seeds. Since real images lack ground-truth videos, we follow the VLM-based protocol of VideoPhy [2, 34] and query GPT-4o for semantic adherence (SA) and physical commonsense (PC) on a 1–5 Likert scale. Push success (the share of pushes that set the object in motion) measures responsiveness, and the median direction error measures whether it moves the right way.

    4.2 Comparison with Baselines

    Quantitative Comparison.

    On Physics-IQ, WorldInteract achieves the highest score under both protocols (Tab.1), 15 points above the strongest baseline, Goal Force, even though Goal Force uses a much larger backbone. The IoU components explain the gain. On spatial IoU, which checks only where motion happens, Goal Force is close to our model. On spatiotemporal IoU, which also checks when it happens, our model scores more than twice as high as any baseline. Both models move objects to similar places, but ours moves them at the right time.

    On real-world images (Tab.2), our model raises push success from 67% (StreamForce, the strongest baseline) to 90%, reduces the median direction error from 10.1∘ to 5.2∘, and obtains the highest SA and PC. The baselines instead trade these criteria off: Wan2.2 attains a high SA but moves the object in only 30% of pushes, whereas Force Prompting achieves a high PC at the cost of the lowest SA.

    Qualitative comparison.

    Figure 4 shows that the baselines fail in three characteristic ways. First, Force Prompting and StreamForce often barely move the pushed object, so the described contact never happens (e.g., the tissue box does not reach the pillow). Second, Goal Force moves objects but violates rigid-body behavior: the rock breaks into fragments, tissues spill out of the tissue box, and the snow heap bursts into a spray. Third, Wan2.2 adds content instead of simulating the push, for instance a hand that enters the food-container scene, which explains its high SA but low PC. Our model keeps each pushed object intact and resolves the contact the prompt describes: the rock stops against the heavy boulder, the tissue box slides into the pillow, and the first food container pushes the second. In streaming rollouts (Fig.5), RealWonder distorts pushed objects, FlashMotion leaves them static, and StreamForce loses scene detail, whereas WorldInteract resolves the glass–can contact.

    4.3 Physics Awareness

    Figure 6 varies one physical factor at a time while holding the others fixed. External interaction intensity: the rock barely moves under the 1× push, travels farther under 3×, and reaches the cushion under 7×. External interaction direction: changing the push direction steers the cue ball toward different billiard balls, transferring motion upon contact. Material: under the same push, the steel box barely moves, the leather box travels a short distance, and the cardboard box reaches the large box, consistent with their estimated masses. Shape: the basketball rolls into the pouf and rebounds, the can reaches it more slowly, and the container slides and stops short, showing distinct rolling and sliding behaviors. The Appendix provides baseline comparisons.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    Component ablations.

    Each component contributes to the final model (Tab.3). Causal state propagation matters most: without Stages 2 and 3, P-IQ falls from 63.0 to 52.4 and push success from 90% to 82%, highlighting the importance of tracking objects as the scene evolves. Material-Aware RL adds a further 2.0 P-IQ points on top of supervised training. The physics controller leaves push success unchanged but adds 4.0 P-IQ points, indicating that explicit contact computation drives the gain in physical accuracy.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that combines material-dependent behavior generation with contact response computation through a shared velocity-increment interface. Interaction-free videos teach reusable material behavior, causal training with scene memory maintains spatial state and object identity, and Material-Aware RL improves the execution of physical controls on generated rollouts. A physics controller composes contact responses from object properties estimated by a VLM, allowing supervised data to focus on individual materials without enumerating every material pairing and contact configuration. The existing evaluations on Physics-IQ and real images support the effectiveness of this decomposition for physical accuracy and control adherence. The current controller uses approximate geometry and a frictionless central collision model; extending the same interface to richer contact models is a direction for future work.

    Appendix

    This appendix complements the main paper. AppendixA describes the interaction-free dataset. AppendixB details the implementation and training settings, while AppendicesC and D explain causal generation and the supervised objectives. AppendixE presents Material-Aware RL, AppendixF describes the physics controller, and AppendixG provides additional qualitative results.

    Appendix A Interaction-free Dataset

    Each clip shows one simulated object pushed horizontally on a textured floor under an HDRI environment map, rendered with Blender Cycles [4] at 480×832 and 16 fps. Training uses 49 frames per clip. Other objects in the scene either stay still or move in their own separate simulation, so no object–object contact occurs. Contact with the floor, friction, and rebounds remain. The 30k clips span 22 material classes across rigid and elastic solids, sand, and fluids (Tabs.S1 and S2).

    Pushes.

    A rigid or elastic push applies a horizontal force for 0.1 s; its impulse J is the force times this duration, and the simulator’s true mass gives the velocity increment Δv=J/mₒ. In clips with several pushes, the later pushes act during motion, including re-pushes of the already moving object.

    Paired groups.

    The rigid and elastic categories also contain clips rendered in paired groups that share the scene. Force ladders repeat a scene at 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0× the push force, and material pairs change the pushed object’s material, making it 2–2.5× heavier or 0.4–0.5× lighter. These groups supply the simulated pairs for Material-Aware RL (AppendixE). Hard negatives, in which the pushed object passes close to other objects without touching them, are also included.

    Appendix B Implementation Details

    Velocity-increment encoding.

    A push (t,o,J) applies a camera-frame impulse J to object o at frame t. During training, the corresponding velocity increment uses the simulator’s true mass; the generator does not receive mass as an input. Velocities are expressed in metric units in the camera frame, using simulator units during training and metric depth from Depth-Anything-3 [20] at inference, so V_\max has the same physical meaning in both. Each component is clipped to [-V_\max,V_\max]. The push control cᵘ={cᵘₜ}ₜ is a sequence of three-channel maps.
