Crucially, the objective is goal and constraint independent, training the dynamics to recover the demonstrated controls required to reproduce X.

    To mitigate controller-induced distribution shift, we use DAgger-style aggregation. At each epoch, the finite-horizon tracking QP used for control-recovery supervision generates control sequences that are executed in simulation. The resulting trajectories are added to a bounded replay buffer and mixed with original demonstrations, adapting the model to controller-visited states while retaining expert data.

    V Experiments

    Unless otherwise noted, models are trained on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 without state normalization, using loss weights λₓ=1, λ_z=0.1, and λᵤ=10⁻² in (29). Desktop experiments use an i9-14900KF and RTX 4090 with JAX dense linear algebra. unless stated otherwise. Reported times are end-to-end MPC latency. We evaluate three claims: (i) KC-QP reduces constrained MPC latency across desktop, edge, and MCU hardware; (ii) DiffQP and DAgger improve finite-horizon control quality; and (iii) the formulation scales to high-dimensional whole-body and visual models and batched collision-constrained multi-agent planning. For constrained MPC, the solver terminates when feasibility and fixed-point residuals meet prescribed tolerances or the maximum iteration count is reached.

    V-ADubins Car

    We first consider a Dubins car [30, Eq. 13.17] with state x=[pₓ,p_y,\sinθ,\cosθ]∈ℝ⁴ and control u=[v,ω]∈ℝ². We learn a 32-dimensional Koopman model using a three-hidden-layer, width-32 GELU encoder, trained for 250 epochs on 55-step rollouts with batch size 8192 using AdamW. Control-constrained Dubins MPC requires 0.054±0.018/0.066±0.019/0.090±0.028 ms on CPU for H=15/30/45, respectively, while GPU latency is 1.426±0.049/1.436±0.053/1.438±0.058 ms, dominated by launch overhead for these small action-space QPs.

    V-A1 Real-Time Multi-Agent Planning

    We deploy the learned model on seven differential-drive robots in a 3.2 m×2.0 m workspace (Fig. 1F). Each robot solves an H=28 KC-QP with the other robots’ predicted trajectories as time-varying collision constraints. We perform five iterative best response (IBR) [7] rounds per control update, with each KC-QP terminating at residual tolerance or after 25 iterations; if the budget is exhausted, IBR proceeds with the current iterate. Using batched NumPy on CPU, the full five-round update takes 18.24±3.96 ms, within the 30 Hz control period. This demonstrates real-time KC-QP solves under changing inter-agent constraints using only CPU-based linear algebra, without GPU acceleration or specialized optimization solvers.

    V-B2D Quadcopter

    We next consider a planar quadcopter [31, Eq. 13] with state x=[pₓ,p_z,θ,vₓ,v_z,ω] and inputs given by collective thrust and torque in a 5 m×5 m workspace. We learn a 128-dimensional Koopman embedding using a three-hidden-layer, width-64 GELU encoder. The model is trained for 250 epochs using 40-step rollouts and a batch size of 8192.

    Table I shows that μMPC achieves 23–40 μs median CPU solve times with control constraints across the tested horizons. For these small condensed KC-QPs, GPU execution is slower because launch and synchronization overhead dominate the solve. With a centered 1 m-radius obstacle and start–goal pairs on opposing sides, we use an empirical model-error margin. Each of two outer updates relinearizes the nonlinear constraints about the previous control-induced trajectory; the inner primal–dual solve terminates when both residuals fall below 10⁻² or after 150 iterations. Median CPU solve time remains below 0.33 ms across all horizons while meeting the prescribed residual tolerance.

    V-C3D Quadcopter

    We consider a 12-state quadcopter [31, Eq. 14] with four control inputs in a 5 m×5 m×5 m workspace. We use a 128-dimensional Koopman embedding with a three-hidden-layer, width-64 GELU encoder, trained for 250 epochs with batch size 4096 and 75-step rollouts.

    We compare against acados/HPIPM [20], Koopman-BoxQP [18], OSQP [19] using both learned Condensed Koopman and analytical dynamics, and GPU-ADMM SQP [4]. Unlike trajectory-space SQP methods that update local dynamics online via relinearization, μMPC reuses a fixed precomputed primal operator across MPC steps and constraint relinearizations. This is enabled by our linear Koopman dynamics and avoids online refactorization.

    Table II shows 58–128 μs median CPU latency with control constraints. At H=100, μMPC is 2.3× faster than acados/HPIPM, 19× faster than OSQP on the identical KC-QP, 64× faster than Koopman-BoxQP, and over 100× faster than GPU-ADMM SQP on CPU. The comparison with OSQP using our condensed dynamics isolates the contribution of our solver, which exploits the fixed primal operator to substantially reduce latency beyond condensation alone.

    For obstacle avoidance, we introduce a spherical obstacle of radius 1.25 m and tighten the collision-avoidance constraints using an empirically determined margin to account for model prediction errors, though this can also be calibrated to achieve probabilistic coverage guarantees [32]. At each MPC step, we linearize the obstacle constraints twice about the latest predicted trajectory, allowing up to 150 primal-dual iterations per KC-QP solve. Median CPU solve times remain below 1.4 ms for horizons up to H=100, while satisfying the prescribed feasibility tolerance for the linearized constraints.

    V-C1 Edge Deployment

    We next deploy the same obstacle-aware controller on a Raspberry Pi 5 and an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano to evaluate embedded execution.

    Table III shows that control-constrained MPC remains below 3.2 ms on every edge configuration through H=100. With obstacle constraints, the Jetson CPU remains below 7.2 ms, while the GPU becomes advantageous at longer horizons as the larger constrained problem better amortizes device overhead.

    V-C2 Differentiable-QP Ablation

    We isolate the contributions of DAgger and differentiable-QP supervision, with numerical results in Table IV.

    To assess how differentiable QP supervision affects the learned control-to-state map Gₓ in (10), we report the condition number κ₂(Q̄_track^1/2Gₓ) and smallest singular value σ_\min(Q̄_track^1/2Gₓ), where Q̄_track is the state-tracking weight matrix in (28). A smaller κ₂ indicates more uniform sensitivity of the predicted state trajectory to perturbations along different control directions, while a larger σ_\min indicates fewer near-degenerate control directions. Both improve the numerical conditioning of recovering control inputs from desired state trajectories. DiffQP raises success from 3.7% to 97.7% at H=75 and retains 85.6% at H=125, while improving conditioning and control-recovery RMSE. Adding DAgger maintains over 95% success through H=125 and reaches the goal in fewer MPC steps at long horizons. Although the combined model has slightly higher control RMSE than DiffQP alone, it has substantially better closed-loop performance, showing that DAgger complements DiffQP by adapting the model to controller-induced states. At batch size 4096, DiffQP incurs only modest additional training overhead, increasing per-epoch time from 21.97 to 26.82 s and peak VRAM from 2082 to 2224 MiB.

    V-C3 Comparison with TinyMPC

    For the unconstrained KC-QP, the optimal control sequence is given by U^⋆=-H⁻¹g(z₀), where H=R̄+G̃^⊤G̃ and G̃=Q̄_y^1/2G_y (16). When G̃ has fewer rows than columns, the Woodbury matrix identity [33] replaces the inversion of the Hnᵤ×Hnᵤ Hessian with that of the smaller matrix I+G̃R̄⁻¹G̃^⊤. Since these matrices are fixed and can be precomputed offline, the optimal control sequence can be recovered exactly using only matrix–vector products online.

    The Woodbury form requires 23–37 μs median latency, comparable to TinyMPC’s median runtime but with substantially lower mean latency and variance. We note that the two methods solve different MPC problems: μMPC solves an unconstrained QP using learned Koopman dynamics that can capture the nonlinear dynamics, whereas TinyMPC enforces actuator bounds and uses dynamics linearized analytically about hover, with a different terminal cost. Thus, Table V compares the computational cost of executing each MPC controller, rather than the efficiency of the two solvers on the same optimization problem.

    V-C4 Crazyflie Deployment

    We deploy μMPC on a Crazyflie Cortex–M4F for the point-to-point task in Fig. 1B using a 128-dimensional Koopman model with H=75 (q=300, 1.875 s horizon). This deployment uses an unconstrained KC-QP, so the optimal action sequence is obtained directly from the fixed quadratic system without primal–dual iterations. For memory efficiency, the MCU stores precompiled float32 quantities and a packed Cholesky factor. The controller requires 601.7 kB of immutable storage and 8.7 kB of runtime workspace; total firmware size is 948.4 kB.

    After hover-thrust calibration, MPC commands normalized thrust and body rates. The MCU averages 20.08 ms over 100 benchmark cases with no 25 ms deadline violations and 24.57 ms during flight. The full radio-mediated experimental loop runs at approximately 15 Hz due to communication, state acquisition, Vicon forwarding, and telemetry.

    V-C5 Scalable Multi-Agent Quadcopter Planning

    We employ Jacobi IBR for multi-agent planning in a 25 m cube; that is, at each IBR iteration, each quadrotor optimizes its trajectory while treating the other agents’ trajectories from the previous iteration as fixed, time-varying collision constraints. This enables all agents’ KC-QPs to be solved simultaneously in a single GPU batch. We reuse the original Koopman model from Sec. V-C without retraining by planning in moving 5m local frames centered on each robot. We use up to 2 IBR sweeps, 1 SQP iteration, and 150 PD iterations per KC-QP, terminating early upon convergence and accepting the current iterate when the budget is exhausted. Goal % denotes agents reaching their assigned goal; Collision % denotes agents experiencing at least one collision.

    Scaling from 50 to 200 quadrotors increases batched MPC/IBR latency from 12.1 to 32.1 ms (2.66× for 4× more agents), while maintaining over 30 Hz operation and above 98% goal reaching. Collision incidence rises to 2.58% at D=200. At large scales, the fixed iteration budget trades full best-response convergence for real-time updates, so residual collision-constraint violations may remain. KC-QP is well suited to IBR because inter-agent constraints change each round while the primal operator remains fixed.

    V-DQuadruped

    V-D1 Control Constrained Planning

    We evaluate whole-body quadruped control using a 4096-dimensional Koopman model of the 61-dimensional robot state, comprising floating-base pose and velocity, joint states, foot positions, and ground-reaction forces, with 12 joint-torque inputs. The three-hidden-layer, width-512 GELU encoder is trained for 100 epochs with batch size 2500 and 55-step rollouts. To avoid out-of-distribution analytical gait references, we distill a PPO locomotion policy into a learned reference generator supplying joint states, foot heights, and vertical ground-reaction forces for KC-QP tracking. Fixed base height and commanded linear and angular velocities are also tracked. We compare against MPX’s primal–dual iLQR [3] and GPU-ADMM SQP [4] using identical reference generation and torque limits. Reported latencies include reference generation for all methods and state encoding for μMPC.

    Table VII shows that at H=100, μMPC is 1.5× faster than MPX and 4.7× faster than GPU-ADMM SQP; the shared reference generator contributes 2.71/5.72/8.53 ms at H=25/65/100. On the Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, μMPC runs in 24–38 ms, versus 28–84 ms for MPX and 173–637 ms for GPU-ADMM SQP. All control-constrained solves terminate within the 150-iteration primal–dual budget at the standard 10⁻² residual tolerance.

    V-D2 Whole-Body Obstacle-Avoidance Filtering

    We filter the same PPO policy, operating within a learned simulator, for state/torque reference and KC-QP obstacle constraints. This harder constrained problem uses up to 750 primal–dual iterations and a relaxed 5×10⁻² residual tolerance to preserve the real-time rate. Across our evaluated rollouts, the filtered controller avoids the obstacle crossed by the nominal policy (Fig. 1A). At H=100, end-to-end latency is 28.18 ms: 7.74 ms reference generation, 0.22 ms encoding, and 20.13 ms KC-QP optimization. Constraint tightenings added for robustness to model mismatch are empirically tuned rather than probabilistically calibrated; formal robust margins remain future work and can be derived following [32] and [34].

    V-ELinear World Models for Visual Planning

    We evaluate all planners on pixel-based bimanual rope manipulation and Reacher [6, Fig. 2c-d] using Koopman-linearized latent world models for planning and control. We evaluate the efficacy of our planner using random workspace start–goal pairs, rather than LeWM [9] and Fast-LeWM’s [10] 25-step same-trajectory goal sampling. Images are encoded by a custom ViT into a 12-dimensional embedding, augmented with first- and second-order differences to form sₜ=[eₜ,Δeₜ,Δ²eₜ]∈ℝ³⁶, and lifted to a 2048-dimensional Koopman model with linear dynamics. For rope manipulation, uₜ=[wₜ,hₜ,rₜ] specifies gripper separation, height, and fore–aft reach and is executed through inverse kinematics. We compile the KC-QP offline, so the 2048-dimensional latent trajectory never appears in the online decision variables; planning optimizes only the action sequence with explicit action bounds enforced as linear inequalities.

    Table VIII shows that μMPC plans in 0.725 ms on bimanual rope manipulation (Fig. 1d) and 0.427 ms on Reacher, while achieving 94% and 62% success, compared with 24%/4% for LeWM and 46%/8% for Fast-LeWM. All evaluated KC-QPs reach the prescribed primal–dual residual tolerances within the real-time iteration budget and respect the imposed action bounds. On the Jetson GPU, the same planners run in approximately 33.060±1.107 ms on both tasks, sustaining about 30 Hz even on edge hardware. These results demonstrate that scaling learned visual representations to 2048 dimensions preserves fast online trajectory optimization via Koopman linearization without requiring repeated expensive nonlinear latent rollouts or sampling-based trajectory search.

    V-E1 Hardware Cube Manipulation

    We validate the same formulation on real cube manipulation with a Kuka iiwa arm, where μMPC commands Cartesian end-effector targets uₜ=[xₜ,yₜ,zₜ] through inverse kinematics to match a goal image taking 0.483±0.130 ms per solve. As shown in Fig. 4, differentiable-QP supervision recovers the vertical control authority required to reach the elevated target, whereas prediction-only training remains below the goal height despite approaching the correct planar configuration.

    VI CONCLUSION

    We presented μMPC, a framework that combines scalable Koopman dynamics learning with fast constrained MPC. By compiling finite-horizon predictions into action-only KC-QPs with a reusable primal operator, μMPC reduces online primal-dual optimization to matrix-vector products and projections, invariant under changing goals and constraints. Lightweight differentiable control-recovery QPs enable fast, batched supervision and scalable DAgger-style data aggregation, directly training dynamics for finite-horizon control. Across experiments, μMPC achieves millisecond-scale whole-body control with 4096-dimensional Koopman models, submillisecond planning with 2048-dimensional linear world models, long horizon MPC onboard Crazyflie MCU, and real-time planning for 200 quadrotors.

    Future work should focus on principled model selection and improved constraint handling. Our reported encoder capacities, lifted dimensions, and training horizons were selected through empirical tuning and retraining, motivating scaling laws relating these choices to prediction and closed-loop performance. In very demanding cases, fixed-budget solves may retain residual constraint violations, incorporating constraints into training could improve constraint response with fewer primal-dual iterations. Current model-error margins also remain empirical rather than formally calibrated.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把有限时域的控制-输出映射预先算好，就能消除抬升状态的轨迹。

要点：

  • 目标：让模型预测控制（MPC）变快，μMPC 用**学到的 Koopman 线性化动力学**来削减在线计算
  • 关键手段：**预先计算有限时域的控制-输出映射**，从而**消除抬升状态（lifted-state）的轨迹**，得到一个只有 `H·n_u` 个决策变量的「动作空间 Koopman 编译 QP」，**维度与抬升维无关**
  • 再配一个固定的、预先算好的原始算子，使原始-对偶迭代只需矩阵-向量乘与投影，**改变目标与约束时不必重新分解**

为什么值得看：「预编译 + 只解动作空间」这个套路在引擎里很熟（着色器预编译、约束预解）。把它用在世界模型控制上，意味着控制器可以在微秒级跑——这是 AI 决策能否进实时循环的分水岭。

中文摘要：μMPC 是一个快速的模型预测控制（MPC）框架，它利用学习得到的 Koopman 线性化动力学来降低在线计算量。其核心是预先计算有限时域内的「控制—输出」映射，从而消除抬升状态（lifted-state）在在线阶段产生的轨迹，最终得到一个只包含动作维决策变量的 Koopman 编译二次规划（KC-QP），其规模与抬升维无关；同时配合一个固定且预先计算好的原始算子，使原始—对偶迭代只需要矩阵—向量乘法和投影运算，更换目标与约束时也无需重新分解。对需要把 AI 决策放进实时循环的系统，这条把「微秒级控制」变成了可能的工程目标。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-26

本期推送：2026-11-28

μMPC: Microsecond-Scale Nonlinear and World Model Control
from Edge to GPU via Koopman-Linearized Precompilation

Abstract

We present μMPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, μMPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with Hnᵤ decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. μMPC achieves solve times as low as 23μs on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, μMPC achieves up to 108× faster constrained MPC and 1907× faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.

Project WebsiteCodeVideo

I Introduction

Optimal control of complex robotic systems requires expressive dynamics models and real-time solvers for deployment, which is particularly difficult for resource-constrained and high-dimensional systems. Embedded aerial robots face strict compute, memory, and power budgets [1, 2]; whole-body legged control requires high-dimensional real-time optimization [3, 4]; visuomotor planning relies on learned world models with thousands of latent states [5, 6]; and multi-agent systems require many concurrent optimizations [7, 8]. Controllers must also plan over long horizons, react rapidly to observations, and satisfy complex constraints. Nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) addresses these requirements, but its computational cost grows with problem dimension, horizon length, and constraint complexity. Despite advances in sparsity exploitation, factorization caching, and GPU parallelism [4, 3], real-time deployment remains challenging.

This computational challenge is particularly pronounced for learned dynamics and world models. While these models can capture complex dynamics from high-dimensional observations, planning often requires repeated computationally-expensive evaluations of candidate action sequences through the learned dynamics [5, 9, 10]. One approach to reducing this cost is via Koopman linearization, which learns dynamics that are linear in a lifted space, yielding an affine dependence of finite-horizon predictions on the control sequence [11] that simplifies both prediction and trajectory optimization. However, nonlinear constraints can still require iterative linearization and expensive matrix refactorizations, limiting the computational benefits. This motivates an MPC framework that moves expensive computations offline while allowing goals and constraints to be updated efficiently online.

Another challenge is learning dynamics models that are suitable for control rather than prediction alone. Conventional Koopman dynamics learning emphasizes state-prediction accuracy [12], but low prediction error may not translate to high control performance. Moreover, training on fixed demonstrations neglects controller-induced distribution shifts, potentially degrading prediction accuracy at inference time. Differentiable MPC offers a way to address these limitations [13] by incorporating the learned Koopman dynamics into the MPC optimization during training, enabling direct supervision of control performance and generating training data arising from controller-induced state distributions. However, repeatedly solving and differentiating through MPC problems can be prohibitively expensive during training.

To address these challenges, we present μMPC, an MPC framework for nonlinear systems that exploits learned Koopman-linearized dynamics to formulate Koopman-Compiled Quadratic Programs (KC-QPs) that can be solved in microseconds. We develop a tailored primal-dual solver that precomputes a fixed primal operator offline, reducing online constrained optimization to efficient matrix-vector products and projections. This operator can be reused across changing constraints, goals, and MPC steps, substantially reducing online computation. The efficiency of KC-QPs also enables scalable control-aware learning: we solve batches of KC-QPs in parallel, evaluate the resulting control performance under the original nonlinear dynamics, and differentiate through the optimization to train Koopman representations directly for control performance rather than prediction accuracy alone. Furthermore, fast batched KC-QP solves enable DAgger-style on-policy data aggregation, improving coverage of controller-induced state distributions and mitigating inference-time distribution shift. Together, this scalable learning of high-dimensional Koopman representations tailored to closed-loop control enables microsecond-scale online MPC. Our contributions are:

  • •

    μMPC exploits the linear structure of learned Koopman dynamics to eliminate state variables and formulate MPC as an action-only QP (KC-QP). We precompute a fixed primal operator offline, enabling fast, “precompiled” primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, even as goals and constraints change, without requiring online matrix refactorization.

  • •

    We exploit the compact, parallelizable structure of KC-QPs to train the Koopman dynamics to produce MPC control sequences that match expert demonstration data, by differentiating through the optimization. Batched KC-QP solves also enable fast DAgger-style data aggregation, reducing controller-induced distribution shift.

  • •

    We demonstrate μMPC across embedded, high-dimensional, multi-agent, and visual control. Our solver achieves MPC runtimes as low as 23 μs on Dubins car and quadrotor systems, solves H=75 MPC onboard a resource-limited Crazyflie microcontroller in 24 ms, and performs 4096-dimensional quadruped control in under 5 ms. We further demonstrate real-time collision-aware multi-agent planning for 200 quadrotors, with hardware validation on a system of seven differential-drive robots. For visual control, we train 2048D linear world models enabling sub-millisecond planning, outperforming evaluated baselines on navigation and bimanual rope manipulation, with hardware cube-manipulation validation.

    • II Related Work

    Koopman MPC and fast optimal control. Koopman methods lift nonlinear dynamics into approximately linear coordinates for linear MPC [11, 14], with recent extensions to robotic systems [15, 16]. Existing formulations retain important online computational overhead:  [11] employ a prescribed lifting basis, which may not adequately represent nonlinear costs and constraints in a form amenable to efficient quadratic programming;  [17] condense Koopman MPC but specialize to input constraints; and  [18] eliminates high-dimensional observables but keeps physical states and controls as decision variables under box structure. More broadly, fast MPC exploits sparsity, condensing, cached factorizations, and specialized solvers [19, 20, 1], while recent GPU methods parallelize dynamics and optimization [3, 4, 2]. In contrast, μMPC compiles Koopman dynamics into an action-only KC-QP. For fixed horizon, quadratic weights, and primal regularization, its precomputed primal operator remains reusable across changing goals and constraints, reducing online constrained optimization to matrix–vector products and projections without refactorization.

    Differentiable control learning. Differentiable optimization and MPC support end-to-end learning through constrained control [13, 21, 22, 23]. KCPO [24] combines deep Koopman dynamics with differentiable MPC under hard box control constraints. We instead differentiate an efficient control-recovery KC-QP that directly supervises the finite-horizon control response, then pair it with DAgger-style on-policy aggregation. This efficiently targets control relevant model error and controller-induced distribution shift without differentiating through a full expensive nonlinear MPC solve.

    World models and latent planning. World models plan through learned latent dynamics [25, 26, 27, 5, 9]. DINO-WM and LeWorldModel optimize action sequences through repeated latent prediction; Fast-LeWM parallelizes prediction but retains CEM search [10]; learned planners instead amortize refinement from imagined rollouts [28]. Historically, these world model dynamics have been represented with high-dimensional nonlinear functions that are expensive to evaluate. μMPC instead learns linear world model dynamics, enabling compiliation of the full-horizon response into a compact KC-QP for sub-millisecond planning, avoiding repeated latent rollouts at planning time while permitting explicit linearized state/task constraints and action bounds.

    III Problem Statement

    We consider a discrete-time nonlinear system

    xₖ₊₁=f(xₖ,uₖ), xₖ∈ℝ^nₓ, uₖ∈ℝ^nᵤ.

    		(1)

    At each control step, we seek a horizon-H input sequence U=[u₀^⊤ ⋯ u_H-1^⊤]^⊤ that drives a task-relevant output yₖ toward a goal y^\rmgoal while satisfying state, task, and input constraints. Locally linearizing the nonlinear constraints about the current nominal trajectory gives

    \undersetx_1:H, u_0:H-1minimize∑ₖ₌₁^H-1∥yₖ-y^\rmgoal∥_Q_y,k²+∑ₖ₌₀^H-1∥uₖ∥_Rₖ²+∥y_H-y^\rmgoal∥_Q_f²(2)
    subject toxₖ₊₁=f(xₖ,uₖ),\hskip9.24994ptk=0,…,H-1,
    D_y,kyₖ₊₁+D_u,kuₖ+Δₖ≤bₖ,\hskip9.24994ptk=0,…,H-1,
    D_fy_H+Δ_f≤b_f.

    Here yₖ=S_yxₖ selects task-relevant coordinates, with S_y=I recovering the full state. We linearize nonlinear state and task constraints about the nominal trajectory, incorporating the constant terms from their first-order Taylor expansions into bₖ and b_f. Nonnegative margins Δₖ and Δ_f then tighten these bounds to account for neglected higher-order terms and prediction errors from the learned dynamics (Sec. IV-C). Since (2) remains nonlinear through f, our goal is to solve (2) by seeking an approximately linear lifted predictive model that moves expensive algebraic operations needed for optimization offline, leaving only fixed linear algebra and projections online.

    IV Method

    Our method proceeds in four stages. First, we learn a nonlinear lifting with control affine linear latent dynamics. Second, we compile its finite-horizon response into precomputed maps and eliminate the latent trajectory from the optimization variables. Third, we solve the resulting action-only KC-QP with a primal–dual method whose primal update operator is fixed for a given model, horizon, objective, and primal regularization, and can therefore be precomputed offline and reused as constraints are relinearized online. Finally, we train the representation with differentiable QP for direct control supervision, and DAgger aggregation to improve its finite-horizon control behavior on the distribution induced by its own controller.

    IV-ALearned Dynamics

    In Koopman models [12], the physical state xₖ is encoded as

    zₖ=enc_θ(xₖ), zₖ∈ℝ^n_z,

    		(3)

    with latent state zₖ, learned globally linear latent dynamics

    zₖ₊₁=Azₖ+Buₖ, A∈ℝ^n_z×n_z, B∈ℝ^n_z×nᵤ,

    		(4)

    and affine decoder

    xₖ=Czₖ+c, C∈ℝ^nₓ×n_z, c∈ℝ^nₓ.

    		(5)

    At each MPC step only the measured physical state is encoded, z₀=enc_θ(x₀); all subsequent predictions follow from the linear latent rollout and decoding into the physical state space in (4). Hereafter, xₖ and yₖ denote states and outputs predicted by the learned Koopman dynamics, unless otherwise specified. We explicitly distinguish measured or demonstrated states from model predictions when both appear.

    IV-BPrecomputed Maps

    To accelerate online computation, all horizon operators that depend only on A, B, C, and H are constructed offline.

    IV-B1 Condensed latent and physical prediction

    Define

    U=\beginbmatrixu₀^⊤⋯u_H-1^⊤\endbmatrix^⊤ ∈ℝ^Hnᵤ, Z=\beginbmatrixz₁^⊤⋯z_H^⊤\endbmatrix^⊤ ∈ℝ^Hn_z.

    		(6)

    Repeatedly applying (4) over a prediction horizon of H yields

    Z=Φz₀+ΓU,

    		(7)

    where

    Φ=\beginbmatrixA A² ⋮ A^H\endbmatrix,\hskip18.49988ptΓ=\beginbmatrixB&0&⋯&0 AB&B&⋯&0 ⋮&⋮&⋱&⋮ A^H-1B&A^H-2B&⋯&B\endbmatrix.

    		(8)

    Thus, the latent trajectory is affine in only (z₀,U). Stacking X=[x₁^⊤ ⋯ x_H^⊤]^⊤ and applying (5) yields

    X=aₓ(z₀)+GₓU

    		(9)

    with,

    aₓ(z₀)=(I_H ⊗C)Φz₀+1_H ⊗c, Gₓ=(I_H ⊗C)Γ.(10)

    Here, ⊗ denotes the Kronecker product, I_H is the H×H identity matrix, and 1_H∈ℝ^H is the vector of ones. Note that neither Z nor X must appear as optimization variables since they are defined implicitly through U in (7) and (9). In implementation, we avoid constructing the full latent prediction matrices Φ and Γ. Instead, we directly assemble the physical-state prediction maps from the blocks CAᵏ and CAᵏB, for k=0,…,H, reducing the need to store intermediate high-dimensional latent trajectories.

    IV-B2 Finite horizon output maps

    Let S_y∈ℝ^n_y×nₓ select the physical-state coordinates relevant to the control objective or constraints, so that yₖ=S_yxₖ. Define

    C_y=S_yC, c_y=S_yc, yₖ=C_yzₖ+c_y.

    		(11)

    For Y=[y₁^⊤ ⋯ y_H^⊤]^⊤

    Y=a_y(z₀)+G_yU

    		(12)

    with,

    a_y(z₀)=F_yz₀+1_H ⊗c_y, F_y=(I_H ⊗C_y)Φ,(13)
    G_y=(I_H ⊗C_y)Γ.

    For each choice of task-relevant outputs yₖ=S_yxₖ, we precompute F_y and G_y offline using the learned dynamics, so that online predictions depend only on the initial latent state z₀ and control sequence U.

    IV-CKoopman Compiled Quadratic Program (KC-QP)

    IV-C1 Linear surrogate OCP

    We replace the nonlinear rollout in (2) by the learned linear dynamics while retaining the locally linearized constraints:

    \undersetz_1:H,u_0:H-1minimize∑ₖ₌₁^H-1∥yₖ-yᵍᵒᵃˡ∥_Q_y,k²+∑ₖ₌₀^H-1∥uₖ∥_Rₖ²+∥y_H-yᵍᵒᵃˡ∥_Q_f²(14)
    subject tozₖ₊₁=Azₖ+Buₖ,\hskip9.24994ptk=0,…,H-1,
    D_y,kyₖ₊₁+D_u,kuₖ+Δₖ≤bₖ,\hskip9.24994ptk=0,…,H-1,
    D_fy_H+Δ_f≤b_f.

    The nonnegative margins Δₖ,Δ_f tighten linearized constraints for approximation error, combining linearization and model mismatch terms. Since (14) is a QP, substituting the precomputed maps (12) eliminates z_1:H from the decision variables.

    IV-C2 Condensed objective and constraints

    Let q=Hnᵤ, Y^\rmgoal=1_H⊗y^\rmgoal, Q̄_y=blkdiag(Q_y,1,…,Q_y,H-1,Q_f), and R̄=blkdiag(R₀,…,R_H-1). Substituting in the finite-horizon prediction map (12) into the objective of (14) yields a quadratic function of only the control sequence U:

    J(U)=1/2∥a_y(z₀)+G_yU-Y^\rmgoal∥_Q̄_y²+1/2∥U∥_R̄²
    =1/2U^⊤HU+g^⊤U+c,(15)

    with

    H=G_y^⊤Q̄_yG_y+R̄, g=G_y^⊤Q̄_y(a_y(z₀)-Y^\rmgoal),(16)
    c=1/2(a_y(z₀)-Y^\rmgoal)^⊤Q̄_y(a_y(z₀)-Y^\rmgoal).

    Since c(z₀) is independent of the decision variables U, it is dropped. For a fixed model, horizon, and cost weights, changing the goal modifies only the linear term g (and the discarded constant term), while the Hessian H and its factorization remain unchanged. Stacking stage, terminal, and input inequalities gives D̄_yY+D̄ᵤU≤b̄-Δ̄. Using (12),

    (D̄_yG_y+D̄ᵤ)U≤b̄-Δ̄-D̄_ya_y(z₀),(17)

    which we can rewrite as MU≤r(z₀) as shorthand, where M=D̄_yG_y+D̄ᵤ and r(z₀)=b̄-Δ̄-D̄_ya_y(z₀). Putting the condensed cost (15) and constraints (17) together, the complete online QP is therefore

    \undersetU∈ℝ^qminimize1/2U^⊤HU+g(z₀)^⊤U(18)
    subject toMU≤r(z₀).

    Crucially, only U is optimized; the latent and physical trajectories Z and X have been analytically eliminated.

    IV-C3 Fixed Operator primal–dual solve

    We efficiently solve (18) using a tailored primal-dual solver. Primal-dual methods [29] seek a saddle point of the Lagrangian, alternating between descent over the primal decision variables and ascent over the dual variables associated with the constraints. Introducing Lagrange multipliers λ≥0 for the inequality constraints in (18), we define the Lagrangian

    L(U,λ)=\tfrac12U^⊤HU+g(z₀)^⊤U+λ^⊤(MU-r(z₀)).

    		(19)

    At iteration j, we first perform projected gradient ascent on L with respect to λ, with step size σ>0:

    λʲ⁺¹=[λʲ+σ(MUʲ-r(z₀))]₊.

    		(20)

    This increases the multipliers associated with violated constraints, increasing the penalty for their violation in the subsequent primal update, while the elementwise projection [·]₊ maintains nonnegativity of the multipliers. We then minimize L(U,λʲ⁺¹) with respect to U, adding a proximal regularization term with ρ>0 to stabilize the update by penalizing deviations from the previous iterate:

    Uʲ⁺¹=\undersetUargmin\tfrac12U^⊤HU+g(z₀)^⊤U+(λʲ⁺¹)^⊤MU(21)
    +\tfracρ2∥U-Uʲ∥₂²,

    where we omit terms independent of U. Since (24) is an unconstrained, strongly convex quadratic minimization, its unique solution satisfies the stationarity condition

    (H+ρI_q)Uʲ⁺¹=ρUʲ-g(z₀)-M^⊤λʲ⁺¹.

    		(22)

    Defining the Hessian of the proximal primal objective as

    K=H+ρI_q,

    		(23)

    we obtain the closed-form primal update

    Uʲ⁺¹=K⁻¹ [ρUʲ-g(z₀)-M^⊤λʲ⁺¹].

    		(24)

    Crucially, K depends only on the learned dynamics, horizon, objective weights, and ρ, and is independent of the constraint matrix M and bounds r(z₀). We therefore compute and store K⁻¹ offline, reducing the online primal and dual updates to matrix–vector products and elementwise projections. Although SQP relinearization may change M and r(z₀), these changes enter the updates through matrix–vector products and vector additions, without requiring online matrix inversion or factorization. For each linearized KC-QP, we set σ=0.99 ρ/∥M∥_F², satisfying the step-size condition σ∥M∥₂²/ρ<1. To assess convergence, we monitor both primal feasibility and changes in the primal and dual iterates using the residuals

    r_feasʲ⁺¹=∥(MUʲ⁺¹-r(z₀))₊∥₂,(25)
    r_fpʲ⁺¹=(ρ²∥Uʲ⁺¹-Uʲ∥₂²+σ⁻²∥λʲ⁺¹-λʲ∥₂²)^1/2.

    The former measures constraint violation, while the latter measures convergence to a fixed point of the primal-dual updates. For each linearized KC-QP, we terminate the solver when both residuals fall below prescribed tolerances or when a fixed real-time iteration budget is exhausted. In the latter case, we return the current iterate, which may be suboptimal or violate constraints.

    IV-DScalability

    The KC-QP decision dimension is q=Hnᵤ, independent of the lifted dimension n_z, compared to Hn_z+Hnᵤ variables in a non-condensed formulation. The fixed primal operator is precomputed offline in O(q³) time with O(q²) storage. Our implementations precompute the dense inverse K⁻¹, so each primal update is a dense matrix-vector product; on memory-constrained hardware, the fixed operator can instead be stored through a factorization. For m inequalities, each primal-dual iteration requires only O(q²+mq) work. With N_PD inner iterations and N_SQP constraint-linearization iterations, the online optimization complexity is

    O (N_SQPN_PD(q²+mq)),

    		(26)

    excluding constraint linearization and model evaluation. These matrix-vector products and projections are GPU-parallelizable, particularly when solving large batches of KC-QPs. However, CPUs often achieve lower latency for small problems due to GPU launch and synchronization overhead.

    The lifted dimension enters online through encoding and affine prediction terms which still scale with n_z. Thus, increasing representation capacity does not enlarge the KC-QP decision vector or its primal operator, although encoding and prediction-map evaluation retain a dependence on n_z.

    IV-ETraining via Differentiable QP (DiffQP) and DAgger

    We train on demonstrations (x₀,U,X), with U=[u₀^⊤ ⋯ u_H-1^⊤]^⊤ and X=[x₁^⊤ ⋯ x_H^⊤]^⊤. Rolling out the learned dynamics under U yields ẑ_1:H and x̂_1:H, while demonstrated states are encoded as z_1:H=enc_θ(X). We initialize A=I and B with Xavier initialization to avoid initially amplifying latent dynamics or control couplings. We use the multi-step losses

    Lₓ=1/H∑ₖ₌₁^H∥x̂ₖ-xₖ∥₂², L_z=1/H∑ₖ₌₁^H∥ẑₖ-zₖ∥₂².(27)

    To supervise finite-horizon control response, we solve

    Û=\undersetVargmin 1/2∥aₓ(z₀)+GₓV-X∥_Q̄_track²+1/2∥V∥_R̄_track²,

    		(28)

    and optimize

    Lᵤ=∥Û-U∥₂², L=λₓLₓ+λ_zL_z+λᵤLᵤ.

    		(29)

    Here, Q̄_track\succeq0 weights deviations from the demonstrated state trajectory, while R̄_track\succ0 regularizes the control sequence. Positive control regularization makes (28) strongly convex with a unique solution. By differentiating through the optimal control sequence Û, we train the encoder and dynamics parameters (A,B,C,c) so that optimizing the learned model recovers the demonstrated control inputs. Crucially, the objective is goal and constraint independent, training the dynamics to recover the demonstrated controls required to reproduce X.

    To mitigate controller-induced distribution shift, we use DAgger-style aggregation. At each epoch, the finite-horizon tracking QP used for control-recovery supervision generates control sequences that are executed in simulation. The resulting trajectories are added to a bounded replay buffer and mixed with original demonstrations, adapting the model to controller-visited states while retaining expert data.

    V Experiments

    Unless otherwise noted, models are trained on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 without state normalization, using loss weights λₓ=1, λ_z=0.1, and λᵤ=10⁻² in (29). Desktop experiments use an i9-14900KF and RTX 4090 with JAX dense linear algebra. unless stated otherwise. Reported times are end-to-end MPC latency. We evaluate three claims: (i) KC-QP reduces constrained MPC latency across desktop, edge, and MCU hardware; (ii) DiffQP and DAgger improve finite-horizon control quality; and (iii) the formulation scales to high-dimensional whole-body and visual models and batched collision-constrained multi-agent planning. For constrained MPC, the solver terminates when feasibility and fixed-point residuals meet prescribed tolerances or the maximum iteration count is reached.

    V-ADubins Car

    We first consider a Dubins car [30, Eq. 13.17] with state x=[pₓ,p_y,\sinθ,\cosθ]∈ℝ⁴ and control u=[v,ω]∈ℝ². We learn a 32-dimensional Koopman model using a three-hidden-layer, width-32 GELU encoder, trained for 250 epochs on 55-step rollouts with batch size 8192 using AdamW. Control-constrained Dubins MPC requires 0.054±0.018/0.066±0.019/0.090±0.028 ms on CPU for H=15/30/45, respectively, while GPU latency is 1.426±0.049/1.436±0.053/1.438±0.058 ms, dominated by launch overhead for these small action-space QPs.

    V-A1 Real-Time Multi-Agent Planning

    We deploy the learned model on seven differential-drive robots in a 3.2 m×2.0 m workspace (Fig. 1F). Each robot solves an H=28 KC-QP with the other robots’ predicted trajectories as time-varying collision constraints. We perform five iterative best response (IBR) [7] rounds per control update, with each KC-QP terminating at residual tolerance or after 25 iterations; if the budget is exhausted, IBR proceeds with the current iterate. Using batched NumPy on CPU, the full five-round update takes 18.24±3.96 ms, within the 30 Hz control period. This demonstrates real-time KC-QP solves under changing inter-agent constraints using only CPU-based linear algebra, without GPU acceleration or specialized optimization solvers.

    V-B2D Quadcopter

    We next consider a planar quadcopter [31, Eq. 13] with state x=[pₓ,p_z,θ,vₓ,v_z,ω] and inputs given by collective thrust and torque in a 5 m×5 m workspace. We learn a 128-dimensional Koopman embedding using a three-hidden-layer, width-64 GELU encoder. The model is trained for 250 epochs using 40-step rollouts and a batch size of 8192.

    Table I shows that μMPC achieves 23–40 μs median CPU solve times with control constraints across the tested horizons. For these small condensed KC-QPs, GPU execution is slower because launch and synchronization overhead dominate the solve. With a centered 1 m-radius obstacle and start–goal pairs on opposing sides, we use an empirical model-error margin. Each of two outer updates relinearizes the nonlinear constraints about the previous control-induced trajectory; the inner primal–dual solve terminates when both residuals fall below 10⁻² or after 150 iterations. Median CPU solve time remains below 0.33 ms across all horizons while meeting the prescribed residual tolerance.

    V-C3D Quadcopter

    We consider a 12-state quadcopter [31, Eq. 14] with four control inputs in a 5 m×5 m×5 m workspace. We use a 128-dimensional Koopman embedding with a three-hidden-layer, width-64 GELU encoder, trained for 250 epochs with batch size 4096 and 75-step rollouts.

    We compare against acados/HPIPM [20], Koopman-BoxQP [18], OSQP [19] using both learned Condensed Koopman and analytical dynamics, and GPU-ADMM SQP [4]. Unlike trajectory-space SQP methods that update local dynamics online via relinearization, μMPC reuses a fixed precomputed primal operator across MPC steps and constraint relinearizations. This is enabled by our linear Koopman dynamics and avoids online refactorization.

    Table II shows 58–128 μs median CPU latency with control constraints. At H=100, μMPC is 2.3× faster than acados/HPIPM, 19× faster than OSQP on the identical KC-QP, 64× faster than Koopman-BoxQP, and over 100× faster than GPU-ADMM SQP on CPU. The comparison with OSQP using our condensed dynamics isolates the contribution of our solver, which exploits the fixed primal operator to substantially reduce latency beyond condensation alone.

    For obstacle avoidance, we introduce a spherical obstacle of radius 1.25 m and tighten the collision-avoidance constraints using an empirically determined margin to account for model prediction errors, though this can also be calibrated to achieve probabilistic coverage guarantees [32]. At each MPC step, we linearize the obstacle constraints twice about the latest predicted trajectory, allowing up to 150 primal-dual iterations per KC-QP solve. Median CPU solve times remain below 1.4 ms for horizons up to H=100, while satisfying the prescribed feasibility tolerance for the linearized constraints.

    V-C1 Edge Deployment

    We next deploy the same obstacle-aware controller on a Raspberry Pi 5 and an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano to evaluate embedded execution.

    Table III shows that control-constrained MPC remains below 3.2 ms on every edge configuration through H=100. With obstacle constraints, the Jetson CPU remains below 7.2 ms, while the GPU becomes advantageous at longer horizons as the larger constrained problem better amortizes device overhead.

    V-C2 Differentiable-QP Ablation

    We isolate the contributions of DAgger and differentiable-QP supervision, with numerical results in Table IV.

    To assess how differentiable QP supervision affects the learned control-to-state map Gₓ in (10), we report the condition number κ₂(Q̄_track^1/2Gₓ) and smallest singular value σ_\min(Q̄_track^1/2Gₓ), where Q̄_track is the state-tracking weight matrix in (28). A smaller κ₂ indicates more uniform sensitivity of the predicted state trajectory to perturbations along different control directions, while a larger σ_\min indicates fewer near-degenerate control directions. Both improve the numerical conditioning of recovering control inputs from desired state trajectories. DiffQP raises success from 3.7% to 97.7% at H=75 and retains 85.6% at H=125, while improving conditioning and control-recovery RMSE. Adding DAgger maintains over 95% success through H=125 and reaches the goal in fewer MPC steps at long horizons. Although the combined model has slightly higher control RMSE than DiffQP alone, it has substantially better closed-loop performance, showing that DAgger complements DiffQP by adapting the model to controller-induced states. At batch size 4096, DiffQP incurs only modest additional training overhead, increasing per-epoch time from 21.97 to 26.82 s and peak VRAM from 2082 to 2224 MiB.

    V-C3 Comparison with TinyMPC

    For the unconstrained KC-QP, the optimal control sequence is given by U^⋆=-H⁻¹g(z₀), where H=R̄+G̃^⊤G̃ and G̃=Q̄_y^1/2G_y (16). When G̃ has fewer rows than columns, the Woodbury matrix identity [33] replaces the inversion of the Hnᵤ×Hnᵤ Hessian with that of the smaller matrix I+G̃R̄⁻¹G̃^⊤. Since these matrices are fixed and can be precomputed offline, the optimal control sequence can be recovered exactly using only matrix–vector products online.

    The Woodbury form requires 23–37 μs median latency, comparable to TinyMPC’s median runtime but with substantially lower mean latency and variance. We note that the two methods solve different MPC problems: μMPC solves an unconstrained QP using learned Koopman dynamics that can capture the nonlinear dynamics, whereas TinyMPC enforces actuator bounds and uses dynamics linearized analytically about hover, with a different terminal cost. Thus, Table V compares the computational cost of executing each MPC controller, rather than the efficiency of the two solvers on the same optimization problem.

    V-C4 Crazyflie Deployment

    We deploy μMPC on a Crazyflie Cortex–M4F for the point-to-point task in Fig. 1B using a 128-dimensional Koopman model with H=75 (q=300, 1.875 s horizon). This deployment uses an unconstrained KC-QP, so the optimal action sequence is obtained directly from the fixed quadratic system without primal–dual iterations. For memory efficiency, the MCU stores precompiled float32 quantities and a packed Cholesky factor. The controller requires 601.7 kB of immutable storage and 8.7 kB of runtime workspace; total firmware size is 948.4 kB.

    After hover-thrust calibration, MPC commands normalized thrust and body rates. The MCU averages 20.08 ms over 100 benchmark cases with no 25 ms deadline violations and 24.57 ms during flight. The full radio-mediated experimental loop runs at approximately 15 Hz due to communication, state acquisition, Vicon forwarding, and telemetry.

    V-C5 Scalable Multi-Agent Quadcopter Planning

    We employ Jacobi IBR for multi-agent planning in a 25 m cube; that is, at each IBR iteration, each quadrotor optimizes its trajectory while treating the other agents’ trajectories from the previous iteration as fixed, time-varying collision constraints. This enables all agents’ KC-QPs to be solved simultaneously in a single GPU batch. We reuse the original Koopman model from Sec. V-C without retraining by planning in moving 5m local frames centered on each robot. We use up to 2 IBR sweeps, 1 SQP iteration, and 150 PD iterations per KC-QP, terminating early upon convergence and accepting the current iterate when the budget is exhausted. Goal % denotes agents reaching their assigned goal; Collision % denotes agents experiencing at least one collision.

    Scaling from 50 to 200 quadrotors increases batched MPC/IBR latency from 12.1 to 32.1 ms (2.66× for 4× more agents), while maintaining over 30 Hz operation and above 98% goal reaching. Collision incidence rises to 2.58% at D=200. At large scales, the fixed iteration budget trades full best-response convergence for real-time updates, so residual collision-constraint violations may remain. KC-QP is well suited to IBR because inter-agent constraints change each round while the primal operator remains fixed.

    V-DQuadruped

    V-D1 Control Constrained Planning

    We evaluate whole-body quadruped control using a 4096-dimensional Koopman model of the 61-dimensional robot state, comprising floating-base pose and velocity, joint states, foot positions, and ground-reaction forces, with 12 joint-torque inputs. The three-hidden-layer, width-512 GELU encoder is trained for 100 epochs with batch size 2500 and 55-step rollouts. To avoid out-of-distribution analytical gait references, we distill a PPO locomotion policy into a learned reference generator supplying joint states, foot heights, and vertical ground-reaction forces for KC-QP tracking. Fixed base height and commanded linear and angular velocities are also tracked. We compare against MPX’s primal–dual iLQR [3] and GPU-ADMM SQP [4] using identical reference generation and torque limits. Reported latencies include reference generation for all methods and state encoding for μMPC.

    Table VII shows that at H=100, μMPC is 1.5× faster than MPX and 4.7× faster than GPU-ADMM SQP; the shared reference generator contributes 2.71/5.72/8.53 ms at H=25/65/100. On the Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, μMPC runs in 24–38 ms, versus 28–84 ms for MPX and 173–637 ms for GPU-ADMM SQP. All control-constrained solves terminate within the 150-iteration primal–dual budget at the standard 10⁻² residual tolerance.

    V-D2 Whole-Body Obstacle-Avoidance Filtering

    We filter the same PPO policy, operating within a learned simulator, for state/torque reference and KC-QP obstacle constraints. This harder constrained problem uses up to 750 primal–dual iterations and a relaxed 5×10⁻² residual tolerance to preserve the real-time rate. Across our evaluated rollouts, the filtered controller avoids the obstacle crossed by the nominal policy (Fig. 1A). At H=100, end-to-end latency is 28.18 ms: 7.74 ms reference generation, 0.22 ms encoding, and 20.13 ms KC-QP optimization. Constraint tightenings added for robustness to model mismatch are empirically tuned rather than probabilistically calibrated; formal robust margins remain future work and can be derived following [32] and [34].

    V-ELinear World Models for Visual Planning

    We evaluate all planners on pixel-based bimanual rope manipulation and Reacher [6, Fig. 2c-d] using Koopman-linearized latent world models for planning and control. We evaluate the efficacy of our planner using random workspace start–goal pairs, rather than LeWM [9] and Fast-LeWM’s [10] 25-step same-trajectory goal sampling. Images are encoded by a custom ViT into a 12-dimensional embedding, augmented with first- and second-order differences to form sₜ=[eₜ,Δeₜ,Δ²eₜ]∈ℝ³⁶, and lifted to a 2048-dimensional Koopman model with linear dynamics. For rope manipulation, uₜ=[wₜ,hₜ,rₜ] specifies gripper separation, height, and fore–aft reach and is executed through inverse kinematics. We compile the KC-QP offline, so the 2048-dimensional latent trajectory never appears in the online decision variables; planning optimizes only the action sequence with explicit action bounds enforced as linear inequalities.

    Table VIII shows that μMPC plans in 0.725 ms on bimanual rope manipulation (Fig. 1d) and 0.427 ms on Reacher, while achieving 94% and 62% success, compared with 24%/4% for LeWM and 46%/8% for Fast-LeWM. All evaluated KC-QPs reach the prescribed primal–dual residual tolerances within the real-time iteration budget and respect the imposed action bounds. On the Jetson GPU, the same planners run in approximately 33.060±1.107 ms on both tasks, sustaining about 30 Hz even on edge hardware. These results demonstrate that scaling learned visual representations to 2048 dimensions preserves fast online trajectory optimization via Koopman linearization without requiring repeated expensive nonlinear latent rollouts or sampling-based trajectory search.

    V-E1 Hardware Cube Manipulation

    We validate the same formulation on real cube manipulation with a Kuka iiwa arm, where μMPC commands Cartesian end-effector targets uₜ=[xₜ,yₜ,zₜ] through inverse kinematics to match a goal image taking 0.483±0.130 ms per solve. As shown in Fig. 4, differentiable-QP supervision recovers the vertical control authority required to reach the elevated target, whereas prediction-only training remains below the goal height despite approaching the correct planar configuration.

    VI CONCLUSION

    We presented μMPC, a framework that combines scalable Koopman dynamics learning with fast constrained MPC. By compiling finite-horizon predictions into action-only KC-QPs with a reusable primal operator, μMPC reduces online primal-dual optimization to matrix-vector products and projections, invariant under changing goals and constraints. Lightweight differentiable control-recovery QPs enable fast, batched supervision and scalable DAgger-style data aggregation, directly training dynamics for finite-horizon control. Across experiments, μMPC achieves millisecond-scale whole-body control with 4096-dimensional Koopman models, submillisecond planning with 2048-dimensional linear world models, long horizon MPC onboard Crazyflie MCU, and real-time planning for 200 quadrotors.

    Future work should focus on principled model selection and improved constraint handling. Our reported encoder capacities, lifted dimensions, and training horizons were selected through empirical tuning and retraining, motivating scaling laws relating these choices to prediction and closed-loop performance. In very demanding cases, fixed-budget solves may retain residual constraint violations, incorporating constraints into training could improve constraint response with fewer primal-dual iterations. Current model-error margins also remain empirical rather than formally calibrated.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 材质贴图里藏着一个没人说的选择：它到底是金属还是绝缘体——ReMeDi 把这个「意图金属度」显式化 ｜ ReMeDi: Single-Image PBR Material Estimation via Reparameterization between Metal and Dielectric Hypotheses
item.description:
一句话：任何决定反照率的贴图都隐含一个金属度判断，判断错了材质就会被误读或物理上不成立。

要点：

  • 把 PBR 材质估计里最容易被忽略的一点讲清了：表面的反射特性**高度取决于它是金属还是绝缘体**，因此**任何决定反照率的贴图都隐含一个「意图金属度」的判断**
  • 代价很直接：**意图金属度不匹配的贴图会导致物理上不成立或被误读的材质**；而 metallic–roughness 工作流又让金属度变得难以从单图推断
  • ReMeDi 因此把问题重新参数化为**「金属假设」与「绝缘体假设」之间的重参数化**，让这个隐含选择变显式、可解

为什么值得看：PBR 贴图进引擎前最大的坑就是金属度判断错误——反照率看着对，换光照就崩。这条把「意图金属度」这个隐含量拿出来显式建模，比再涨一点 PSNR 更接近生产需求。

中文摘要：基于物理的渲染（PBR）材质估计服务于重打光、材质编辑与三维内容创作。作者指出一个常被忽略的关键点：表面的反射特性高度依赖于它是金属还是绝缘体，因此任何决定反照率的贴图都隐含着一个「意图金属度（intended metalness）」的判断；当贴图的意图金属度与实际不符时，渲染出的材质会显得物理上不成立或被误读。与此同时，metallic–roughness 工作流又让金属度难以从单张图像中直接推断。ReMeDi 因此把问题重新参数化为「金属假设」与「绝缘体假设」之间的重参数化，让这个隐含的选择变得显式且可解。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

ReMeDi: Single-Image PBR Material Estimation via
Reparameterization between Metal and Dielectric Hypotheses

Abstract

Physically based rendering (PBR) material estimation facilitates relighting, material editing, and 3D content creation. As the reflectance of a surface heavily depends on whether it is a metal or a dielectric, producing any map that determines albedo involves a decision on metalness, which we call the “intended metalness” of the map. Rendering maps with mismatched intended metalness yields physically implausible or misinterpreted materials. The metallic–roughness workflow makes metalness explicit and thus encourages base color to match it, but does not enforce this match, especially for automated methods directly predicting each map. Therefore, we propose ReMeDi, which enforces the match through two components. First, we reparameterize base color as a metalness-weighted blend of its two variants, estimated under the all-metal and all-dielectric hypothesis, respectively. Second, as available supervision cannot teach a single network both hypotheses at every pixel, we restrict each of two separate networks to one hypothesis, so that each variant is ensured to follow its hypothesis. Besides enforcing the match, this also improves each estimated material map. Experiments show that ReMeDi outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both material accuracy and relighting fidelity. Project page: https://costrice.github.io/remedi/

††footnotetext: This work was done when Fan Fei and Yixin Zhu were interning at Tencent Hunyuan3D.$\dagger$$\dagger$footnotetext: Corresponding authors: chunchaoguo@tencent.com, shiboxin@pku.edu.cn

1 Introduction

Physically based rendering (PBR) materials, represented as spatially varying bidirectional reflectance distribution function (SVBRDF) maps, enable image-space relighting [60, 34, 33] and material editing [31, 52], provide tileable textures [63, 49, 59], and paint 3D assets with view- and lighting-dependent appearance [18, 57, 29, 53, 66, 13]. Recovering them from a single image, a readily available input whether photographed or generated, has therefore long been an important task [2, 30, 32, 10, 24, 16, 19].

The reflective property of a surface heavily depends on whether it is a metal or a dielectric (i.e., its metalness): A dielectric reflects light diffusely in its own color and specularly with a weak, colorless reflectance of about 4%, whereas a metal has no diffuse reflection and a strong, often colored specular reflectance [28]. Therefore, any map that determines albedo, whether authored or estimated and in whichever SVBRDF parameterization, is produced with a decision on metalness. For each such map X, we call this often implicit decision its “intended metalness” μ_X, i.e., the metalness of the material that the map’s producer means to describe with the map. For example, a diffuse albedo map D produced to describe a painted surface has μ_D=0.

We note that the intended metalness of different maps describing the same surface may not match, and this mismatch may yield physically implausible or misinterpreted materials. The specular–glossiness (SG) workflow stores diffuse albedo D and specular albedo S directly, leaving μ_D and μ_S implicit and unconstrained by each other (Tab.1, SG). As a result, it may describe a material that is highly dielectric and metallic at once, e.g., a bright D with a colored S, where the low μ_D does not match the high μ_S[38]. The metallic–roughness (MR) workflow [4] makes the decision explicit as a metalness map M, which is usually binary and directly shows its own intended metalness, i.e., μ_M=M (Tab.1, MR direct). The renderer then interprets a base color map C as diffuse albedo where M=0 and as specular albedo where M=1. This parameterization encourages μ_C to match M, as authors are required to produce M and can directly refer to it when producing C. Nevertheless, the match is not enforced. The surface can look darker than expected if a C intended as diffuse albedo (μ_C=0) is rendered as metal (M=1), and brighter in the opposite case (Fig.1, top). The mismatch problem is more pronounced for learning-based methods that directly produce each map [10, 63, 59, 66, 60, 18] than for human artists, as nothing but the learned data distribution, which only loosely reflects the match, relates the intended metalness of different maps (Fig.1, middle).

To this end, we propose ReMeDi to estimate material maps from a single image via Reparameterization between Metal and Dielectric hypotheses, which enforces the match by design through two components, (1) a reparameterization of base color between all-metal and all-dielectric hypotheses and (2) a hypothesis-specific supervision and estimation pipeline (Tab.1, MR + (1)(2) and Fig.1, bottom).

As component (1), instead of producing C directly with its μ_C left implicitly to the network, we reparameterize C as a blend of its two variants Cᵐ and Cᵈ, meant to be produced under the all-metal hypotheses (μ_Cᵐ=1) and the all-dielectric (μ_Cᵈ=0), respectively, according to M. We form C by selecting Cᵐ where M=1 and Cᵈ where M=0, and generalize this selection to intermediate values of M, interpreting these values as metal coverage. Through this reparameterization, as long as μ_Cᵐ=1 and μ_Cᵈ=0 are actually fulfilled, μ_C is ensured to match M.

Component (1) alone, however, is not sufficient, as ensuring the premise instead of leaving it to chance is not straightforward (Tab.1, MR + (1)). As no existing asset provides two sets of material maps that have opposite metalness and render to the same appearance, each hypothesis can only be supervised on pixels where it holds, leaving the predictions elsewhere unconstrained. Thus, a single network that learns to estimate under both hypotheses is not guaranteed to fully follow the hypothesis required by Cᵐ or Cᵈ. As component (2), we guarantee this by restricting each of two separate networks to learn under a single and fixed hypothesis, so that it can only estimate under that hypothesis, whether it holds at a pixel or not. This ensures that the premise is fulfilled, i.e., μ_Cᵐ=1 and μ_Cᵈ=0.

As shown in the bottom of Fig.1, the reparameterization and the hypothesis-specific estimation together enforce the intended metalness of the blended C to be M by design, eliminating the mismatch and its consequences. Moreover, the separate networks also improve the estimated materials maps, mitigating problems such as highlights baked into base color. This is because metals and dielectrics follow different distributions of base color and roughness, thus calling for different ways of inferring the intrinsic material from the observed appearance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReMeDi outperforms existing methods in both material accuracy and relighting fidelity, reducing the base color and relighting errors by 2.86 dB and 2.74 dB, respectively, and validate the necessity of both components.

2 Related Work

As shown in Tab.2, in this section, we review SVBRDF parameterizations and summarize methods producing them, mostly from a single image.

SVBRDF parameterizations.

SVBRDF maps typically parameterize a microfacet BRDF [7, 51], which sums a diffuse lobe and a specular lobe shaped by the normal and roughness (R) at each surface point. The SG workflow [38] specifies the reflectance of the two lobes with two independent color maps D and S, which do not prevent physically implausible combinations. The MR workflow [4, 21] instead derives both from C and M, using M as the weight for linearly blending dielectric and metallic reflection models. It builds in that dielectrics share an achromatic S of about 0.04 and metals have no diffuse reflection, leading to

D=lerp(C,0;M), S=lerp(0.04,C;M),

(1)

where lerp(·,·;·) is linear interpolation. This makes plausible materials easier to author and the maps more compact, as a single-channel M replaces the three-channel S[38]. MR has thus become the default in asset formats such as glTF [44], USD [40], and OpenPBR [1].

SVBRDF estimation under SG.

Methods in the SG workflow (Tab.2, rows 1–4) estimate R together with D, S, or both from a single image. Most predict D and S jointly, either pixel-aligned with the input [10, 14, 64, 65, 48, 39, 58] or as tileable textures [63, 49], while others predict only D and fix S to the dielectric value of 0.04 [32, 5, 55, 36], which cannot represent metals. Neither the workflow nor the pipelines constrain μ_D and μ_S to match.

SVBRDF estimation under MR.

Unlike D and S, C takes its meaning from M, which encourages, but not enforces, μ_C to match μ_M≡M. We thus organize methods in the MR workflow (rows 5–12), which estimate R together with C and M, by when M is determined relative to C, i.e., how they relate the two. Several first produce C and add M afterwards (rows 5–7). CHORD [59] motivates this order by noting that C most resembles the input among all attributes, and searches over M of 0 and 1 per pixel while keeping the same C. MuMA [66] generates C along with a shaded image, from which IDArb [33] derives M, and Boosting3D [53] assigns M to segmented parts with values suggested by a vision-language model. Many others produce C and M jointly (rows 8–10), whether pixel-aligned [60, 61, 24, 16, 19, 33, 22, 34], tileable [47, 50, 37], or as UV textures [18, 13, 15, 6, 67]. A few encourage μ_C to match M by first predicting M then conditioning C on M (rows 11–12). Rhee and Lee [43] route the whole image to a dedicated metal or non-metal network, which is the closest to our method that restricts a network to a single kind of material, but their decision is per image. In contrast, ReMeDi applies the two hypotheses per pixel by M and thus enforces the match by design, even on images containing both kinds of materials.

3 Proposed Method

Given a single image I∈[0,1]^H×W×3 of an object, ReMeDi estimates pixel-aligned base color C∈[0,1]^H×W×3, metalness M∈[0,1]^H×W, and roughness R∈[0,1]^H×W in the MR workflow (Fig.2). We first show how to reparameterize C under two fixed hypotheses so that its intended metalness μ_C matches the used metalness map M (component (1), Sec.3.1). After introducing the conditional generation model on which our networks are built (Sec.3.2), we describe how each variant is supervised only where its hypothesis holds (Sec.3.3). We then show how separate networks ensure that each variant follows its hypothesis at every pixel (component (2), Sec.3.4), followed by the implementation details (Sec.3.5).

3.1 Reparameterization between Hypotheses

As discussed in previous sections, base color is the diffuse albedo of a dielectric but the specular albedo of a metal, so a base color map C comes with its intended metalness map μ_C. When base color C is produced directly, its μ_C is left to the producer and may not match the explicit metalness map M, leading to materials that appear too dark or too bright. To eliminate this potential mismatch, we reparameterize C as a combination of two variants by M so that μ_C=M holds as long as a premise is fulfilled.

Picking one from two hypotheses about metalness.

We first introduce two variants of base color, Cᵈ and Cᵐ, which describe the input as if every pixel were dielectric or metal, respectively. Thus, their intended metalness is 0 and 1, respectively, whatever the actual material is. C then picks at every pixel p the exact hypothesis that M indicates:

C(p)=\begincasesCᵈ(p),&whereM(p)=0 Cᵐ(p),&whereM(p)=1\endcases.

(2)

This ensures μ_C=M where M is binary. Note that Cᵈ and Cᵐ do not equal the diffuse albedo D or specular albedo S, which depend on the actual metalness. For example, D should be 0 at a metal pixel while Cᵈ is meant to describe this pixel as dielectric and predict its diffuse albedo under that hypothesis, which is generally non-zero.

Generalization to intermediate metalness.

When M is not binary, combining the two variants of C so that μ_C is still M is not as trivial as in Eq.2. In the MR workflow [4, 21], intermediate metalness values indicate a spatial mixture of dielectric and metal surfaces, such as material boundaries and partially rusted metals. The value of metalness is interpreted as the fraction covered by the metal, and thus serves as the linear blending weight between the two reflection models in rendering (Eq.1). The same linear blending of different materials is also used in material-layering works [11, 46]. Thus, we follow this convention and use M to linearly blend the two base color variants at every pixel, which generalizes Eq.2:

C(p)=lerp(Cᵈ(p),Cᵐ(p);M(p)), ∀p,

(3)

The blended C thus has μ_C=M, as long as Cᵈ and Cᵐ indeed follow their respective hypotheses, which we enforce by the pipeline design described in Secs.3.3 and 3.4.

3.2 Preliminary: Conditional Generation

Our networks are built on a pretrained diffusion transformer (DiT) for conditional image generation [42], fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [17]. In this subsection, we describe a single module Gʰ that generates a set of target maps Xʰ from a set of condition images Yʰ. For all modules of ReMeDi, Yʰ={I}, while some variants in Sec.4.3 additionally condition on M.

Image tokens.

The DiT generates images as sequences of tokens, which a frozen variational autoencoder (VAE) [23] encodes from images and decodes back. Its encoder 𝔼 downsamples an image X by a factor of 16 into d=64 channels, so that 𝔼(X)∈ℝ^H/16×W/16×d, i.e., N=HW/16² tokens, each covering a 16×16 pixel patch. We replicate single-channel maps such as roughness and metalness to three channels as we empirically find that keeping them as separate maps instead of a combined map gives sharper and cleaner generation results.

Conditioning.

The DiT processes text and image tokens in a single sequence, whose prefix holds the condition tokens. A frozen vision-language model (VLM) encoder [3] jointly encodes I and a fixed text prompt into a sequence of embeddings, of which those at the text positions, eₜₑₓₜ, are kept, and those at the image positions are replaced by 𝔼(I). Any other condition image is encoded by the VAE into a further block, so that the condition tokens of module h are

z_condʰ=concat{ eₜₑₓₜ, 𝔼(Y):Y∈Yʰ }.

(4)

Target.

The original backbone generates only a single target image after the prefix. We extend it to multiple target maps by appending their tokens after the prefix, each map with its own positional embedding, and letting all of them attend to the whole prefix and to each other, so that the maps of a module are generated jointly. Specifically, the target tokens z₀ʰ are formed by encoding each target map into a grid of tokens and concatenating the flattened grids:

z₀ʰ=concat{ 𝔼(X):X∈Xʰ }∈ℝ^|Xʰ|N×d.

(5)

Denoising.

Following flow matching [35], we sample a time t∈[0,1] and standard Gaussian noise ε of the same shape as z₀ʰ and interpolate into noised targets,

zₜʰ=(1-t) z₀ʰ+t ε∈ℝ^|Xʰ|N×d,

(6)

which are then appended to z_condʰ. The transformer v_θ,Δθʰ, with frozen backbone weights θ and the LoRA weights Δθʰ of module h, predicts the velocity ε-z₀ʰ of the target. At inference, we start from pure noise at t=1, integrate the predicted velocity to t=0, and decode each block of the result ẑ₀ʰ with the frozen VAE decoder D:

X̂=D(ẑ₀ʰ[X])∈[0,1]^H×W×3, X∈Xʰ,

(7)

where ẑ₀ʰ[X]∈ℝ^N×d is the block corresponding to X. As the single-channel maps are replicated before encoding, we average the three channels of their decoded output.

3.3 Hypothesis-Specific Supervision

The effectiveness of the reparameterization relies on that the two base color variants, Cᵈ and Cᵐ, follow their respective hypotheses, i.e., describing every pixel as the same kind of material. However, the ground-truth (GT) material maps of a training asset follow its actual material. The GT base color map is thus a valid target for a variant only on pixels where its hypothesis holds, e.g., metal pixels for Cᵐ, and misleads it elsewhere. We therefore supervise each variant only on regions of its own kind of material.

As the generation operates on tokens, we weight each token by the pixels it covers. We call a pixel dielectric if its GT metalness is below τᵈ=0.2 and metal if it exceeds τᵐ=0.8, which gives the sets of target pixels Tᵈ and Tᵐ of the two hypotheses. For each token k of a variant map under hypothesis h∈{d,m}, covering the 16×16 pixels ℙₖ, we compute the fraction of target pixels:

fₖʰ=(|ℙₖ∩F∩Tʰ|)/(|ℙₖ∩F|)∈[0,1],

(8)

where F is the set of foreground pixels. Tokens dominated by the target pixels are supervised with the weight

wₖʰ=clamp (fₖʰ-τᵖ/1-τᵖ, 0, 1),

(9)

where τᵖ=0.9 is the purity threshold of the target material for a token to participate in training. We apply wₖʰ to get a weighted flow matching objective of the module Gʰ that generates the variant maps under hypothesis h:

L_WFM=(∑ₖwₖʰ∥v_θ,Δθʰ(zₜʰ,t,z_condʰ)ₖ-(ε-z₀ʰ)ₖ∥²)/(∑ₖwₖʰ).

(10)

For both variants, the target tokens z₀ʰ correspond to the same GT map, and their difference comes from wₖʰ.

3.4 Restricting One Network to One Hypothesis

The supervision in Sec.3.3 leaves the output of each variant on pixels of the other kind of material to the extrapolation of the network. For example, outputting the actual base color for both variants fits the supervision perfectly, though they do not fully follow the hypotheses. Thus, a single network that learns under both hypotheses may apply either of them to each variant, and the produced two variants are not ensured to follow their own hypotheses, as shown in Sec.4.3.

Imposing more complete supervisions by constraining both variants on the same pixels would require two sets of material maps that have opposite metalness and render to the same appearance, which existing assets do not provide. An alternative to constrain every pixel is thus required.

Separate hypothesis networks.

We therefore restrict each network to learn under a single hypothesis, using a dielectric module Gᵈ and a metal module Gᵐ built on Sec.3.2, together with a metalness module G^M described below. The modules share the frozen backbone but have their own LoRA weights. As each module never learns to estimate under the other hypothesis, it surely follows its own hypothesis at every pixel, fulfilling the requirement of Sec.3.1.

Separate modules also improve the estimated materials of both kinds, as dielectrics and metals follow different distributions of material values and call for different ways to infer the material from appearance. For example, the metal variant requires stronger ability to identify and remove metallic highlights, while the dielectric variant should focus more on retaining detailed textures in the input.

Roughness.

Roughness R keeps its meaning for both dielectrics and metals, but its typical values differ significantly between them, e.g., a high roughness is far more common on dielectrics. A roughness map thus also carries an intended metalness, though more weakly tied to its values than that of base color. We therefore let Gᵈ and Gᵐ estimate roughness under their own hypotheses as well, i.e., Xᵈ={Cᵈ,Rᵈ} and Xᵐ={Cᵐ,Rᵐ}, and combine the two in the same way as base color:

R(p)=lerp(Rᵈ(p),Rᵐ(p);M(p)), ∀p.

(11)

Metalness predictor.

The metalness module G^M, with X^M={M}, estimates the metalness that blends the two hypotheses. Besides Eq.10, a binarization penalty keeps its estimate near-binary where the GT is binary:

L_bin=(1)/(|Ω|)∑_p∈Ω|M̂₀(p)-[M_GT(p)>0.5]|,

(12)

where M̂₀ is the metalness decoded from the clean estimate zₜ^M-t v_θ,Δθ^M, Ω⊆F is the set of foreground pixels whose GT metalness is clearly binary, i.e., below τᵈ or above τᵐ, and [·] is the indicator function. The penalty is applied only at small t, where M̂₀ is reliable. As pixels with intermediate GT metalness are left out of Ω, the predicted metalness remains continuous where the GT is. The metalness module is trained with L_WFM+λ L_bin, where wₖ^M=1 on all foreground tokens and λ balances the two terms.

3.5 Implementation Details

Training and inference.

We train each module separately at a resolution of 1024×1024, with LoRA of rank 64 on the transformer, AdamW at a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵ after a linear warm-up of 500 iterations, and λ=0.3. Each module is trained for 30K iterations with a batch size of 1 per GPU and a sequence parallelism (SP) size of 2, on 24 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The training set contains about 95K assets. At inference, the three modules take the same 1024×1024 input and use 20 sampling steps each, which takes about 60 s in total for an average case on a single GPU.

4 Experiments

The experiments are conducted on two test sets: SynTest containing rendered images of 3D assets with GT material maps and WildTest containing in-the-wild images without GT material (Sec.4.1). We compare our ReMeDi with existing methods (Sec.4.2) and validate the proposed components through controlled ablation studies (Sec.4.3). For more details and results, please refer to the supplement.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Test set with GT material maps.

Our synthetic test set, SynTest, contains 365 high-quality objects curated from Objaverse-XL [8], each rendered from one view under one lighting condition, with GT base color, metalness, roughness, and normal maps at 1024×1024. The fraction of metal pixels in the foreground varies widely across images: 80 images have less than 1% metal pixels, and 93 have more than 50%. We exclude assets appearing in the available training-asset lists of the compared baselines, and hold out the selected test assets from our own training data, so that all comparing methods should not have seen these data.

In-the-wild test set.

We additionally curate WildTest, an in-house set of high-quality in-the-wild images without GT materials, for qualitative comparison. For relighting, all methods share normals estimated using MoGe-3 [25].

Metrics.

We report metrics for both material maps and relit images, which show how the material maps work together. For base color, we report PSNR, scale-invariant PSNR (si-PSNR, where the prediction is aligned to the GT with per-channel least squares), SSIM [54], and LPIPS [62]; for metalness, we report RMSE and classification accuracy at a threshold of 0.5 on foreground pixels whose GT metalness is below τᵈ or above τᵐ; and for roughness, we report RMSE. For relit results, we render the predicted and GT material maps with the same single-view-based renderer and GT normals, under a neutral-color environment map that is rotated in 36 steps about the viewing axis and, separately, about the world vertical axis, resulting in 72 relit frames per object per method. Then we measure the PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS between the rendered images and GT.

Scope.

We report metrics on the whole foreground (Overall) and restricted to metal pixels (Metal, GT metalness above τᵐ) and dielectric pixels (Dielectric, below τᵈ). Pixel-wise errors are evaluated within the mask of the scope. SSIM and LPIPS are computed on the whole image, where all pixels outside the mask of the scope are replaced by the mean GT value over these pixels, in both the prediction and the GT. Each metric is computed per image and then averaged over the images, where a restricted scope only counts the images that contain at least 5% such pixels.

4.2 Comparison with Existing Methods

Baselines.

We compare with methods that estimate pixel-aligned metallic–roughness maps from a single image with available model weights, including RGB↔X [60], Intrinsic Image Diffusion (IID) [24], IDArb [33], SuperMat [16], Marigold-IID [22], and the inverse renderer of DiffusionRenderer [34], which is a video generator and applied to single frames. We run each baseline with its released checkpoint and default inference settings.

Quantitative comparison.

Tab.3 reports the overall metrics on SynTest. As shown in Tab.3, ReMeDi outperforms all baselines on every metric. Compared with the strongest baseline, SuperMat [16], ReMeDi improves the PSNR of base color by 2.86 dB and reduces its LPIPS by 57.6%. The RMSEs of metalness and roughness are also reduced by 25.9% and 10.5%, respectively. These gains carry over to relighting, where PSNR is improved by 2.74 dB and LPIPS drops from 0.065 to 0.031, indicating that the estimated maps combine into a more faithful appearance.

Qualitative comparison.

Fig.3 shows the estimated base color and metalness by the two strongest baselines [16, 33] and our ReMeDi, together with the relit results, on both SynTest and WildTest.
