On the photosniper (left), IDArb and SuperMat estimate base color on its silver gunstock that is too dark and does not match the medium or high metalness, so that the body is rendered too dark, whereas ReMeDi correctly estimates the materials closest to the GT. On the diving helmet (right), IDArb combines a bright base color with scattered metalness, which makes the helmet appear overly bright and noisy when relit, whereas SuperMat and ReMeDi produce plausible results that give metallic appearances. On both examples, the base color of ReMeDi matches its metalness, leading to relit results that faithfully preserve the appearance of the input.

4.3 Ablation Studies

一句话：任何决定反照率的贴图都隐含一个金属度判断，判断错了材质就会被误读或物理上不成立。

要点：

  • 把 PBR 材质估计里最容易被忽略的一点讲清了：表面的反射特性**高度取决于它是金属还是绝缘体**，因此**任何决定反照率的贴图都隐含一个「意图金属度」的判断**
  • 代价很直接：**意图金属度不匹配的贴图会导致物理上不成立或被误读的材质**；而 metallic–roughness 工作流又让金属度变得难以从单图推断
  • ReMeDi 因此把问题重新参数化为**「金属假设」与「绝缘体假设」之间的重参数化**，让这个隐含选择变显式、可解

为什么值得看：PBR 贴图进引擎前最大的坑就是金属度判断错误——反照率看着对，换光照就崩。这条把「意图金属度」这个隐含量拿出来显式建模，比再涨一点 PSNR 更接近生产需求。

中文摘要：基于物理的渲染（PBR）材质估计服务于重打光、材质编辑与三维内容创作。作者指出一个常被忽略的关键点：表面的反射特性高度依赖于它是金属还是绝缘体，因此任何决定反照率的贴图都隐含着一个「意图金属度（intended metalness）」的判断；当贴图的意图金属度与实际不符时，渲染出的材质会显得物理上不成立或被误读。与此同时，metallic–roughness 工作流又让金属度难以从单张图像中直接推断。ReMeDi 因此把问题重新参数化为「金属假设」与「绝缘体假设」之间的重参数化，让这个隐含的选择变得显式且可解。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

ReMeDi: Single-Image PBR Material Estimation via
Reparameterization between Metal and Dielectric Hypotheses

Abstract

Physically based rendering (PBR) material estimation facilitates relighting, material editing, and 3D content creation. As the reflectance of a surface heavily depends on whether it is a metal or a dielectric, producing any map that determines albedo involves a decision on metalness, which we call the “intended metalness” of the map. Rendering maps with mismatched intended metalness yields physically implausible or misinterpreted materials. The metallic–roughness workflow makes metalness explicit and thus encourages base color to match it, but does not enforce this match, especially for automated methods directly predicting each map. Therefore, we propose ReMeDi, which enforces the match through two components. First, we reparameterize base color as a metalness-weighted blend of its two variants, estimated under the all-metal and all-dielectric hypothesis, respectively. Second, as available supervision cannot teach a single network both hypotheses at every pixel, we restrict each of two separate networks to one hypothesis, so that each variant is ensured to follow its hypothesis. Besides enforcing the match, this also improves each estimated material map. Experiments show that ReMeDi outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both material accuracy and relighting fidelity. Project page: https://costrice.github.io/remedi/

††footnotetext: This work was done when Fan Fei and Yixin Zhu were interning at Tencent Hunyuan3D.$\dagger$$\dagger$footnotetext: Corresponding authors: chunchaoguo@tencent.com, shiboxin@pku.edu.cn

1 Introduction

Physically based rendering (PBR) materials, represented as spatially varying bidirectional reflectance distribution function (SVBRDF) maps, enable image-space relighting [60, 34, 33] and material editing [31, 52], provide tileable textures [63, 49, 59], and paint 3D assets with view- and lighting-dependent appearance [18, 57, 29, 53, 66, 13]. Recovering them from a single image, a readily available input whether photographed or generated, has therefore long been an important task [2, 30, 32, 10, 24, 16, 19].

The reflective property of a surface heavily depends on whether it is a metal or a dielectric (i.e., its metalness): A dielectric reflects light diffusely in its own color and specularly with a weak, colorless reflectance of about 4%, whereas a metal has no diffuse reflection and a strong, often colored specular reflectance [28]. Therefore, any map that determines albedo, whether authored or estimated and in whichever SVBRDF parameterization, is produced with a decision on metalness. For each such map X, we call this often implicit decision its “intended metalness” μ_X, i.e., the metalness of the material that the map’s producer means to describe with the map. For example, a diffuse albedo map D produced to describe a painted surface has μ_D=0.

We note that the intended metalness of different maps describing the same surface may not match, and this mismatch may yield physically implausible or misinterpreted materials. The specular–glossiness (SG) workflow stores diffuse albedo D and specular albedo S directly, leaving μ_D and μ_S implicit and unconstrained by each other (Tab.1, SG). As a result, it may describe a material that is highly dielectric and metallic at once, e.g., a bright D with a colored S, where the low μ_D does not match the high μ_S[38]. The metallic–roughness (MR) workflow [4] makes the decision explicit as a metalness map M, which is usually binary and directly shows its own intended metalness, i.e., μ_M=M (Tab.1, MR direct). The renderer then interprets a base color map C as diffuse albedo where M=0 and as specular albedo where M=1. This parameterization encourages μ_C to match M, as authors are required to produce M and can directly refer to it when producing C. Nevertheless, the match is not enforced. The surface can look darker than expected if a C intended as diffuse albedo (μ_C=0) is rendered as metal (M=1), and brighter in the opposite case (Fig.1, top). The mismatch problem is more pronounced for learning-based methods that directly produce each map [10, 63, 59, 66, 60, 18] than for human artists, as nothing but the learned data distribution, which only loosely reflects the match, relates the intended metalness of different maps (Fig.1, middle).

To this end, we propose ReMeDi to estimate material maps from a single image via Reparameterization between Metal and Dielectric hypotheses, which enforces the match by design through two components, (1) a reparameterization of base color between all-metal and all-dielectric hypotheses and (2) a hypothesis-specific supervision and estimation pipeline (Tab.1, MR + (1)(2) and Fig.1, bottom).

As component (1), instead of producing C directly with its μ_C left implicitly to the network, we reparameterize C as a blend of its two variants Cᵐ and Cᵈ, meant to be produced under the all-metal hypotheses (μ_Cᵐ=1) and the all-dielectric (μ_Cᵈ=0), respectively, according to M. We form C by selecting Cᵐ where M=1 and Cᵈ where M=0, and generalize this selection to intermediate values of M, interpreting these values as metal coverage. Through this reparameterization, as long as μ_Cᵐ=1 and μ_Cᵈ=0 are actually fulfilled, μ_C is ensured to match M.

Component (1) alone, however, is not sufficient, as ensuring the premise instead of leaving it to chance is not straightforward (Tab.1, MR + (1)). As no existing asset provides two sets of material maps that have opposite metalness and render to the same appearance, each hypothesis can only be supervised on pixels where it holds, leaving the predictions elsewhere unconstrained. Thus, a single network that learns to estimate under both hypotheses is not guaranteed to fully follow the hypothesis required by Cᵐ or Cᵈ. As component (2), we guarantee this by restricting each of two separate networks to learn under a single and fixed hypothesis, so that it can only estimate under that hypothesis, whether it holds at a pixel or not. This ensures that the premise is fulfilled, i.e., μ_Cᵐ=1 and μ_Cᵈ=0.

As shown in the bottom of Fig.1, the reparameterization and the hypothesis-specific estimation together enforce the intended metalness of the blended C to be M by design, eliminating the mismatch and its consequences. Moreover, the separate networks also improve the estimated materials maps, mitigating problems such as highlights baked into base color. This is because metals and dielectrics follow different distributions of base color and roughness, thus calling for different ways of inferring the intrinsic material from the observed appearance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReMeDi outperforms existing methods in both material accuracy and relighting fidelity, reducing the base color and relighting errors by 2.86 dB and 2.74 dB, respectively, and validate the necessity of both components.

2 Related Work

As shown in Tab.2, in this section, we review SVBRDF parameterizations and summarize methods producing them, mostly from a single image.

SVBRDF parameterizations.

SVBRDF maps typically parameterize a microfacet BRDF [7, 51], which sums a diffuse lobe and a specular lobe shaped by the normal and roughness (R) at each surface point. The SG workflow [38] specifies the reflectance of the two lobes with two independent color maps D and S, which do not prevent physically implausible combinations. The MR workflow [4, 21] instead derives both from C and M, using M as the weight for linearly blending dielectric and metallic reflection models. It builds in that dielectrics share an achromatic S of about 0.04 and metals have no diffuse reflection, leading to

D=lerp(C,0;M), S=lerp(0.04,C;M),

(1)

where lerp(·,·;·) is linear interpolation. This makes plausible materials easier to author and the maps more compact, as a single-channel M replaces the three-channel S[38]. MR has thus become the default in asset formats such as glTF [44], USD [40], and OpenPBR [1].

SVBRDF estimation under SG.

Methods in the SG workflow (Tab.2, rows 1–4) estimate R together with D, S, or both from a single image. Most predict D and S jointly, either pixel-aligned with the input [10, 14, 64, 65, 48, 39, 58] or as tileable textures [63, 49], while others predict only D and fix S to the dielectric value of 0.04 [32, 5, 55, 36], which cannot represent metals. Neither the workflow nor the pipelines constrain μ_D and μ_S to match.

SVBRDF estimation under MR.

Unlike D and S, C takes its meaning from M, which encourages, but not enforces, μ_C to match μ_M≡M. We thus organize methods in the MR workflow (rows 5–12), which estimate R together with C and M, by when M is determined relative to C, i.e., how they relate the two. Several first produce C and add M afterwards (rows 5–7). CHORD [59] motivates this order by noting that C most resembles the input among all attributes, and searches over M of 0 and 1 per pixel while keeping the same C. MuMA [66] generates C along with a shaded image, from which IDArb [33] derives M, and Boosting3D [53] assigns M to segmented parts with values suggested by a vision-language model. Many others produce C and M jointly (rows 8–10), whether pixel-aligned [60, 61, 24, 16, 19, 33, 22, 34], tileable [47, 50, 37], or as UV textures [18, 13, 15, 6, 67]. A few encourage μ_C to match M by first predicting M then conditioning C on M (rows 11–12). Rhee and Lee [43] route the whole image to a dedicated metal or non-metal network, which is the closest to our method that restricts a network to a single kind of material, but their decision is per image. In contrast, ReMeDi applies the two hypotheses per pixel by M and thus enforces the match by design, even on images containing both kinds of materials.

3 Proposed Method

Given a single image I∈[0,1]^H×W×3 of an object, ReMeDi estimates pixel-aligned base color C∈[0,1]^H×W×3, metalness M∈[0,1]^H×W, and roughness R∈[0,1]^H×W in the MR workflow (Fig.2). We first show how to reparameterize C under two fixed hypotheses so that its intended metalness μ_C matches the used metalness map M (component (1), Sec.3.1). After introducing the conditional generation model on which our networks are built (Sec.3.2), we describe how each variant is supervised only where its hypothesis holds (Sec.3.3). We then show how separate networks ensure that each variant follows its hypothesis at every pixel (component (2), Sec.3.4), followed by the implementation details (Sec.3.5).

3.1 Reparameterization between Hypotheses

As discussed in previous sections, base color is the diffuse albedo of a dielectric but the specular albedo of a metal, so a base color map C comes with its intended metalness map μ_C. When base color C is produced directly, its μ_C is left to the producer and may not match the explicit metalness map M, leading to materials that appear too dark or too bright. To eliminate this potential mismatch, we reparameterize C as a combination of two variants by M so that μ_C=M holds as long as a premise is fulfilled.

Picking one from two hypotheses about metalness.

We first introduce two variants of base color, Cᵈ and Cᵐ, which describe the input as if every pixel were dielectric or metal, respectively. Thus, their intended metalness is 0 and 1, respectively, whatever the actual material is. C then picks at every pixel p the exact hypothesis that M indicates:

C(p)=\begincasesCᵈ(p),&whereM(p)=0 Cᵐ(p),&whereM(p)=1\endcases.

(2)

This ensures μ_C=M where M is binary. Note that Cᵈ and Cᵐ do not equal the diffuse albedo D or specular albedo S, which depend on the actual metalness. For example, D should be 0 at a metal pixel while Cᵈ is meant to describe this pixel as dielectric and predict its diffuse albedo under that hypothesis, which is generally non-zero.

Generalization to intermediate metalness.

When M is not binary, combining the two variants of C so that μ_C is still M is not as trivial as in Eq.2. In the MR workflow [4, 21], intermediate metalness values indicate a spatial mixture of dielectric and metal surfaces, such as material boundaries and partially rusted metals. The value of metalness is interpreted as the fraction covered by the metal, and thus serves as the linear blending weight between the two reflection models in rendering (Eq.1). The same linear blending of different materials is also used in material-layering works [11, 46]. Thus, we follow this convention and use M to linearly blend the two base color variants at every pixel, which generalizes Eq.2:

C(p)=lerp(Cᵈ(p),Cᵐ(p);M(p)), ∀p,

(3)

The blended C thus has μ_C=M, as long as Cᵈ and Cᵐ indeed follow their respective hypotheses, which we enforce by the pipeline design described in Secs.3.3 and 3.4.

3.2 Preliminary: Conditional Generation

Our networks are built on a pretrained diffusion transformer (DiT) for conditional image generation [42], fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [17]. In this subsection, we describe a single module Gʰ that generates a set of target maps Xʰ from a set of condition images Yʰ. For all modules of ReMeDi, Yʰ={I}, while some variants in Sec.4.3 additionally condition on M.

Image tokens.

The DiT generates images as sequences of tokens, which a frozen variational autoencoder (VAE) [23] encodes from images and decodes back. Its encoder 𝔼 downsamples an image X by a factor of 16 into d=64 channels, so that 𝔼(X)∈ℝ^H/16×W/16×d, i.e., N=HW/16² tokens, each covering a 16×16 pixel patch. We replicate single-channel maps such as roughness and metalness to three channels as we empirically find that keeping them as separate maps instead of a combined map gives sharper and cleaner generation results.

Conditioning.

The DiT processes text and image tokens in a single sequence, whose prefix holds the condition tokens. A frozen vision-language model (VLM) encoder [3] jointly encodes I and a fixed text prompt into a sequence of embeddings, of which those at the text positions, eₜₑₓₜ, are kept, and those at the image positions are replaced by 𝔼(I). Any other condition image is encoded by the VAE into a further block, so that the condition tokens of module h are

z_condʰ=concat{ eₜₑₓₜ, 𝔼(Y):Y∈Yʰ }.

(4)

Target.

The original backbone generates only a single target image after the prefix. We extend it to multiple target maps by appending their tokens after the prefix, each map with its own positional embedding, and letting all of them attend to the whole prefix and to each other, so that the maps of a module are generated jointly. Specifically, the target tokens z₀ʰ are formed by encoding each target map into a grid of tokens and concatenating the flattened grids:

z₀ʰ=concat{ 𝔼(X):X∈Xʰ }∈ℝ^|Xʰ|N×d.

(5)

Denoising.

Following flow matching [35], we sample a time t∈[0,1] and standard Gaussian noise ε of the same shape as z₀ʰ and interpolate into noised targets,

zₜʰ=(1-t) z₀ʰ+t ε∈ℝ^|Xʰ|N×d,

(6)

which are then appended to z_condʰ. The transformer v_θ,Δθʰ, with frozen backbone weights θ and the LoRA weights Δθʰ of module h, predicts the velocity ε-z₀ʰ of the target. At inference, we start from pure noise at t=1, integrate the predicted velocity to t=0, and decode each block of the result ẑ₀ʰ with the frozen VAE decoder D:

X̂=D(ẑ₀ʰ[X])∈[0,1]^H×W×3, X∈Xʰ,

(7)

where ẑ₀ʰ[X]∈ℝ^N×d is the block corresponding to X. As the single-channel maps are replicated before encoding, we average the three channels of their decoded output.

3.3 Hypothesis-Specific Supervision

The effectiveness of the reparameterization relies on that the two base color variants, Cᵈ and Cᵐ, follow their respective hypotheses, i.e., describing every pixel as the same kind of material. However, the ground-truth (GT) material maps of a training asset follow its actual material. The GT base color map is thus a valid target for a variant only on pixels where its hypothesis holds, e.g., metal pixels for Cᵐ, and misleads it elsewhere. We therefore supervise each variant only on regions of its own kind of material.

As the generation operates on tokens, we weight each token by the pixels it covers. We call a pixel dielectric if its GT metalness is below τᵈ=0.2 and metal if it exceeds τᵐ=0.8, which gives the sets of target pixels Tᵈ and Tᵐ of the two hypotheses. For each token k of a variant map under hypothesis h∈{d,m}, covering the 16×16 pixels ℙₖ, we compute the fraction of target pixels:

fₖʰ=(|ℙₖ∩F∩Tʰ|)/(|ℙₖ∩F|)∈[0,1],

(8)

where F is the set of foreground pixels. Tokens dominated by the target pixels are supervised with the weight

wₖʰ=clamp (fₖʰ-τᵖ/1-τᵖ, 0, 1),

(9)

where τᵖ=0.9 is the purity threshold of the target material for a token to participate in training. We apply wₖʰ to get a weighted flow matching objective of the module Gʰ that generates the variant maps under hypothesis h:

L_WFM=(∑ₖwₖʰ∥v_θ,Δθʰ(zₜʰ,t,z_condʰ)ₖ-(ε-z₀ʰ)ₖ∥²)/(∑ₖwₖʰ).

(10)

For both variants, the target tokens z₀ʰ correspond to the same GT map, and their difference comes from wₖʰ.

3.4 Restricting One Network to One Hypothesis

The supervision in Sec.3.3 leaves the output of each variant on pixels of the other kind of material to the extrapolation of the network. For example, outputting the actual base color for both variants fits the supervision perfectly, though they do not fully follow the hypotheses. Thus, a single network that learns under both hypotheses may apply either of them to each variant, and the produced two variants are not ensured to follow their own hypotheses, as shown in Sec.4.3.

Imposing more complete supervisions by constraining both variants on the same pixels would require two sets of material maps that have opposite metalness and render to the same appearance, which existing assets do not provide. An alternative to constrain every pixel is thus required.

Separate hypothesis networks.

We therefore restrict each network to learn under a single hypothesis, using a dielectric module Gᵈ and a metal module Gᵐ built on Sec.3.2, together with a metalness module G^M described below. The modules share the frozen backbone but have their own LoRA weights. As each module never learns to estimate under the other hypothesis, it surely follows its own hypothesis at every pixel, fulfilling the requirement of Sec.3.1.

Separate modules also improve the estimated materials of both kinds, as dielectrics and metals follow different distributions of material values and call for different ways to infer the material from appearance. For example, the metal variant requires stronger ability to identify and remove metallic highlights, while the dielectric variant should focus more on retaining detailed textures in the input.

Roughness.

Roughness R keeps its meaning for both dielectrics and metals, but its typical values differ significantly between them, e.g., a high roughness is far more common on dielectrics. A roughness map thus also carries an intended metalness, though more weakly tied to its values than that of base color. We therefore let Gᵈ and Gᵐ estimate roughness under their own hypotheses as well, i.e., Xᵈ={Cᵈ,Rᵈ} and Xᵐ={Cᵐ,Rᵐ}, and combine the two in the same way as base color:

R(p)=lerp(Rᵈ(p),Rᵐ(p);M(p)), ∀p.

(11)

Metalness predictor.

The metalness module G^M, with X^M={M}, estimates the metalness that blends the two hypotheses. Besides Eq.10, a binarization penalty keeps its estimate near-binary where the GT is binary:

L_bin=(1)/(|Ω|)∑_p∈Ω|M̂₀(p)-[M_GT(p)>0.5]|,

(12)

where M̂₀ is the metalness decoded from the clean estimate zₜ^M-t v_θ,Δθ^M, Ω⊆F is the set of foreground pixels whose GT metalness is clearly binary, i.e., below τᵈ or above τᵐ, and [·] is the indicator function. The penalty is applied only at small t, where M̂₀ is reliable. As pixels with intermediate GT metalness are left out of Ω, the predicted metalness remains continuous where the GT is. The metalness module is trained with L_WFM+λ L_bin, where wₖ^M=1 on all foreground tokens and λ balances the two terms.

3.5 Implementation Details

Training and inference.

We train each module separately at a resolution of 1024×1024, with LoRA of rank 64 on the transformer, AdamW at a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵ after a linear warm-up of 500 iterations, and λ=0.3. Each module is trained for 30K iterations with a batch size of 1 per GPU and a sequence parallelism (SP) size of 2, on 24 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The training set contains about 95K assets. At inference, the three modules take the same 1024×1024 input and use 20 sampling steps each, which takes about 60 s in total for an average case on a single GPU.

4 Experiments

The experiments are conducted on two test sets: SynTest containing rendered images of 3D assets with GT material maps and WildTest containing in-the-wild images without GT material (Sec.4.1). We compare our ReMeDi with existing methods (Sec.4.2) and validate the proposed components through controlled ablation studies (Sec.4.3). For more details and results, please refer to the supplement.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Test set with GT material maps.

Our synthetic test set, SynTest, contains 365 high-quality objects curated from Objaverse-XL [8], each rendered from one view under one lighting condition, with GT base color, metalness, roughness, and normal maps at 1024×1024. The fraction of metal pixels in the foreground varies widely across images: 80 images have less than 1% metal pixels, and 93 have more than 50%. We exclude assets appearing in the available training-asset lists of the compared baselines, and hold out the selected test assets from our own training data, so that all comparing methods should not have seen these data.

In-the-wild test set.

We additionally curate WildTest, an in-house set of high-quality in-the-wild images without GT materials, for qualitative comparison. For relighting, all methods share normals estimated using MoGe-3 [25].

Metrics.

We report metrics for both material maps and relit images, which show how the material maps work together. For base color, we report PSNR, scale-invariant PSNR (si-PSNR, where the prediction is aligned to the GT with per-channel least squares), SSIM [54], and LPIPS [62]; for metalness, we report RMSE and classification accuracy at a threshold of 0.5 on foreground pixels whose GT metalness is below τᵈ or above τᵐ; and for roughness, we report RMSE. For relit results, we render the predicted and GT material maps with the same single-view-based renderer and GT normals, under a neutral-color environment map that is rotated in 36 steps about the viewing axis and, separately, about the world vertical axis, resulting in 72 relit frames per object per method. Then we measure the PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS between the rendered images and GT.

Scope.

We report metrics on the whole foreground (Overall) and restricted to metal pixels (Metal, GT metalness above τᵐ) and dielectric pixels (Dielectric, below τᵈ). Pixel-wise errors are evaluated within the mask of the scope. SSIM and LPIPS are computed on the whole image, where all pixels outside the mask of the scope are replaced by the mean GT value over these pixels, in both the prediction and the GT. Each metric is computed per image and then averaged over the images, where a restricted scope only counts the images that contain at least 5% such pixels.

4.2 Comparison with Existing Methods

Baselines.

We compare with methods that estimate pixel-aligned metallic–roughness maps from a single image with available model weights, including RGB↔X [60], Intrinsic Image Diffusion (IID) [24], IDArb [33], SuperMat [16], Marigold-IID [22], and the inverse renderer of DiffusionRenderer [34], which is a video generator and applied to single frames. We run each baseline with its released checkpoint and default inference settings.

Quantitative comparison.

Tab.3 reports the overall metrics on SynTest. As shown in Tab.3, ReMeDi outperforms all baselines on every metric. Compared with the strongest baseline, SuperMat [16], ReMeDi improves the PSNR of base color by 2.86 dB and reduces its LPIPS by 57.6%. The RMSEs of metalness and roughness are also reduced by 25.9% and 10.5%, respectively. These gains carry over to relighting, where PSNR is improved by 2.74 dB and LPIPS drops from 0.065 to 0.031, indicating that the estimated maps combine into a more faithful appearance.

Qualitative comparison.

Fig.3 shows the estimated base color and metalness by the two strongest baselines [16, 33] and our ReMeDi, together with the relit results, on both SynTest and WildTest. On the photosniper (left), IDArb and SuperMat estimate base color on its silver gunstock that is too dark and does not match the medium or high metalness, so that the body is rendered too dark, whereas ReMeDi correctly estimates the materials closest to the GT. On the diving helmet (right), IDArb combines a bright base color with scattered metalness, which makes the helmet appear overly bright and noisy when relit, whereas SuperMat and ReMeDi produce plausible results that give metallic appearances. On both examples, the base color of ReMeDi matches its metalness, leading to relit results that faithfully preserve the appearance of the input.

4.3 Ablation Studies

item.title: 一张肖像就能实时动、还能换光：LuxAvatar 把「可动的高斯代理」与「因果神经着色器」分开 ｜ LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies
item.description:
一句话：既要三维可控，又要复杂的面部光传输——这两件事被拆给两个组件。

要点：

  • 任务：从单张肖像出发，做**实时**的头部 avatar 动画与重打光
  • 分解方式：把合成拆成**可动画的三维本征高斯代理**与一个**因果自回归神经着色器**；代理负责**解耦标准几何与反射属性**，并把形变后的高斯**快速光栅化成视角与运动一致的 PBR 缓冲**
  • 着色器再基于这些本征缓冲做因果的神经着色，从而拿到复杂面部光传输

为什么值得看：按 11-12 定下的 B4 细则：**高斯的「表示改进」不收，重打光的「管线能力」收**。这条属于后者——高斯只是本征代理，真正的新东西是「光栅化出 PBR 缓冲 + 因果神经着色」这条实时重打光管线。

中文摘要：LuxAvatar 提出一个前馈框架，能从单张肖像出发，实时生成可动画、可重打光的头部 avatar。为实现三维可控性与复杂面部光传输，它把合成任务分解为两部分：一个可动画的三维本征高斯代理，以及一个因果自回归神经着色器。代理负责解耦标准几何与反射属性，并把形变后的高斯快速光栅化为视角与运动一致的 PBR 缓冲；神经着色器则在这些本征缓冲之上做因果着色，从而再现复杂的面部光传输。按现行判定，这类工作的价值不在「高斯表示更好」，而在实时重打光这条管线能力本身。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies

Abstract

We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. To achieve both 3D controllability and complex facial light transport, we factorize avatar synthesis into an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy and a causal autoregressive neural shader. This proxy disentangles canonical geometry and reflectance attributes, rapidly rasterizing deformed Gaussians into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Conditioned on these buffers, our neural shader formulates forward rendering as a conditional video diffusion process, bypassing explicit PBR computation to synthesize realistic shading effects under target illumination. We achieve real-time streaming through heterogeneous distillation from a pretrained multi-step bidirectional relighting teacher to a two-step causal autoregressive neural shader, inheriting broad synthetic lighting priors while minimizing conditioning and decoding latency. To further specialize these priors to human heads, we construct a hybrid relighting dataset for domain-specific fine-tuning, capturing authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded light transport. Extensive experiments show that our framework enables 3D-controllable, real-time portrait animation and relighting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy.

22footnotetext: Project lead.11footnotetext: Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Creating animatable and relightable head avatars is crucial for telepresence, immersive communication, and digital content creation. Seamless integration into virtual environments demands not only faithful facial motion, but also photorealistic appearance that adapts naturally to novel illumination. However, convincing head relighting is inherently difficult, as it requires modeling the intricate light transport among dynamic facial geometry, complex skin reflectance, and environmental lighting. Without costly acquisition setups or heavy rendering overhead, capturing and representing these complex effects with high visual fidelity remains a fundamental challenge.

Traditional approaches [10, 45, 20] to relightable head modeling either reconstruct facial meshes and reflectance maps for physically based rendering or linearly combine images captured under basis lighting. However, they often struggle with complex structures such as hair and detailed appearance. Subsequent neural volumetric head models [83, 62, 29, 78, 49, 58, 59] capture fine geometry and lighting effects via learned volumetric fields, at the cost of slow ray marching. Recently, relightable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods [61, 37, 63, 44, 80] have accelerated rendering by rasterizing explicit Gaussian primitives augmented with material properties or learned light transport. Despite these rendering advances, reconstructing a new subject still requires time-consuming per-subject optimization and faces a fundamental trade-off in data acquisition. Light stages provide controlled illumination but entail prohibitive hardware costs, whereas monocular approaches [72, 1, 88, 79] operate under unknown lighting via ill-posed inverse rendering, often suffering from baked-in shading residuals and simplified analytical shaders that struggle to model realistic light transport.

To enable instant avatar creation from a single portrait, recent feed-forward Gaussian head models [8, 24, 92, 52, 32, 75, 31] learn cross-identity priors for rapid 3D reconstruction and animation. However, these methods focus solely on motion control under baked-in ambient lighting, leaving the avatars non-relightable. Alternatively, 2D conditional diffusion models [41, 27] directly synthesize portraits under target motion and lighting, yet struggle with precise 3D control and cross-frame identity consistency [21]. Moreover, their multi-step denoising incurs high computational overhead, prohibiting real-time interaction.

To address these challenges, we introduce LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time streaming head animation and relighting from a single image, as shown in Fig. 1. Our key insight is to couple an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy with a causal autoregressive neural shader that models complex light transport from 4D-consistent PBR buffers in real time. Specifically, given a single reference image, we first reconstruct 3D Gaussians anchored on a canonical UV manifold in a feed-forward manner, augmenting each primitive with decoupled geometric and material attributes, including surface normals, base color, and roughness. Driven by target FLAME and camera parameters, these canonical primitives are deformed and rapidly rasterized into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Such a Gaussian proxy imposes a prior on 3D consistency and temporal material coherence.

Crucially, since the proxy already accounts for 3D geometry and viewpoint changes, our neural shader primarily addresses how to model intricate light transport efficiently and accurately. Rather than explicitly formulating analytical PBR equations, we cast forward shading as a conditional video diffusion process that directly synthesizes complex illumination effects, such as subsurface scattering, specular highlights, and soft shadows. However, standard video diffusion suffers from multi-step sampling overhead and bidirectional frame dependencies. To achieve both high fidelity and efficiency, we distill a pre-trained multi-step bidirectional teacher tailored for video relighting into a two-step causal autoregressive generator with lightweight channel-wise conditioning and fast latent decoding. Since the pre-trained teacher is designed for general relighting, we subsequently fine-tune the distilled generator on portrait relighting data to specialize it for human portraits.

Both training our feed-forward Gaussian proxy and fine-tuning the distilled shader require paired portrait videos under varying illumination. To overcome the high cost of acquiring such paired data at scale, we further construct a hybrid dataset from three complementary sources: (i) synthetic intrinsic supervision for the proxy and relit video targets for the shader, (ii) dynamic portraits under static lighting via reverse reference editing to provide real video targets with authentic facial dynamics, and (iii) static portraits under rotating illumination from public OLAT captures for physically grounded light transport.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time streaming head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait, supporting explicit motion and viewpoint control alongside photorealistic light transport without per-subject optimization.

  • •

    We introduce an animatable intrinsic Gaussian proxy that predicts decoupled canonical geometry and material attributes, providing view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers as explicit 4D guidance for neural shading.

  • •

    We develop a two-step causal neural shader via heterogeneous distillation and curate a hybrid dataset that adapts the general relighting prior with real portrait dynamics and OLAT supervision, enabling efficient streaming with realistic facial appearance and dynamic shading.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Feed-Forward 3D Head Avatars

    Feed-forward head avatar methods learn cross-identity priors to reconstruct animatable heads from one or a few images without per-identity optimization. Early radiance-field head avatars [39, 40, 9, 85, 13, 14, 71, 70] represent identity and motion through deformable fields or triplanes, supporting novel-view animation at the cost of expensive ray sampling for volumetric rendering.

    Recently, 3D Gaussian representations have mitigated this rendering bottleneck through efficient splatting, while exploring diverse animation and rendering designs. To model facial dynamics, expression-conditioned Gaussian predictors [34, 28, 52, 32, 31] directly regress motion-dependent Gaussian attributes. Alternatively, canonical Gaussian models [24, 67] achieve efficient animation via FLAME-based rigging and direct RGB splatting. Along this line, UIKA [75] constructs a Gaussian avatar from unposed images by leveraging facial correspondences and attention across screen and UV spaces for high-quality animation. Beyond direct color splatting, GAGAvatar [8] enhances image synthesis by coupling explicit Gaussian feature splatting with a neural image decoder. Despite their efficiency, these methods bake illumination into reconstructed appearance without explicit reflectance–illumination disentanglement, thereby precluding relighting.

    2.2 Relightable 3D Head Models

    Methods using light stages or other calibrated capture rigs [2, 78, 83, 62, 61, 63] build detailed relightable head models from controlled multi-view observations, but require dedicated capture and per-subject training. To relax capture requirements, inverse-rendering approaches [72, 79, 1, 88] recover geometry, reflectance, and lighting from monocular observations through subject-specific optimization. Given only a single image, parametric face reconstruction methods [82, 65, 35, 36, 16, 4, 51, 15] leverage morphable priors to infer these intrinsic properties, yet the decomposition remains ambiguous under unknown illumination.

    Beyond surface reflectance recovery, generative and feed-forward head models [68, 29, 57, 11, 49, 44, 66, 58, 59] learn cross-identity priors over volumetric or Gaussian representations to support joint view synthesis and relighting. However, to achieve high-fidelity facial animation, existing frameworks still rely on costly test-time optimization for each new subject. VRMM [84] fits an animatable volumetric head model to a single image via latent inversion, URAvatar [37] adapts a universal Gaussian avatar to a phone video with joint lighting estimation, and RelightAnyone [80] reconstructs a neutral-expression head from a single image through identity and lighting inversion.

    2.3 Generative Relighting and Rendering

    Generative portrait relighting methods [54, 55, 5, 81, 7] synthesize novel illumination while preserving the observed pose and expression. Similarly, portrait harmonization approaches [50, 60, 89] adapt foreground illumination to match replacement backgrounds. Portrait video relighting methods [23, 48, 91] extend image relighting to dynamic facial performances using flat-lit sequences that retain the recorded motion. They promote temporal coherence through dynamic Gaussian reconstruction and temporal blending, or by jointly denoising multiple frames with video diffusion. More broadly, diffusion-based neural renderers [87, 6, 19, 42, 76, 46] synthesize photorealistic RGB images or videos under target illumination, using conditions such as geometry and material buffers, depth-aware irradiance maps, and RGB references.

    For joint control of pose, expression, and lighting, 3DMM-guided diffusion models [17, 41, 27] use parametric face renderings as spatial conditions for portrait synthesis. LCVD [21] extends this paradigm to video diffusion, conditioning on reference appearance and FLAME shading sequences to synthesize relightable portrait animation over overlapping temporal windows. However, many existing video relighting and rendering frameworks still incur substantial latency from multi-step denoising.

    3 Method

    Given a reference image I, a sequence of driving FLAME parameters, and target camera parameters, our goal is to synthesize photorealistic, 3D-consistent portrait videos conditioned on either a target environment map for relighting or a target background for harmonization. As illustrated in Fig. 2, LuxAvatar consists of two core components: (1) a feed-forward intrinsic Gaussian head proxy (Sec. 3.1) that lifts the input portrait into an animatable 3D representation to provide view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers, and (2) a causal autoregressive neural shader (Sec. 3.2) first distilled from a pre-trained bidirectional teacher for two-step streaming and relighting priors and then adapted on paired portrait data to achieve realistic facial shading and enable background harmonization. To effectively supervise the intrinsic proxy and support paired portrait adaptation without costly dynamic light stage captures, we further detail our hybrid training dataset construction in Sec. 3.3.

    3.1 3D Intrinsic Gaussian Head Proxy

    To provide explicit 3D geometric and material guidance from a single reference image I, we reconstruct a canonical head proxy parameterized by N 3D Gaussians [30], where each primitive is augmented with intrinsic PBR attributes:

    Gᶜ={(μᵢ,sᵢ,qᵢ,αᵢ,nᵢ,aᵢ,rᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^N.

    		(1)

    Here, μᵢ, sᵢ, qᵢ, and αᵢ denote the canonical 3D center, scale, orientation quaternion, and opacity of the i-th Gaussian, while nᵢ∈[-1,1]³, aᵢ∈[0,1]³, and rᵢ∈[0,1] represent its unit normal, base color, and roughness.

    UV-anchored intrinsic reconstruction. We organize the canonical Gaussians on a 2D UV manifold anchored to an identity-shaped FLAME template [38]. Given the reference image I, we first employ a frozen pretrained dense correspondence predictor to map foreground pixels onto the canonical UV grid, averaging colors within each occupied texel and zero-padding unobserved regions to form a partial UV texture Iᵤᵥ. Both I and Iᵤᵥ are encoded by a shared frozen DINOv3 [64] backbone, followed by separate trainable adapters that fuse multi-layer intermediate features into image-space and UV-space token streams. Learnable queries anchored at canonical UV coordinates then integrate both token streams via a transformer, after which a DPT-style decoder [56] combines intermediate query features with RGB cues from Iᵤᵥ to produce a dense canonical feature map F. Finally, for the i-th Gaussian at UV coordinate uᵢ, two decoupled prediction heads regress its geometric and material attributes in parallel:

    D_geo(F(uᵢ))=(Δμᵢ,sᵢ,qᵢ,αᵢ,nᵢ),(2)
    Dₘₐₜ(F(uᵢ))=(aᵢ,rᵢ).

    Each canonical center is defined as μᵢ=vᵢ+Δμᵢ, where vᵢ is the 3D surface point barycentrically interpolated from the FLAME mesh at uᵢ.

    Deformation and PBR buffer rasterization. Given the driving FLAME motion parameters at frame t, we animate the canonical proxy via expression blendshapes and linear blend skinning (LBS), utilizing deformation bases and skinning weights barycentrically interpolated at uᵢ. Specifically, this deformation process updates the canonical centers μᵢ and transforms the normals nᵢ into the posed space using blended linear transforms followed by unit-length normalization, whereas the intrinsic material attributes (aᵢ,rᵢ) remain unchanged. This yields the animated proxy Gₜ with view- and motion-consistent reflectance. Under the target camera πₜ, we then rasterize Gₜ into per-frame PBR buffers via fast differentiable splatting:

    ℂₜ=(Aₜ,Rₜ,Nₜ)=ℝₐₜₜᵣ(Gₜ,πₜ),

    		(3)

    where Aₜ, Rₜ, and Nₜ denote the rendered base color, roughness, and normal maps, respectively, and ℝₐₜₜᵣ is the differentiable attribute rasterizer. By projecting the driven 3D proxy into 2D screen space, the rendered buffers {ℂₜ} encode explicit camera and motion control alongside shading-free intrinsic cues, providing dense per-frame guidance for the subsequent neural shader.

    Training objectives. We train the proxy by supervising the rendered PBR buffers {ℂₜ} at sampled target frames against the intrinsic labels detailed in Sec. 3.3, using L1 (L_L1), SSIM [73] (L_SSIM), and LPIPS [90] (L_LPIPS) losses across all buffers. Combined with an offset regularizer L_off that constrains the Gaussians near their FLAME anchors, the overall objective is:

    L_off=1/3N∑ᵢ₌₁^N∥Δμᵢ∥₂²,(4)
    L=L_L1+λₛL_SSIM+λₚL_LPIPS+λ_offL_off,

    with λₛ=0.1, λₚ=0.5, and λ_off=0.1.

    3.2 Two-Step Causal Neural Shader

    Analytical shading of the rasterized PBR buffers {ℂₜ} is sensitive to geometry and material inaccuracies, struggling to reproduce complex light transport and fine facial details. We therefore formulate neural shading as a real-time causal video generation process, where {ℂₜ} provides view-aligned 3D geometry and intrinsic guidance, allowing the shader to focus on synthesizing photorealistic illumination and high-frequency appearance.

    Multi-modal conditioning. Built upon Wan2.1-1.3B [69], our shader adopts TAEHV [3], a compact video autoencoder with 2D convolutions and temporal memory blocks, for fast latent encoding and decoding. It integrates multi-modal conditions according to their structural roles:

    (1) Per-frame intrinsic and lighting cues: Each modality in the PBR buffers {ℂₜ} is encoded and concatenated with the noisy video latents along the channel dimension to preserve spatial alignment in latent space. For dynamic illumination control, the environment map Eₜ is represented by LDR, log-HDR, and direction maps, whose encoded features are injected via both channel concatenation and cross-attention. By associating environment-map texels with fixed 3D directions and jointly conditioning on posed-space normals Nₜ, the shader learns how incident illumination interacts with surface orientation across motion and viewpoint changes.

    (2) Global context prefixes: The static reference I is encoded as a token prefix to anchor subject identity and appearance details across the sequence. For background harmonization, the target background plate B is encoded as an additional token prefix before the reference tokens to provide scene context, while Eₜ is estimated from B at inference via DiffusionLight [53].

    Causal autoregressive distillation. To enable real-time streaming, we formulate the shader as a causal generator that synthesizes video chunks autoregressively in just two denoising steps per chunk, caching keys and values (KV) of the global context prefixes and past chunks. To inherit broad relighting priors, we distill a pre-trained multi-step bidirectional teacher (Relit-LiVE [76]) into our streamlined causal student. Specifically, we first warm up the student on teacher ODE trajectories and then apply distribution matching distillation (DMD) [86] over self-forced autoregressive student rollouts [25]. During distillation, the teacher uses its native Wan-VAE to encode intrinsic conditions obtained from DiffusionRenderer [42], including additional depth and metallic maps, and retains its original joint video–environment interface. We encode the target log-HDR environment maps with Wan-VAE and perturb both the environment and student-generated video latents to the same noise level, updating the student via DMD using only the video component of the score difference between the frozen teacher and a trainable auxiliary score model.

    Paired portrait adaptation. As the general-purpose teacher lacks domain priors for subtle facial dynamics and skin reflectance, we fine-tune the distilled shader on our paired portrait dataset (Sec. 3.3) via:

    Lₚₐᵢᵣ=λ_zLₗₐₜₑₙₜ+λ_L1L_L1+λₚL_LPIPS+λ_advL_adv,

    		(5)

    where Lₗₐₜₑₙₜ and L_L1 measure latent MSE and RGB ℓ₁ distance, and L_adv denotes a patch-based adversarial loss [26]. We set λ_z=λ_L1=1, λₚ=0.5, and λ_adv=0.01. This stage also activates the background prefix stream, unifying environment-map relighting and background harmonization within a single generator via shared illumination conditioning and distilled lighting priors. More architectural and training details are provided in the supplementary material.

    3.3 Hybrid Relighting Data Curation

    Training our framework requires dynamic portrait videos paired with intrinsic buffers and varying illumination, which are prohibitively costly to capture at scale. As illustrated in Fig. 3, we curate three complementary data sources from in-the-wild videos and static OLAT captures to jointly supervise intrinsic decomposition, authentic facial dynamics, and physically accurate light transport.

    Intrinsic and relit video synthesis. We first leverage DiffusionRenderer [42] to generate both intrinsic labels and relit video pairs. Its inverse renderer extracts temporally consistent base color, roughness, and normal maps from VFHQ [77] to supervise our Gaussian proxy (Sec. 3.1), while its forward renderer relights VFHQ clips under diverse HDR environment maps to provide paired relighting supervision for the shader.

    Reverse pair construction via reference editing. To prevent the shader from overfitting to synthetic artifacts in synthesized relit targets, we invert the pairing direction by keeping original VFHQ videos as real ground-truth targets while editing sampled reference frames. For environment-map relighting, we estimate the target HDR illumination from the initial frame via DiffusionLight [53] and relight the reference frame under random HDR maps using UniRelight [22]. For background harmonization, we employ Qwen-Image-Edit [74] to extract the clean background plate B of the original video and composite the reference portrait onto a newly synthesized background.

    Physically grounded OLAT relighting. As in-the-wild videos mainly capture facial motion under static lighting, we further introduce continuous illumination changes using public captures from FaceOLAT [59]. Exploiting the linearity of light transport, we continuously rotate HDR environment maps over 360^∘ and linearly combine the OLAT basis images at each step, yielding physically accurate relit sequences under dynamic lighting.

    4 Experiment

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Implementation details. We train our framework in two stages. First, the intrinsic Gaussian head proxy uses a frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone with a 48×48 UV query grid to predict 192×192 canonical attribute maps. It is trained on 512×512 images for 100K iterations using AdamW with a learning rate of 4×10⁻⁴ and a batch size of 64. Second, the causal video shader is distilled via 3K ODE regression and 2K DMD steps, and then fine-tuned on our hybrid dataset for 5K iterations across 32 NVIDIA H20 GPUs (batch size 32) using Muon (10⁻⁴ learning rate) and auxiliary AdamW updates (10⁻⁵). Paired adaptation uses 57-frame clips for synthesized relit videos and OLAT sequences, and 81-frame clips for reverse-paired data. At inference, we reconstruct the canonical proxy once and autoregressively generate chunks of three latent frames using two denoising steps per chunk with KV-cache reuse. To bound the attention context during streaming, self-attention accesses the current and preceding chunks together with up to two uniformly selected chunks from earlier history. More details are provided in the supplementary material.

    Datasets. Public benchmarks for head animation under dynamic illumination remain limited. Following Sec. 3.3, we construct training and held-out test sets from VFHQ [77] and FaceOLAT [59] for qualitative and quantitative evaluation. To assess cross-dataset generalization, we further conduct qualitative comparisons on NeRSemble [33], which is unseen during training.

    Baselines. We primarily evaluate single-portrait head animation jointly with relighting or background harmonization. For environment-map relighting, we compare against 2D generative models CapHuman [41], ControlFace [27], and LCVD [21], and construct cascaded baselines by pairing the 3D head animator UIKA [75] with the video relighting models UniRelight [22] or Relit-LiVE [76]. For background harmonization, we similarly pair the 2D animator Follow-Your-Emoji (FYE) [47] or UIKA with the video harmonization models RelightVid [18] or UniLumos [43]. We omit comparisons with RelightAnyone [80] and URAvatar [37] due to the lack of public implementations.

    Evaluation metrics. We measure foreground reconstruction quality via PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, identity preservation via ArcFace [12] cosine similarity (CSIM), and motion accuracy via average expression and pose distances (AED/APD). CSIM is averaged over frames with valid face detections across all methods. We benchmark inference throughput in FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 D GPU.

    4.2 Comparisons with Existing Methods

    Environment-map relighting. As shown in Fig. 4, CapHuman, ControlFace and LCVD struggle with identity preservation and lighting control. UIKA-based cascades inherit upstream deformation artifacts, as downstream video relighters are trained to preserve input structure. Moreover, their general-scene priors often yield less convincing facial shading. In contrast, our full pipeline achieves more faithful lighting responses with superior identity preservation and reconstruction quality, consistent with the metrics in Table 1. The supplementary material provides additional qualitative results for the above comparisons, as well as evaluations of direct relighting methods (3DPR [59], Lite2Relight [58], DiffusionRenderer [42], Relit-LiVE, and UniRelight) using target-pose RGB frames as input.

    Background harmonization. Figure 5 compares harmonization results on backgrounds synthesized by GPT Image 2. Under challenging illumination, both 2D and 3D cascades paired with RelightVid or UniLumos exhibit appearance distortions or unnatural shading. By sharing a common relighting prior across environment-map relighting and background harmonization, our method produces more realistic facial appearance and natural lighting effects, with quantitative results reported in the supplementary material.

    Furthermore, our method runs substantially faster than baselines, achieving 20.31 FPS on a single GPU and 26.02 FPS on two GPUs with inference optimization. Finally, since predicted target illumination on VFHQ may deviate from the true lighting, quantitative metrics alone cannot fully reflect perceptual quality. We thus provide a user study in the supplementary material.

    4.3 Ablation Studies

    Effect of training strategy and intrinsic proxy. Table 2 ablates our training strategy and intrinsic proxy on the VFHQ and FaceOLAT test sets.

    Training strategy. We compare our full training pipeline against two variants: (1) DMD-only, which evaluates the causal shader after 2K distillation steps without paired portrait adaptation, and (2) Direct SF, which fine-tunes a generic Self-Forcing initialization on our paired data, bypassing relighting distillation. Our full model consistently outperforms both variants across all metrics, confirming that distilling relighting priors and adapting to paired portrait data are both essential and complementary.

    Intrinsic proxy. We replace our full PBR buffers {ℂₜ} with three alternatives while keeping all other conditions unchanged: (1) GS-RGB, which renders standard RGB Gaussians with baked-in source lighting; (2) GS-N, which provides only our Gaussian normal maps {Nₜ}; and (3) FLAME-N, which rasterizes coarse FLAME mesh normals. GS-N and FLAME-N show mixed results on FaceOLAT, whose static portraits do not fully reflect the benefits of animated normals. These benefits are more evident on VFHQ, where GS-N outperforms FLAME-N across all metrics. Conditioning on the full PBR buffers consistently achieves the best results across all datasets, demonstrating the necessity of shading-free material cues {Aₜ,Rₜ} and fine-grained geometry {Nₜ}.

    Effect of the causal neural shader. On the unseen NeRSemble dataset (Fig. 6), the LBS-driven Gaussian proxy fails to produce expression-dependent forehead wrinkles missing from the reference image and introduces non-rigid bending along the eyeglass rims. Our neural shader leverages learned video priors to synthesize realistic dynamic wrinkles and preserve the structural rigidity of the glasses under novel illumination, generalizing effectively to unseen domains without per-subject optimization.

    Effect of hybrid training data. Fig. 7 demonstrates the complementary roles of our three training data sources. While synthesized relit videos from DiffusionRenderer provide diverse illumination supervision, removing reverse pairs visibly degrades mouth and tooth details, as real video targets are crucial for preserving high-frequency appearance and faithful motion adherence. Furthermore, incorporating static OLAT captures under rotating illumination provides physically grounded supervision for continuous lighting transitions, significantly improving dynamic shading fidelity on moving heads without requiring costly dynamic light stage captures.

    Long-sequence stability. To assess error accumulation during streaming, we evaluate five VFHQ test sequences of 982–984 frames at rollout lengths of 81, 333, and the full sequence. Shorter rollouts periodically reset the inference state between segments, whereas the full rollout streams continuously without resetting the KV cache. Table 3 shows minimal foreground degradation, with an average PSNR drop of only 0.27 dB from 81-frame to full rollouts, while the background drift largely stems from inherent camera jitter in the ground-truth VFHQ videos.

    Runtime ablation. Table 4(a) evaluates our standalone shader over 57 frames, excluding Gaussian reconstruction and rasterization. Our two-step shader takes only 4.19 s versus 556.51 s for the 50-step Relit-LiVE (132.82× speedup), while outperforming two-step variants with Wan-VAE and token concatenation by up to 18.60×. Inference optimization, detailed in the supplementary material, further cuts runtime to 2.42 s at 23.55 FPS. Table 4(b) evaluates the end-to-end dual-GPU pipeline over 984 frames, where GPU 1 performs two-step denoising while GPU 2 concurrently executes Gaussian reconstruction, rasterization, condition encoding, and latent decoding, achieving 26.02 FPS.

    5 Conclusion

    We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. By coupling an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy with a causal neural shader, our approach leverages view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers as 4D guidance to synthesize fine-scale appearance and complex light transport beyond coarse 3D representations. Heterogeneous distillation further enables low-latency autoregressive streaming, while our hybrid training strategy adapts general relighting priors to authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded lighting changes. Extensive experiments demonstrate temporally coherent, real-time head animation, relighting, and background harmonization, without requiring per-subject optimization or dynamic light stage captures.

    Acknowledgments

    We thank Zijian Wu, Qiuyu Wang, and Hao Ouyang for valuable discussions.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    This supplementary material provides architectural, training, and data-curation details (Sec. A), streaming and inference optimizations (Sec. B), additional evaluations (Sec. C), and limitations (Sec. D).

    A Architecture and Training Details

    A.1 Intrinsic Gaussian Head Proxy

    Architecture and attribute parameterization. In our canonical proxy, image-space and UV-space DINOv3 ViT-L/16 [64] token streams are fused by a 4-layer transformer (1024-dim tokens) using 48×48 learnable UV queries, and upsampled by the DPT-style decoder [56] into a 192×192×128 canonical feature map F. Gaussians are instantiated exclusively at texels within the valid FLAME UV mask [38], with base color aᵢ and roughness rᵢ bounded to [0,1] via sigmoid activations and canonical normals nᵢ normalized to unit length.

    Deformation and attribute splatting. At frame t, we deform the canonical Gaussians using FLAME [38] expression coefficients ψₜ, joint poses, and global translation tₜ. The expression basis Bₑₓₚᵣ(uᵢ) and blended skinning transform are barycentrically interpolated at each Gaussian’s UV coordinate uᵢ. Writing the latter’s linear and translation components as M_i,t∈ℝ^3×3 and d_i,t∈ℝ³, respectively, we obtain the posed center μ_i,t and unit normal n_i,t as follows:

    μ_i,t=M_i,t (μᵢ+Bₑₓₚᵣ(uᵢ)ψₜ)+d_i,t+tₜ,(S1)
    n_i,t=(M_i,tnᵢ)/(∥M_i,tnᵢ∥₂),

    while (sᵢ,qᵢ,αᵢ,aᵢ,rᵢ) remain shared across frames. Under the target camera πₜ, we render each PBR buffer using 3DGS [30]. Its value Cₜ(x) at pixel x is obtained by alpha-compositing the corresponding Gaussian attributes c_i,t from front to back:

    Cₜ(x)=∑_i∈ℕ(x)α̃_i,t(x)T_i,t(x) c_i,t+T_bg,t(x) b.

    		(S2)

    Here, ℕ(x) indexes the contributing Gaussians in depth order, and α̃_i,t(x) is the projected opacity of Gaussian i. The transmittance before Gaussian i is T_i,t(x)=∏_j

    A.2 Causal Neural Shader

    Latent grid and multi-modal conditioning. The frozen TAEHV autoencoder [3] applies 8× spatial downsampling and 4× temporal compression into a 16-channel latent space (mapping 57- and 81-frame RGB clips to 15 and 21 latent frames), which our Wan2.1-1.3B [69] backbone generates autoregressively in 3-frame latent chunks. In the channel-concatenation branch, the three PBR buffers and three illumination maps (LDR, log-HDR, and 3D direction maps) are independently encoded at the input video scale into six spatially aligned 16-channel latents and concatenated with the 16-channel noisy video latent, forming a 112-channel patch-embedding input without increasing the video token count. In the parallel environment cross-attention branch, the three lighting maps are spatially downsampled before 8× autoencoder compression and 2× strided projection into compact lighting context tokens concatenated with a fixed empty-prompt embedding from the frozen text encoder. Reference and background latents are separately projected into spatial token grids with the same feature dimension as video tokens, increasing sequence length without changing the 112-channel video input. With a background prefix, BG and reference occupy the first two temporal positions, and video RoPE indices and KV-cache offsets are shifted accordingly. Chunk-causal attention allows video tokens to access both prefixes and available video history, while excluding future chunks.

    A.3 Heterogeneous Distillation

    Table S1 summarizes the teacher–student interface differences. The student uses TAEHV for condition encoding, while the Relit-LiVE teacher [76] and auxiliary score model retain Wan-VAE. Since TAEHV is compatible with the Wan video latent space, student-generated video latents can be evaluated directly by both score models.

    ODE warm-up. From precomputed multi-step teacher ODE trajectories, we independently sample a trajectory state for each 3-frame latent chunk. Given a noisy state from the teacher’s ODE trajectory, the student predicts the trajectory’s clean terminal video latent, conditioned on proxy-rendered PBR buffers, the reference portrait, and target illumination. We minimize latent MSE between the prediction and this target.

    Distribution matching. Following DMD [86] and Self-Forcing [25], clean video latents ẑ from self-forced student rollouts are perturbed into noisy latents z_σ at a sampled noise level σ:

    z_σ=(1-σ)ẑ+σε, ε∼ℕ(0,I).

    		(S3)

    Here, ε denotes standard Gaussian noise and I is the identity covariance matrix. To match the teacher’s joint video–environment input, we encode the target log-HDR environment maps with Wan-VAE and perturb the resulting latent at the same noise level σ. Both the frozen teacher and the trainable auxiliary score model receive the noisy video and environment latents, together with the full set of intrinsic conditions extracted by DiffusionRenderer [42]. We convert their video flow predictions into clean-latent estimates ẑ_T (teacher) and ẑ_φ (auxiliary model with parameters φ), and update the student via the surrogate loss:

    g=(ẑ_φ-ẑ_T)/(\tfrac1M∥ẑ-ẑ_T∥₁),(S4)
    L_DMD=𝔼 [(1)/(2|I|)∥ẑ_I-sg[ẑ_I-g_I]∥₂²].

    Here, g is the normalized DMD gradient signal and M is the number of scalar entries per video latent sample. The set I indexes gradient-bearing rollout entries, |I| is their count, subscripts I select these entries, and sg[·] denotes the stop-gradient operator. The expectation averages over conditioning samples, student rollouts, noise levels, and Gaussian noise. The auxiliary model is updated via flow matching on detached noisy student rollouts.

    A.4 Paired Portrait Adaptation

    Patch adversarial supervision. For L_adv, we apply a spectral-normalized 2D PatchGAN discriminator D[26] to all decoded RGB frames using the hinge objective:

    L_D=𝔼[\max(0,1-D(Y))](S5)
    +𝔼[\max(0,1+D(Ŷ))],
    L_adv=-𝔼[D(Ŷ)],

    where L_D is the discriminator loss, Y and Ŷ are real and generated frames, and expectations average over video frames and spatial patches.

    A.5 Training Data and Model Selection

    Data composition. For paired portrait adaptation, we use 1,000 synthesized relit video records, 40,355 reverse-constructed environment-map relighting pairs, 41,777 reverse-constructed background harmonization pairs, and 55,840 OLAT relit sequences. These pools are sampled with weights of 5%, 45%, 20%, and 30%, respectively. Synthesized relit and OLAT clips contain 57 frames, while reverse-constructed clips contain 81 frames.

    Data use across training stages. The intrinsic Gaussian proxy is trained on 46,795 VFHQ clip groups using original RGB frames and DiffusionRenderer intrinsic pseudo-labels. ODE warm-up and DMD use VFHQ clips with sampled HDR environment maps. The student receives proxy-rendered PBR buffers, while the teacher and auxiliary score model use DiffusionRenderer intrinsics. ODE warm-up learns from teacher-generated trajectories, whereas DMD transfers the teacher’s relighting prior without paired relit RGB targets. For paired adaptation, the student continues to use proxy-rendered PBR buffers and is supervised by synthesized relit videos, original videos from reverse-constructed pairs, and OLAT relit sequences.

    Teacher selection. Relit-LiVE generally produces softer, more natural facial lighting. DiffusionRenderer is more prone to producing an overly specular, metallic appearance on faces. We therefore use Relit-LiVE as the distillation teacher to transfer its broad relighting prior to our shader. However, Relit-LiVE may miss subtle expression changes, so we use DiffusionRenderer to synthesize paired relit targets that better preserve the source video’s facial motion. We visually inspect the synthesized relit videos before including them in the training set.

    Reference editing for reverse pairs. The edited reference should replace the original illumination, including its cast shadows, while the original video remains the real target. In our experience, UniRelight [22] achieves more pronounced and realistic lighting changes than Qwen-Image-Edit [74], reducing residual source shading that would weaken relighting supervision. We therefore use UniRelight for environment-map reference editing. For background pairs, we favor Qwen-Image-Edit for its clean background extraction and coherent joint editing of backgrounds and portrait lighting. Since these edits can alter identity, we use ArcFace [12] cosine similarity to flag potential identity changes, followed by visual review to exclude failed edits.

    B Streaming and Inference Optimization

    Bounded attention context. To keep attention cost bounded during streaming, each chunk attends to itself, its immediate predecessor, and up to two uniformly spaced chunks from the earlier history. The reference and optional background prefixes remain accessible throughout generation and do not count toward this four-chunk budget. Numbering chunks from 1, we select m=\min(2,k-2) earlier chunks for the current chunk k>2, with indices:

    hⱼ=1+⌊((j+\tfrac12)(k-2))/(m)⌋, j=0,…,m-1,

    		(S6)

    where hⱼ is the index of the j-th selected history chunk and ⌊·⌋ denotes the floor operation. For the first two chunks, all available video chunks are used. Selected chunks retain their original temporal indices under RoPE.

    After the two denoising steps, we run a clean-latent forward pass to cache the completed chunk’s keys and values for subsequent chunks, following Self-Forcing [25]. This extra pass can be skipped for the final chunk of the sequence.

    Condition caching and kernel fusion. We compute reference, optional background, and empty-prompt text projections once per stream and cache them across chunks. For each chunk, we compute lighting projections and joint text–lighting cross-attention K/V once, sharing them across the two denoising steps and the clean-latent KV update. We also fuse QKV projections, RoPE, AdaLN modulation, and gated residual updates using torch.compile and custom CUDA kernels.

    Exact tiered KV management. Historical chunks may be selected again by Eq. (S6), so their KV states must remain available until their last use. Since this selection depends only on chunk indices, we can determine cache lifetimes without accessing future frames. For short clips of known length, we precompute the access schedule and recycle GPU slots after each chunk’s last use. For long streams, inactive KV blocks are offloaded to CPU memory and reloaded on demand, keeping GPU memory bounded. Under our selection rule, chunk i can be discarded once generation advances beyond chunk 4i+1, independently of the final sequence length. These storage operations preserve the BF16 cache values and the selected attention context.

    C Additional Evaluation

    C.1 Environment-Map Relighting

    Figure S1 presents additional qualitative comparisons with the joint animation-and-relighting baselines from the main paper. Across varied identities and target illumination, our method better preserves facial appearance and produces more plausible directional shading while following the driving expressions.

    C.2 Direct Environment-Map Relighting

    Table S2 compares LuxAvatar with five direct relighting baselines: 3DPR [59], Lite2Relight [58], DiffusionRenderer [42], Relit-LiVE [76], and UniRelight [22]. These baselines receive target-pose RGB frames as input. For DiffusionRenderer and Relit-LiVE, we first use DiffusionRenderer’s inverse rendering model to extract intrinsic buffers from these frames for subsequent relighting. LuxAvatar instead synthesizes both target head motion and novel illumination from a single reference portrait. Figure S3 provides qualitative comparisons.

    Despite the baselines’ access to target-pose RGB frames, LuxAvatar performs best in PSNR, LPIPS, CSIM, and AED on both benchmarks. With inference optimization, LuxAvatar achieves approximately 6–360× the FPS of these baselines. In particular, paired portrait adaptation substantially improves facial shading fidelity and color accuracy over general-scene video relighting methods, especially on physically captured FaceOLAT sequences.

    C.3 Background Harmonization

    In our harmonization comparison against two-stage cascades (Follow-Your-Emoji (FYE) [47] or UIKA [75] followed by RelightVid [18] or UniLumos [43]), the driven video from each animation method is shared across both downstream harmonization methods under identical source, motion, and background inputs. We evaluate on VFHQ test clips, following the evaluation protocol detailed in the main paper. As shown in Table S3, LuxAvatar outperforms all four cascades across reconstruction, identity, and motion metrics. Figure S2 provides additional qualitative comparisons across diverse target backgrounds.

    C.4 Training Strategy and Intrinsic Proxy

    Figure S4 complements the quantitative ablations in the main paper. DMD-only loses fine facial details, while Direct SF and the normal-only variants show discrepancies in eye appearance and shadows around the nose. Our full model better preserves these details under target lighting.

    C.5 Long-Sequence Stability

    Figure S5 shows cross-reenactment over continuous 984-frame rollouts. We animate the same reference identity using another subject’s FLAME motion and camera parameters under two fixed environment maps, generating each sequence without resetting the KV cache. The displayed frames retain consistent identity and distinct lighting while following changes in the driving expression.

    C.6 User Study

    We evaluate 20 video cases: 10 for environment-map relighting with six methods and 10 for background harmonization with five methods. The interface displays synchronized, looping videos alongside the reference portrait, driving video, and target illumination or background. Case order and anonymous method labels are randomized for each session. For each case, respondents rank all methods from best to worst, without ties, on overall visual quality, lighting or background consistency, and identity preservation.

    Table S4 summarizes mean ranks over 21 completed questionnaires, with the two tasks evaluated separately. LuxAvatar achieves the lowest mean rank for overall visual quality, lighting or background consistency, and identity preservation in both tasks.

    D Limitations

    Two aspects of LuxAvatar remain to be addressed in future work. The FLAME-driven proxy lacks an explicit tongue model, so tongue motions such as protrusion cannot be directly controlled. In addition, our training data lack multi-view coverage of the entire head, leaving the geometry and appearance of the back of the head underconstrained and limiting reliable synthesis of rear views.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：既要三维可控，又要复杂的面部光传输——这两件事被拆给两个组件。

要点：

  • 任务：从单张肖像出发，做**实时**的头部 avatar 动画与重打光
  • 分解方式：把合成拆成**可动画的三维本征高斯代理**与一个**因果自回归神经着色器**；代理负责**解耦标准几何与反射属性**，并把形变后的高斯**快速光栅化成视角与运动一致的 PBR 缓冲**
  • 着色器再基于这些本征缓冲做因果的神经着色，从而拿到复杂面部光传输

为什么值得看：按 11-12 定下的 B4 细则：**高斯的「表示改进」不收，重打光的「管线能力」收**。这条属于后者——高斯只是本征代理，真正的新东西是「光栅化出 PBR 缓冲 + 因果神经着色」这条实时重打光管线。

中文摘要：LuxAvatar 提出一个前馈框架，能从单张肖像出发，实时生成可动画、可重打光的头部 avatar。为实现三维可控性与复杂面部光传输，它把合成任务分解为两部分：一个可动画的三维本征高斯代理，以及一个因果自回归神经着色器。代理负责解耦标准几何与反射属性，并把形变后的高斯快速光栅化为视角与运动一致的 PBR 缓冲；神经着色器则在这些本征缓冲之上做因果着色，从而再现复杂的面部光传输。按现行判定，这类工作的价值不在「高斯表示更好」，而在实时重打光这条管线能力本身。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

LuxAvatar: Real-Time Relightable Head Avatars via Causal Neural Shading of 3D Intrinsic Proxies

Abstract

We present LuxAvatar, a feed-forward framework for real-time head avatar animation and relighting from a single portrait. To achieve both 3D controllability and complex facial light transport, we factorize avatar synthesis into an animatable 3D intrinsic Gaussian proxy and a causal autoregressive neural shader. This proxy disentangles canonical geometry and reflectance attributes, rapidly rasterizing deformed Gaussians into view- and motion-consistent PBR buffers. Conditioned on these buffers, our neural shader formulates forward rendering as a conditional video diffusion process, bypassing explicit PBR computation to synthesize realistic shading effects under target illumination. We achieve real-time streaming through heterogeneous distillation from a pretrained multi-step bidirectional relighting teacher to a two-step causal autoregressive neural shader, inheriting broad synthetic lighting priors while minimizing conditioning and decoding latency. To further specialize these priors to human heads, we construct a hybrid relighting dataset for domain-specific fine-tuning, capturing authentic facial dynamics and physically grounded light transport. Extensive experiments show that our framework enables 3D-controllable, real-time portrait animation and relighting, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity, motion control, and lighting accuracy.
