一句话：自回归方法一个网格要几十到几百秒；扩散/流式方法快，但网格达不到美术级。

要点：

  • 要的目标很明确：把稠密三维物体变成**艺术级网格（artist mesh）**——紧凑、以四边形为主、易于编辑
  • 两难：当前多数方法是**自回归**的，逐 token 解码，**一个网格要几十到几百秒**；而**扩散与流式生成**快得多，但产出的网格仍达不到美术级质量
  • PostMesh 因此做**面向流式/扩散艺术网格生成的后训练**方法（自称首个），用自奖励的偏好后训练把质量补上

为什么值得看：「能编辑」比「面数少」更值钱：四边面为主的网格是美术真正能改的东西。把后训练用在流式生成器上，等于在保住速度的同时拿到可用性——这对生成式资产进生产管线是关键一步。

中文摘要：艺术级网格生成器的目标，是把稠密的三维物体转换成一个「美术网格」：紧凑、以四边形为主、并且易于编辑。当前多数方法采用自回归形式，逐 token 解码，每个网格需要数十到数百秒；而基于扩散与流的生成器虽然快得多，产出的网格在美术质量上却仍有欠缺。PostMesh 因此提出一种面向扩散/流式艺术网格生成的后训练方法（作者称其为首个），借助自奖励的偏好后训练来补齐质量差距。对生成式资产进生产管线而言，关键不只是速度快，而是产出的网格真的能被美术改动。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

PostMesh: Self-Rewarded Preference Post-Training
for Flow-Based Artist Mesh Generation

Abstract

Artistic mesh generators turn a dense 3D object into an artist mesh: a compact, quad-dominant mesh that is easy to edit. Most of current models are auto-regressive methods which decode a mesh token by token, take tens to hundreds of seconds per mesh. Diffusion- and flow-based generators are much faster, but their meshes still fall short of artist quality. To our knowledge, PostMesh is the first post-training method for a diffusion- or flow-based artist mesh generator, and it needs no expensive artist-made ground truth: the generator is trained on its own samples, scored by a reward computed from the dense input and the output. We propose an artistic mesh reward that keeps the output consistent with the dense input while making the mesh structure into artistic. We also propose a multi-negative flow preference optimisation that transfers the reward to the generator. After a short LoRA post-training, PostMesh is comparable to or better than slow autoregressive generators on most artist-mesh quality metrics and in a blind VLM preference test, at a fraction of their time (2.53 s against 26.98–471.84 s per mesh).

††footnotetext: †Work done outside Amazon.

1 Introduction

Artist meshes are compact, quad-dominant and laid out in edge loops, which makes them easy to edit, rig and texture. Artists build them by hand, so they are hard and expensive to make.

Recently, there has been model-based approaches which automate artistic mesh creation. PolyGen [22] generates the vertices and then the faces of a mesh with transformers, and MeshGPT [26] encodes faces as learned tokens and decodes them one at a time. Later autoregressive (AR) models condition on the input shape and shorten the token sequence: MeshAnything [3] turns a point cloud of a shape into an artist mesh, MeshAnything V2 [4] represents a face by a single vertex token wherever possible, Mesh Silksong [27] layers and orders the vertices so that each is tokenised only once, and FastMesh [12] generates only the vertices autoregressively and predicts all faces in one pass. The above methods follows auto-regressive (AR) approach which decodes one token at a time. Although these methods can generate high-quality artist meshes, but generating one token at a time makes them expensive and slow.

Diffusion- and flow-based generators instead produce the whole mesh in parallel. PolyDiff [1] denoises a quantised triangle soup by discrete diffusion, TriFlow [13] predicts nearest-vertex vector fields by latent flow matching, and MeshFlow [15] compresses an artist mesh, its vertices and connectivity, into a compact per-vertex latent with a MeshVAE. In MeshFlow, a rectified-flow transformer conditioned on the input shape generates all latent tokens at once, and the MeshVAE decoder turns them into vertices and faces. Because the whole latent is generated in a fixed number of denoising steps instead of token by token, these models are much faster than auto-regressive approaches. Despite their speed, their meshes still fall short of the best AR models, with long, thin triangles (Fig.1) and fragmented parts, so there is room for improvement. These defects live in the decoded mesh, which the flow-matching loss never sees.

For AR models, much of the recent progress came from post-training with preference optimisation or reinforcement learning (RL) on the token likelihood: DeepMesh [34] and Mesh-RFT [17] use Direct Preference Optimization, QuadGPT [18] use tDPO and Mesh-Pro [36] use online RL-based training. Reward and preference optimisation have also been applied to dense 3D generators [33, 14, 37, 23], whose output is an implicit field or an iso-surface. However, to our knowledge, no diffusion- or flow-based artist-mesh generator has been post-trained in this way. Collecting more artist meshes is expensive, and training the flow model on its own best samples helps less: imitating them (RAFT [7]) made outputs more fragmented in our study (Tab.2), and in our ablations, fine-tuning on the reward-selected samples with the flow-matching loss alone loses most of the quad-structure gain of preference optimisation (Sec.4.5). We therefore post-train the generator without ground truth artist meshes, delivering a reward to it directly through preference optimisation.

PostMesh is the first post-training method for a diffusion- or flow-based artist-mesh generator, and its artistic mesh reward is the first reward for such a generator that keeps the output consistent with the dense input while steering it toward the structure of artist meshes, without any artist mesh. For training, we propose a gating algorithm which also rejects samples with more flipped faces than their group, turns each group of samples into one winning and several weighted losing samples. Also we use multi-negative flow preference optimisation, Diffusion-DPO [30] with several losing samples and an RPO likelihood term [19], transfers the reward to the generator. Our contributions are:

  • •

    To our knowledge, the first post-training of a diffusion- or flow-based artist-mesh generator, done by self-training on its own samples without any artist mesh.

  • •

    We propose an artistic mesh reward, to our knowledge the first for guiding the generated mesh to be consistent with the dense input and follows artist-mesh structure: silhouette IoU and depth agreement on renders to keep the shape consistency, and quad strips and tessellation, slivers, vertex valence, tiny and stray components and a face-count bound reward for artist-preferred mesh generation.

  • •

    A gating algorithm and a multi-negative flow preference optimisation that turn the reward into weighted winning and losing samples and transfer it to a flow model.

    • Overall, PostMesh is better than or comparable to slow autoregressive generators on most artist-mesh quality metrics and in a blind VLM preference test, and it is far more efficient in time.

    2 Related Work

    Autoregressive artist-mesh generation.

    Beyond the models above, AR work has mostly restructured the token sequence: MeshXL [2] trains large transformers on coordinate sequences, BPT [32] shortens them by block-wise indexing and patches of faces, EdgeRunner [29] compresses meshes into shorter token sequences, Meshtron [8] trains an hourglass transformer on truncated sequences to reach much larger meshes, and QuadGPT [18] generates quads natively. All decode sequentially, so cost grows with face count.

    Diffusion and flow artist-mesh generation.

    Besides PolyDiff, TriFlow and MeshFlow, MeshCraft [9] runs a flow transformer over VAE face latents for a chosen face count, PolyFlow [31] denoises continuous per-vertex embeddings from which the connectivity is recovered, and LATO [35] encodes vertices and connectivity in a joint sparse-voxel latent, which LATO.2 [20] factorises into a vertex flow followed by a connectivity flow. Our base model is the MeshFlow of Li et al., unrelated to the equivariant MeshFlow of Sun et al.[28]. To our knowledge, none of these reports an RL or preference post-training stage.

    Post-training generative models.

    DPO [25] optimises pairwise preferences without a reward model, and RPO [19, 24] adds a likelihood term on the preferred sample. Diffusion-DPO [30] uses the denoising error of a re-noised sample as the likelihood, Flow-GRPO [16] turns the ODE sampler of a flow model into an SDE to apply GRPO, and RAFT [7] fine-tunes on reward-ranked samples. In 3D, DreamReward [33] learns a human-preference reward for text-to-3D, DSO [14] aligns a 3D generator with feedback from a physics simulator, and concurrent DHO [37] (online RL) and Flow3D-OPD [23] (distillation from DPO teachers) post-train flow-matching generators of iso-surfaced dense geometry. Artist-mesh post-training so far is autoregressive and acts on token likelihoods (Sec.1); Mesh-RFT [17], for instance, uses face-masked DPO with a topology score. Our policy instead is a flow model with no token likelihood, behind a frozen, non-differentiable decoder. To our knowledge, PostMesh is the first to post-train a diffusion- or flow-based artist-mesh generator.

    3 Method

    3.1 Problem and Overview

    MeshFlow [15] encodes an artist mesh as a per-vertex latent z₀. A rectified-flow transformer v_θ(z_σ,σ,c) predicts ε-z₀ along z_σ=(1-σ)z₀+σε, conditioned on surface samples c of a dense input mesh I. A frozen decoder turns z₀ into vertices, edges and 3-clique faces, so topology defects appear only after decoding, out of sight of the flow-matching loss. We improve the model by self-training: it learns only from its own samples, and no artist mesh is added to the training data, the rewards or the selection of winning and losing samples. We train LoRA adapters [11] upon pretrained flow model.

    Training pipeline.

    For each dense input, the model draws a group of samples (16 in our setting). Each sample is decoded and scored by the artistic mesh reward. A gating algorithm then picks the best plausible sample as the winner and turns clearly worse or implausible samples into weighted losing samples, and the preference loss raises the likelihood of the winner under the model relative to the losers (Fig.3). Each round repeats this on fresh inputs with the updated model.

    3.2 Artistic Mesh Reward

    An artist mesh should (i) follow the shape of the dense input and (ii) have the structure artists need: quads laid out in edge loops, no needle-like triangles, no poles, no specks or stray pieces, and a sensible face budget. Since we do not have artist mesh for training, we score (i) against renders of the input and (ii) on the output alone. Figure2 shows each term on real training pairs. For the two input-consistency terms we render the output O and I from fixed views in the frame of I. Per view, S_O,S_I are the silhouettes and d_O,d_I the depths, and scores are averaged over views.

    3.2.1 Silhouette IoU

    tₛᵢₗ scores the intersection over union of the silhouettes,

    IoU=|S_O∩S_I| / |S_O∪S_I|.

    		(1)

    Without an artist mesh, the outline of the dense input is the most direct evidence of what the output must contain. A missing part, such as a chair leg or a handle, or an extra blob changes the outline in some view and lowers the IoU. Although it makes strong shape consistency between dense inputs and outputs, there is clear limit that it sees nothing inside the outline, such as offsets or flipped faces, which is why additional reward is required to complements it.

    3.2.2 Depth Agreement

    t_depth scores the mean depth difference where both silhouettes cover a pixel, in units of the bounding-box diagonal,

    depth_L1=\tfrac1|S_O∩S_I|∑_p∈S_O∩S_I|d_O(p)-d_I(p)|,

    		(2)

    where the p is render from generated mesh within silhouette intersection. Two meshes can share every outline while one has surfaces pushed in or out: a sunken seat, a bulging side, a part of the wrong thickness. The depth maps reveal these offsets. Together with silhouette IoU, depth agreement forms the shape constraint rewards. Because the two terms compares renders, not surfaces, they do not prefer any triangulation or mesh structure.

    3.2.3 Quad Strips & Tessellation

    Artists build meshes from quads arranged in edge loops, which makes selection, UV unwrapping, subdivision and deformation predictable. Both terms first merge adjacent triangle pairs into quads: a pair merges if its two triangles are within 10^∘ of coplanar and their union is a convex quad with all corners in [45^∘,135^∘], greedily in decreasing order of the smallest corner of the quad. Let ℚ be the merged quads and T the triangles left over.

    Quad strips. Stepping from a quad across one of its sides into the neighbouring quad, and on across the opposite side, traces a strip; it ends at a triangle, a boundary or a non-manifold edge, and a strip that closes on itself is a ring. Each quad lies on two strips, one per pair of opposite sides. With Π the set of strips, t_QS scores the quad score

    QS=\tfrac1|ℚ||{q∈π: π∈Π a ring or |π|≥4}|,

    		(3)

    the share of quads on a ring or on a strip of at least four quads, inspired by the quad rings and lines of QuadGPT [18] and Mesh-Pro [36]. It rewards quads that continue into edge loops, so a mesh can have many quads and still a low QS if they are scattered among triangles.

    Tessellation.t_TS scores the Mesh-RFT topology score [17],

    TS=0.4 τ₁+0.2 τ₂+0.3 τ₃+0.1 τ₄,

    		(4)

    with the quad ratio τ₁=|ℚ|/(|ℚ|+|T|), the right-angle score τ₂=1-\tfrac1|ℚ|∑_q∑ₖ₌₁⁴|θ_q,k-90^∘|/360^∘ over the corners θ_q,k of each quad, a score for equal opposite sides and side lengths (τ₃) and one for similar shapes of neighbouring quads (τ₄). Exact definitions are in AppendixD.

    TS thus rewards quads that are well shaped where they are (limited on neighboring mesh connectivity) , and QS measures how well quads continue into strips and rings (larger set mesh connectivity check). Both terms are blind to shape, which is why they are paired with silhouette IoU and depth agreement.

    3.2.4 Sliver Triangles

    tₛₗᵢᵥₑᵣ scores the area share of needle-like triangles that were not merged into quads,

    sₛₗᵢᵥₑᵣ=∑_f∈T, α_f<5^∘A_f /∑_f∈FA_f,

    		(5)

    with F all triangles of O, A_f the area and α_f the smallest corner of triangle f. Such needle-like triangles shade badly, cannot become part of a quad layout, and make editing and subdivision unstable; Fig.1 shows them on outputs of the pretrained model. The term measures sliver area rather than a count, so long slivers that run across a surface cost more than a few tiny ones.

    3.2.5 Vertex Valence

    tᵥₐₗ scores the share of vertices with extreme valence \deg(v), the number of edges at v,

    sᵥₐₗ=|{v∈V:\deg(v)≤2 or \deg(v)≥10}| / |V|,

    		(6)

    with V the vertices that have at least one edge. A vertex with 10 or more edges is a pole, typically the hub of a fan of thin triangles. A vertex with at most 2 edges belongs to a single triangle, a loose corner. Both interrupt edge loops, pinch the surface under subdivision and deform badly when the mesh is animated. Artists do place some poles, for example at corners, so only extreme valences are penalised.

    3.2.6 Tiny & Stray Components

    t_frag-n scores \log(1+n_tiny), with n_tiny the number of components with at most 4 faces, and t_frag-stray scores s_stray, the area share of stray components, those that cover less than 1% of the surface and have a boundary edge or at most 4 faces. Together they prevent specks and floating pieces, which an artist must find and delete by hand and which renders show only as hairline cracks. The two terms complement each other: the count reacts to many specks even when their area is negligible, and the area reacts to a few larger stray pieces. Fusing real parts is not rewarded: artist meshes are multi-part, and the gating algorithm rejects samples with far fewer real parts than their group.

    3.2.7 Face Count Bound

    With F the face count of the output and Fₜ a target predicted from the input,

    r_fc=clip(1-|\log₂(F/Fₜ)|/b, 0, 1),

    		(7)

    which is 1 at the target and falls on both sides within a band of width b. Because the score is on a log scale, twice the target face count costs as much as half of it. It keeps the face budget sensible: it stops the policy from shedding faces, which training did without it, and from copying the dense input.

    Overall reward.

    Each term except r_dens maps its raw score linearly to [0,1] between two fixed anchors. The reward is the weighted sum of all terms,

    r=λₛᵢₗtₛᵢₗ+λ_deptht_depth+λ_QSt_QS+λ_TSt_TS(8)
    +λₛₗᵢᵥₑᵣtₛₗᵢᵥₑᵣ+λᵥₐₗtᵥₐₗ+λ_tinyt_frag-n
    +λ_strayt_frag-stray+λ_Fr_fc,

    with weights λ that sum to 1 (values in AppendixC).

    3.3 Gating Algorithm

    The gating algorithm turns a group of scored samples into preferences. Its rules compare each sample with the other samples of the same input, so they adapt to how hard that input is. A sample fails a gate if it is implausible relative to its group: its Chamfer or Hausdorff distance to I is far above the group median, it has more flipped faces or more tiny components than the group, it has far fewer real parts, or it fails to decode. The winning sample w is the best gate-passing sample under r. The losing samples are every gate-failed sample, with weight 1 whatever its reward, and every gate-passing sample clearly below w, by more than half a group standard deviation. Finally, a pair is dropped if w is worse than the losing sample in fidelity to I, coverage of I, face count or centring, so that no preference teaches the model to trade these away. Figure4 shows a real group of training samples. Detailed thresholds and gating alrogithm criteria are in AppendixB.

    3.4 Preference Loss

    Each kept pair compares w with a losing sample lⱼ of the same input.

    3.4.1 Flow-Matching Error as a Likelihood Proxy

    The loss should make the model more likely to produce w than lⱼ, but a flow model gives no cheap, differentiable likelihood of a finished mesh. As in Diffusion-DPO [30], we re-noise the latent z₀ of the finished sample and measure how well the model denoises it; a lower error means the model finds the sample more likely. The error, averaged over latent entries, stands in for the negative log-likelihood:

    ℓ_θ(z₀)=\tfrac1|z₀|∥v_θ(z_σ,σ,c)-(ε-z₀)∥²,

    		(9)

    with one (ε,σ) per input shared by w and its losing samples, so that differences come from the samples, not the noise.

    3.4.2 Margin Against the Frozen Reference

    The margin asks one question: has fine-tuning made the model better at producing w than at producing lⱼ? Each error is measured against the same error ℓ_ref of the frozen pretrained MeshFlow,

    dⱼ=(ℓ_θ(w)-ℓ_ref(w))-(ℓ_θ(lⱼ)-ℓ_ref(lⱼ)).

    		(10)

    dⱼ<0 when the policy improved its fit to w more than its fit to lⱼ. Because only the genuine change is considered during training, a sample that was easy for the model from the start does not contribute to the training.

    3.4.3 Multi-Negative Weighting

    Instead of one pair per input, every losing sample of the group contributes, and its weight ωⱼ says how bad it is:

    L_DPO=∑ⱼωⱼ φ(dⱼ)/∑ⱼωⱼ,

    		(11)

    with φ a soft loss on the preference margin (defined below). A gate-passing losing sample weighs its reward gap to w divided by the largest gap in the group, so a clearly worse sample pushes harder than a near-tie. A gate-failed one weighs ωⱼ=1, because failing a gate is not a matter of degree. Using several losing samples draws more signal from each group than a single pair; when an input has many, each update uses a random subset, redrawn every update.

    3.4.4 The Scale β and the Log-Sigmoid

    Each losing sample contributes φ(d)=softplus(\tfracβ2d)=-\logsigmoid(-\tfracβ2d). This turns the margin into a soft classification loss: it costs little once w is clearly preferred and grows linearly when lⱼ is preferred, and β sets how sharp that switch is (value in AppendixH).

    3.4.5 RPO Term on the Winning Sample

    The DPO term only looks at the gap between w and lⱼ, so it can be satisfied by letting both errors rise, as long as the error of the losers rises more. The RPO term [19, 24] keeps the winner itself likely by penalising ℓ_θ(w) directly. The per-input loss, averaged over the inputs of an update, with RPO weight γ, is

    L=L_DPO+γ ℓ_θ(w).

    		(12)

    Without the RPO term (DPO only), one training run gave an inconclusive result, so its benefit is not established.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Setup

    Training.

    Training objects come from Objaverse [6] with at most 100k faces. Training inputs come from a 2,000-object pool disjoint from evaluation. We run two rounds of self-training, updating only the LoRA adapters. At each training round, we use 1000 training iterations with 1000 object data. After one training round we use new batch of 1,000 inputs and apply same training protocol to the previous round. More detailes are in AppendixA.

    Test Data.

    For testing and evaluation of the post-trained model, we chose another batch of 300 dense objects randomly collected from Objaverse with proper face count band. For ablation study, we selected another independent batch of 200 objects from Objaverse dataset. The test objects have corresponding artist meshes.

    Metrics.

    Table1 measures fidelity against the artist mesh, topology after the quad merge of Sec.3.2.3. For details, see AppendixD.

  • •

    CD, HD (×100): Chamfer and Hausdorff distance between points sampled on the output and on the artist mesh, the average and the worst-case shape error.

  • •

    ECD[5]: Chamfer distance between points sampled on sharp edges of the two meshes, i.e., how well creases are kept.

  • •

    QS: share of merged quads on a ring or a strip of ≥4 quads, i.e., continuous edge flow (Eq.3).

  • •

    TS[17]: Mesh-RFT score of quad share, right angles, even sides and like neighbours (Eq.4).

  • •

    DFF: area share of defect faces (on a boundary or non-manifold edge, self-intersecting, degenerate or in a stray fragment), i.e., what an artist must repair.

  • •

    Frag.: share of outputs with at least 5 more small components (under 1% of the area) than the artist mesh.

  • •

    SI(×100): share of faces that self-intersect after two levels of Loop subdivision.

  • •

    NME(×100): share of edges shared by more than two faces, which half-edge structures and many tools do not accept.

  • •

    UVΔ: absolute difference to the artist mesh in UV charts per 1k faces after the same automatic unwrap.

  • •

    Faces: mean face count; s/mesh: seconds per mesh on one L40S GPU.

    • Baselines.

    We compare with autoregressive artist-mesh generators that take a dense mesh: MeshAnything [3], MeshAnything V2 [4], Mesh Silksong [27] and FastMesh [12], which decodes vertices autoregressively and faces in one pass. MeshFlow [15], our base model, is the only flow-based one.

    4.2 Quantitative Results

    Table1 compares all methods on the 300 test objects. Against the autoregressive generators, PostMesh has the lowest mean CD and HD of all methods. FastMesh and Mesh Silksong have higher CD and HD than both MeshFlow and PostMesh, which indicates that our outputs keep the shape of the dense input well. For ECD, Mesh Silksong and FastMesh are better than MeshFlow and PostMesh. We conjecture that this is because they generate several times more faces (2344 and 12490 against 728 for PostMesh), which makes sharp edges easier to keep. Against the two MeshAnything models, whose face counts are close to ours, MeshFlow and PostMesh are clearly better on all three shape-consistency metrics (CD, HD and ECD).

    On mesh topology measurement, PostMesh has the highest QS of all methods, and its TS is on par with that of Mesh Silksong, above that of FastMesh and slightly below that of both MeshAnything models. Compared with our main baseline MeshFlow, our Post-trained model shows meaningful improvements in both of QS and TS scores.

    In terms of defective mesh scores, PostMesh has a lower DFF than FastMesh and both MeshAnything models, but slightly higher one than Mesh Silksong. For fragmentation score, ours has similar score to MeshAnything v2, but worse than MeshAnything and Mesh Silksong. However, similar to our topology score cases, our post-trained model can clearly reduce the defective meshes compared to our main baseline MeshFlow.

    Over its base model, PostMesh improves QS, TS, DFF and fragmentation at slightly lower CD and HD, with more faces. Because QS, TS and DFF partly overlap with our reward terms, we also measure, on the same outputs, properties that no reward term computes: robustness to Loop subdivision, non-manifold edges and automatic UV unwrapping. PostMesh improves over MeshFlow overall on these as well: after subdivision it has about half the flipped and self-intersecting faces, it has less than half the non-manifold edges, and its UV unwrapping is slightly better. More experiments are in AppendixF.

    The most important practical difference is speed: PostMesh keeps the cost per mesh of MeshFlow, below that of the autoregressive models.

    4.3 Blind VLM Preference Test

    QS and TS are reward terms, so better scores on them could reflect the reward rather than better meshes, and a check that does not use them is needed. A study with professional artists would be the natural check but is too costly at this scale. We therefore gave a strong vision-language model, Claude Opus 5.5, explicit artist-mesh criteria and asked it to judge blind. Prompted as a senior 3D artist reviewing meshes for production, it weighs edge flow and topology, triangle quality (few slivers, a sensible density), cleanliness (no floating fragments, holes or flipped faces) and fidelity to the input shape.

    In a two-alternative forced choice, the judge saw renders of the dense input and two candidates labelled only A and B, in both orders, on 60 objects separate from the test set. The judge preferred PostMesh over MeshFlow, FastMesh and both MeshAnything models, and slightly preferred it over Mesh Silksong (62.5%, Tab.1). For detailed experiment protocol, see AppendixG.

    4.4 Qualitative Results

    In Figure5, we show the actual generated meshes from baseline and our proposed model.

    For earlier baseline of FastMesh, it suffer from highly fragmented meshes where each face is very tiny and over segmented. In MeshAnything groups, the generated meshes follow the shape of dense inputs while making the meshes into artist-like, but some of the meshes are incomplete and still lots of meshes are thin sliver triangles. In the most recent baseline of Mesh Silksong, it shows high quality artist meshes with proper mesh structure and consistency with input dense mesh, but some cases are suffer from incomplete mesh generation.

    MeshFlow follows the input shapes but lays long, thin triangles across surfaces such as the keg. PostMesh keeps the shapes complete and gives a more regular layout on most rows, without fragmented or irregular shaped meshes.

    Some autoregressive outputs are incomplete because decoding hit the token limit: 51 of the 300 Mesh Silksong outputs (17%) reached its 10240-token cap, and 82 of the 300 MeshAnything V2 outputs (27%) stopped at its token limit.

    4.5 Ablation Study

    Table2 removes one component at a time from the full setting and retrains the model on the same candidates, scoring on 200 testing objects. Among the reward terms, removing the quad-strip and tessellation terms costs the most QS and TS, and removing them together with the sliver and valence terms costs even more. Removing silhouette IoU or depth agreement also lowers QS and TS. Removing the tiny and stray terms lowers QS and raises DFF, which indicates that stray term is related to fragmentation defects. Fine-tuning on the winning samples without the preference objective (SFT only) loses most of the QS gain and raises DFF and fragmentation, so the preference loss, not the selection alone, carries the improvement. RAFT and Flow-GRPO stay far below the full setting, with 0.32 and 0.30 lower QS and higher DFF and fragmentation.

    5 Limitations and Conclusion

    Limitations.

    Failure cases are shown in Fig.7. There is no single standard for an artistic mesh, and artists differ in what they want, so our reward is not a golden standard for everyone. The evaluation of artist mesh is subjective, therefore our automatic metrics and VLM study is not a perfect measurement of artist mesh quality. However, the value of PostMesh lies in the method: it firstly shows how to post-train a fast flow-based generator toward a chosen standard without artist meshes.

    Conclusion.

    PostMesh post-trains a fast flow-based artist-mesh generator on its own samples, with an artistic mesh reward and gated multi-negative preference optimisation, and without artist meshes. It is comparable to or better than slow autoregressive generators on most quality measures and in a blind VLM test while keeping the fast speed of flow-based artist mesh generation model.

    Supplementary Material

    Contents.

    This appendix gives the implementation details (AppendixA), the gating algorithm (AppendixB), the reward constants (AppendixC), how each metric is computed (AppendixD), a comparison with the dense input, mesh decimation and remeshing (AppendixE), additional mesh-quality metrics (AppendixF), the VLM judge with its full prompt (AppendixG), the loss hyperparameters (AppendixH) and further qualitative results (AppendixI).

    Appendix A Implementation details

    MeshFlow [15] is used in geometry mode (dense-mesh condition only), in which the cross-attention (attn2) adapters receive exactly zero gradient and are left out, therefore we only apply lora on attn1. The reference model is the network with the adapters disabled. Table3 lists the settings, and the loss hyperparameters are in Tab.7.

    Rounds.

    We train two rounds. The first uses an earlier version of the reward and gating algorithm, without the silhouette and depth terms; the second, starting from the first-round model, uses the final reward and gating algorithm of Sec.3.

    Appendix B Gating algorithm

    Table4 lists every rule of Sec.3.3 with its threshold. The winning sample w is the best gate-passing sample of the group under r. The losing samples are every gate-failed sample, with ω=1 whatever its reward, and the gate-passing samples that pass the clear-preference rule, with ω equal to their reward gap to w divided by the largest such gap of the input. The fidelity and coverage filters apply to gate-passing losing samples, the face filter to both kinds, and the centre-offset filter, applied last, to all; ω is computed before the centre-offset filter and not rescaled after it. Inputs whose reward standard deviation is below 0.01 are skipped, as are inputs that keep no losing sample. Each update uses at most 3 losing samples per input (Tab.7).

    Appendix C Reward details

    Weights.

    We use the following weights λ in Eq.8 (rounded to two decimals):

    r=0.2 (tₛᵢₗ+t_depth)+0.15 t_QS+0.1 t_TS(13)
    +0.05 tₛₗᵢᵥₑᵣ+0.05 tᵥₐₗ
    +0.1 (t_frag-n+t_frag-stray)+0.15 r_dens.

    Render and component scores.

    Silhouette IoU and depth L1 are computed per view over the union and the intersection of the silhouettes, the latter in units of the bounding-box diagonal, and averaged over the 8 views of the renderer in Tab.3. Components are connected through shared edges after merging duplicate vertices: n_tiny counts components with at most 4 faces, and s_stray is the area share of components with less than 1% of the total area that have a boundary edge or at most 4 faces.

    Face-count target and band.

    r_dens=clip(1-|\log₂(F/Fₜ)|/2.5,0,1) with Fₜ=\exp(4.60+0.471\lnF_ref8), where F_ref8 is the median face count of 8 samples of the pretrained model on the input. The band width is b=2.5, so r_dens is 1 at the target and falls to 0 at 2^2.5≈5.7× too few or too many faces.

    Appendix D Metric computation

    One harness scores every method; Tab.1 and Tab.5 use the 300 test objects.

    CD and HD (×100).

    As in the MeshFlow evaluation protocol: the artist mesh is scaled to the [-0.5,0.5] unit cube and the output gets the same transform; 5,000 surface points are sampled on each, and the Chamfer and Hausdorff distances are computed with point_cloud_utils. The only change is a sampling seed fixed per object.

    ECD (×100).

    100k surface points are sampled per mesh. A point is an edge sample if the minimum of |nᵢ·nⱼ| over its (at most 24) neighbours within ε=0.01 is below 0.2. ECD [5] is the Chamfer distance between the edge samples of the output and of the artist mesh; it is undefined if either has fewer than 50 edge samples, so the means of Tab.1 are over the 290–294 objects where it is defined.

    Quad merge.

    Adjacent triangle pairs within 10^∘ of coplanar whose union is a convex quad with every corner in [45^∘,135^∘] are candidates; they are taken greedily in decreasing order of their smallest corner, each triangle at most once. ℚ are the merged quads and T the remaining triangles. The same merge is used for QS, TS, the sliver term and every method.

    QS (Eq.3).

    Every quad q has two nodes, one per pair of opposite sides. Two nodes are linked when their quads share a side that belongs to the side pairs of both nodes and that side is shared by exactly two quads. A strip π is a connected component of this graph. It is a ring if it has at least 3 nodes and every node has degree 2, and |π| counts its distinct quads. QS is the share of quads in ℚ that lie on a ring or on a strip with |π|≥4, QS =0 if ℚ is empty.

    TS (Eq.4).

    TS [17]=0.4 τ₁+0.2 τ₂+0.3 τ₃+0.1 τ₄. With corners θ_q,k and sides L_q,1,…,L_q,4 (in cyclic order) of quad q: τ₁=|ℚ|/\max(1,|ℚ|+|T|); τ₂=1-\tfrac1|ℚ|∑_q∑ₖ₌₁⁴|θ_q,k-90^∘|/360^∘; with ρ_q=\max(\tfrac\max(L_q,1,L_q,3)\min(L_q,1,L_q,3),\tfrac\max(L_q,2,L_q,4)\min(L_q,2,L_q,4)), τ₃=\tfrac12(\tfrac1|ℚ|∑_qρ_q)⁻¹+\tfrac12|ℚ|∑_qL̄_q/\maxₖL_q,k, L̄_q the mean side; and τ₄=\tfrac1|ℚ^′|∑_q∈ℚ^′(1+\tfrac1|N(q)|∑_j∈N(q)|ρ_q-ρⱼ|)⁻¹ over the quads ℚ^′ that share a side with at least one other quad, N(q) those neighbours (τ₄=0 if ℚ^′ is empty). If ℚ is empty, τ₂=τ₃=τ₄=0.

    Sliver and valence (Eq.5, Eq.6).

    α_f is the smallest corner of triangle f; \deg(v) counts the edges of the triangle mesh at v, quad diagonals included.

    DFF.

    DFF is the area share of faces that are on a boundary or non-manifold edge, self-intersect within a component, belong to a stray fragment (<0.5% of the area and open or with ≤4 faces) or are degenerate (area below 10⁻⁹ of the total). Self-intersections are tested within each of the components that cover 95% of the area (at most 50). FastMesh keeps every 3-clique of its predicted adjacency, so most of its area lies on non-manifold edges (DFF 0.990).

    Frag.

    An output has introduced fragmentation if it has at least 5 more small components (<1% of the area) than the GT. Frag. is the share of such outputs. Fragmentation does not change monotonically: on V_obj (3-seed mean component counts), the final model is closer to the GT component count than the pretrained MeshFlow on 156 of 200 objects (5 ties), and on 35 objects the pretrained count is above the GT count and that of the final model below it.

    Faces and s/mesh.

    Faces is the mean face count. s/mesh is the generation time per mesh recorded by the harness, averaged over the 300 test objects on one L40S GPU at batch 1. The classical methods of Tab.5 run on the CPU.

    Appendix E Comparison with Classical baselines.

    Since many graphic artists use classical remeshing algorithm on dense meshes, we compare our proposed model-based artist mesh generation performance with classical algorithm-based remeshing methods. QEM is pymeshlab quadric edge collapse (preserving boundary, face orientation and topology) to the face count of the MeshFlow. Isotropic remeshing is pymeshlab explicit isotropic remeshing with the edge length chosen so that face count is within MeshFlow’s meshcount range (feature angle 60^∘, surface-distance check 1%).

    Table5 compares them with MeshFlow and PostMesh on the same objects. Our model based methods shows better performance compared to algorithmic mesh generation in terms of QS and TS , which indicates that our proposed method is better in generating artist-preferred meshes. In algorithmic generation methods, they show extremely low fragmentation and DFF score, because algorithmic remeshing strongly keep the dense mesh structure so those are strictly following the shape of dense inputs.

    Appendix F Additional mesh-quality metrics

    QS, TS and DFF of Tab.1 partly overlap with the terms of our reward. We therefore also measure three properties that no reward term computes: robustness to subdivision, non-manifold edges and automatic UV unwrapping.

    Loop subdivision.

    We apply two levels of Loop subdivision [21]. Edges with one or more than two incident faces are kept as creases [10]. On the subdivided surface we measure the share of faces whose normal points against the normal of their original parent face (flip), the share of faces selected by the self-intersection test of pymeshlab (self-int.) and the share of faces that touch an extreme crease, an edge whose two face normals differ by more than 120^∘ (crease). An artist’s 90^∘ hard edge is not an extreme crease.

    Non-manifold edges.

    NM edge is the share of edges with more than two incident faces.

    UV unwrapping.

    No method outputs UVs, so we unwrap every mesh with one fixed automatic unwrapper, xatlas 0.0.11 with its default chart and packing options. Charts is the number of charts per 1,000 faces. Artist meshes have no ideal chart count, so we report the per-object distance |x-xₐᵣₜᵢₛₜ| to the chart count of the artist mesh of the same object.

    Results.

    Table6 shows the results. After Loop subdivision, PostMesh has about half the flipped faces (0.51% vs. 1.10%), less than half the self-intersecting faces (1.50% vs. 3.43%) and less than half the faces at extreme creases (0.16% vs. 0.39%) of MeshFlow. Its self-intersection share is the lowest of all methods, and its flip and crease shares are the lowest except for FastMesh, whose very dense meshes dilute per-face shares. PostMesh also has less than half the non-manifold edges of MeshFlow (4.78% vs. 11.04%), far fewer than FastMesh and on par with MeshAnything V2, though more than MeshAnything and Mesh Silksong. On UV unwrapping, its chart count is closer to that of the artist mesh than that of MeshFlow (70.1 vs. 84.3), a slight improvement, and closer than that of every other method except Mesh Silksong.

    Appendix G VLM judge

    Setup.

    The judge compares PostMesh with one other method at a time on 60 objects independent of the 300 test objects of Tab.1. Each call shows three images: the dense input, shaded only, and the two candidates, labeled only A and B, each as a 2×2 sheet of four fixed views (azimuth 30^∘,120^∘,210^∘,300^∘, elevation 25^∘) with flat shading, a 1-px wireframe and back faces tinted red, all in the frame of the dense input. Every pair is judged in both orders. The per-object score is the share of the two orders in which PostMesh was chosen, and W is its mean over objects, so an object judged differently in the two orders counts half.

    Our judgement model is the state-of-the-art commercial VLM Claude Opus 5.5, since the VLM critic must mimic the expertised graphic artist. Figure6 shows the full prompt.

    Appendix H Loss hyperparameters

    Table7 lists the settings of the loss of Eq.12 of the final model.

    Appendix I Additional qualitative results

    Figure8 shows outputs of the ablation study of Tab.2 on two validation objects, and Figs.9 and 10 show further generated outputs from test objects.

    In Fig.8, each row shows the dense input, the full setting and five arms: without the tessellation, sliver and valence terms, without silhouette IoU, without depth agreement, without the tiny and stray terms, and SFT only. The full setting covers the sides of the school bus and the floor slab under the desk with fairly even faces. Without the tessellation, sliver and valence terms, or without the tiny and stray terms, long thin triangles and fans appear on the same surfaces, and SFT only gives an irregular layout with many small triangles. Without depth agreement the layout is denser and less even; without silhouette IoU it is the closest to the full setting on these two objects. On average, every arm has a lower QS than the full setting in Tab.2, with the largest losses without the tessellation, sliver and valence terms and with SFT only.

    Fig.7 is failure case. Although our method can improve the mesh structure and shape consistency compared to baseline MeshFlow, our method can still shows unbalanced meshes or tiny components. Due to the property of flow based model, the output can be worse with different seeds.

item.title: 无位姿图像直接出连续曲面：FoundSurface 把 pointmap 与「射线」两种表示接起来 ｜ FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images
item.description:
一句话：前馈 pointmap 方法免了位姿，但输出的是离散、稀疏的表示。

要点：

  • 现状：从**无位姿图像**做精确的三维表面重建仍是基础难题；近期前馈 pointmap 方法虽然**免去了相机位姿**，但**本质产出的是离散、稀疏的表示**
  • FoundSurface 因此提出一条可泛化的管线：把 **pointmap 表示与射线（ray-based）表示融合**，直接从无位姿图像恢复**连续、高保真的三维表面**
  • 做法是先提取显式几何先验，再在射线表示上求解连续表面

为什么值得看：「免位姿」与「连续曲面」长期二选一：pointmap 给点，网格要面。把两种表示接起来，才能让「拍一段视频→拿到可用曲面」这条路真正闭环——对 real-to-sim 与资产重建都是前置能力。

中文摘要：从无位姿图像中精确重建三维表面，一直是计算机视觉的基础难题。近期的前馈 pointmap 方法免去了对相机位姿的依赖，但它们本质上产出的是离散、稀疏的表示。FoundSurface 提出一条可泛化的管线：把 pointmap 表示与基于射线的表示无缝结合，直接从无位姿图像恢复连续、高保真的三维表面。其做法是先提取显式的几何先验，再在射线表示上求解连续表面。对「拍一段视频就拿到可用曲面」这类 real-to-sim 与资产重建流程，这补的是从离散点到连续面之间的那一步。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-27

本期推送：2026-11-28

FoundSurface: Feedforward Ray-Based 3D Scene Surface Reconstruction from Unposed Images

Abstract

Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation. Code and data are available at: https://vlar-group.github.io/FoundSurface.html

1 Introduction

Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from multiple images plays a key role in emerging applications such as embodied AI and augmented reality. In recent years, significant progress has been made in the field of 3D reconstruction through the development of various 3D representation techniques [82]. These include coordinate-based methods such as radiance fields (NeRF) [56], and point-based methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [43], and their variants [29, 12]. While these approaches achieve impressive results in novel view synthesis, they usually rely on highly accurate camera poses, which are often unavailable in practice, and typically struggle to recover precise 3D surfaces. Furthermore, they generally require time-consuming per-scene optimization rather than functioning as generalizable, feed-forward models [99].

Recently, the pioneering feedforward method DUSt3R [81] has enabled precise 3D geometry reconstruction by directly predicting pixel-aligned pointmaps from unposed image pairs. Subsequent methods [101] have extended this pointmap representation to handle multiple views [78, 92], to improve computational efficiency [65, 52], etc.. Leveraging powerful Transformer architectures and large-scale training datasets, these approaches achieve excellent accuracy in recovering surface points from image collections. However, the reconstructed pointmaps are inherently discrete and sparse, lacking the continuous and fine-grained geometric details required for many downstream applications, such as robot manipulation and scene editing.

Another recent line of work focuses on ray-based representations such as RayDF [53] and RayletDF [84]. Their key innovation is learning a ray-surface distance field for any query light ray conditioned on visual inputs, thus enabling the recovery of continuous and high-fidelity surfaces. However, they still rely on accurate camera poses or sparse point clouds as inputs to reconstruct detailed surfaces.

In this paper, we present a generalizable, feed-forward 3D surface reconstruction pipeline that takes only a set of unposed images as input and directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces. We achieve this by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. In particular, as illustrated in Figure 2, our pipeline comprises four key components: 1) a pre-trained pointmap-based model such as VGGT [78], which extracts visual tokens and generates pixel-aligned pointmaps along with estimated camera poses; 2) a query-view-centric selection module designed to identify geometrically relevant reference views; 3) a coarse ray-surface distance regressor utilizing cross-attention layers; and 4) a raylet-based surface module for refining surface details and normals.

Among the four modules of our pipeline, the core is the second and third modules, which seamlessly integrate pointmap- and ray-based representations, effectively estimating continuous surfaces for any query views conditioned on the recovered pointmaps from unposed input images. In contrast, directly applying RayletDF to VGGT pointmaps can lead to inaccurate raylet initialization, resulting in multi-surface artifacts and missing regions.

Our pipeline is based on large Transformer and standard neural layers with sufficient capacity, without relying on domain specific assumptions. Therefore, it is rather suitable to consume various indoor and outdoor datasets. We train a single foundation 3D surface model on a mixture of 9 public datasets with depth annotations, including BlendMVS [94], WildRGB [86], ScanNet [21], HyperSim [63], MVS-Synth [37], ARKitScenes [4], S3DIS [1], SceneNN [33], and GTASfM [79]. Our model is termed FoundSurface and Figure 1 shows qualitative results. Our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce a large feed-forward model to recover continuous 3D scene surfaces from an arbitrary number of images without needing poses.

  • •

    We design a query-view-centric selection module together with a cross attention based fusion module to seamlessly integrate pointmap- and ray-based 3D representations.

  • •

    We train a single foundation model and demonstrate superior 3D surface reconstruction accuracy across multiple datasets, clearly surpassing existing baselines.

    • 2 Related Work

    To recover 3D surfaces from images, classical SfM [59] and SLAM [9] systems extract sparse point clouds that can be smoothed into continuous surfaces, though they often fail to capture fine details. Early deep learning methods utilized explicit 3D representations such as voxel grids [17, 90, 91], point clouds [24], octrees [72], and meshes [41]. Nevertheless, the quality of these discrete structures is inherently bottlenecked by memory footprints and resolution constraints. Comprehensive surveys of these methods are available in [5, 32].

    Implicit Representations for Surface Reconstruction: To bypass the resolution limits of explicit 3D formats, implicit representations use simple MLPs to parameterize continuous 3D shapes [Fried2020]. Techniques such as occupancy fields (OF) [15, 55], un/signed distance fields (U/SDF) [16, 60, 75, 22], vector fields (VF) [93, 61], and NeRF [56, 73] operate by mapping 3D coordinates to local geometric or visual properties. While these approaches and their variants [82] yield highly accurate surface reconstructions and 2D renderings, they rely on dense 3D spatial sampling and exhaustive network evaluations per view and often require images with accurate poses as input. In this paper, our FoundSurface learns a feedforward model from unposed images, directly regressing surface points for any query viewing rays in single pass.

    Point-based Representations for Surface Reconstruction: A recent breakthrough is 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [43], which models environments as a set of 3D Gaussians with optimizable positions, covariances, and colors. Supported by a custom tile-based rasterizer, 3DGS delivers real-time 2D view synthesis. Nevertheless, because it inherently lacks tight geometric constraints, 3DGS falls short in extracting fine surface details and generating highly accurate depth maps. While a multitude of recent works [13, 25, 85, 31, 34, 18, 89, 48, 35, 98, 87, 58, 97, 67, 11, 102, 30] have attempted to enforce surface alignment and improve depth quality, they generally require time-consuming per-scene optimization and images with accurate poses as input.

    Another breakthrough is DUSt3R [81] which demonstrates 3D geometry can be represented by pixel-aligned pointmaps and recovered from unposed image pairs in a single forward pass. A series of succeeding methods [101, 47, 8, 23, 14, 78, 80, 92, 38, 100, 50, 88, 39, 104, 46, 26, 49] extend it from different perspectives, including handling more views , modeling videos, processing faster, etc.. Although these methods achieve impressive results, they are limited to recovering discrete and sparse point clouds, falling short of producing continuous, high-fidelity surfaces.

    Ray-based Representations for Surface Reconstruction: Another line of work models 3D shapes through ray-based neural functions. By taking individual rays as input, these models directly regress either RGB values [51, 27, 57, 69, 10] or explicit surface points [28, 2, 53, 84, 45, 70, 40, 71, 96]. Despite their impressive rendering efficiency and surface accuracy, most of these methods require posed images as input and struggle to generalize across diverse 3D scenes. In this paper, we leverage the robust surface representation capabilities of RayDF [53] and RayletDF [84] and seamlessly integrate them with pointmap-based representations. This synergistic approach enables feedforward 3D surface reconstruction directly from sets of images.

    3 FoundSurface

    FoundSurface recovers continuous high-fidelity 3D scene surfaces through a coarse-to-fine, discrete-to-continuous progression. Given a set of unposed and uncalibrated multi-view images I={Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3 | i=1,...,K}, we first extract an explicit geometric prior using a pre-trained pointmap-based model elaborated in Section 3.1. Next, we filter out redundant information by selecting geometrically relevant views for any target query in Section 3.2. We then transition from 3D points to rays by regressing an initial, continuous coarse surface, which resolves global geometry and occlusions detailed in Section 3.3. Finally, we refine this coarse surface using a raylet-based module that aggregates high-resolution local 3D features to recover fine-grained details, yielding the final high-fidelity surfaces, discussed in Section 3.4.

    3.1 Pre-trained Pointmap-based Model

    This model aims to establish a reliable spatial anchor for building continuous surfaces without camera poses. Given a set of input images I={Iᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3}, we employ the pre-trained VGGT model [78] to predict explicit geometric priors. Specifically, the network’s prediction heads output a pixel-aligned pointmap Pᵢ∈ℝ^H×W×3, a camera pose matrix Tᵢ∈ℝ^4×4, and an intrinsic matrix Cᵢ∈ℝ^3×3 for each input image Iᵢ.

    During this forward pass, we concurrently retain intermediate patch features to capture rich contextual information. Let F_i,l∈ℝ^h×w×dₗ denote the patch feature extracted from the l-th layer of VGGT, where h=H/s and w=W/s are the patch-level spatial dimensions downsampled from H and W by ratio s, and dₗ is the channel depth. We specifically collect features from four layers, defined as the set L={4,11,17,23}. To prepare compact and geometry-aware visual tokens for subsequent modules, we fuse these multi-scale patch features using a two-layer MLP, denoted as f_fuse. The entire extraction and fusion process can be succinctly formulated as:

    {Pᵢ,Tᵢ,Cᵢ,{F_i,l}_l∈L}←VGGT(Iᵢ), Fᵢ=f_fuse([F_i,4,F_i,11,F_i,17,F_i,23])

    		(1)

    where the operator [·] denotes concatenation along the channel dimension, yielding the final fused visual feature Fᵢ∈ℝ^h×w×dₒᵤₜ. The discrete geometric predictions Pᵢ/Tᵢ/Cᵢ and the fused visual tokens Fᵢ constitute the foundation for our continuous ray-based formulation.

    3.2 Query-View-Centric Selection Module

    As shown in the leftmost block of Figure 3, when reconstructing the geometry of a novel query view, which is defined explicitly by a given target camera pose T_target and C_target, intuitively, not all input views are helpful. Views that do not observe the target surfaces will only introduce noise and computational overhead. Therefore, instead of globally querying features of all input views, we design a selection module to identify only the overlapping, geometrically relevant reference views by a surfel-based voting mechanism, ensuring the selected views provide reliable geometric coverage.

    Specifically, we first establish a canonical geometric reference for this novel query view. We project all available input pointmaps onto the camera plane defined by the target query pose, and apply a standard depth buffer (z-buffer) to render a dense target pseudo-depth map, Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ. We then uniformly divide Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ into non-overlapping patches, conceptualized as target surfels.

    To evaluate a candidate view j out of all input views, we similarly divide its pointmap Pⱼ into candidate surfels and project them onto the target view. For each pixel (x,y) within a projected candidate surfel, we compare its depth value Dʲ_x,y against the canonical target depth Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ_x,y. The pixel casts a valid match vote according to an indicator function:

    v_x,y=I(|Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ_x,y-Dʲ_x,y|<δ_depth)

    		(2)

    A candidate surfel is considered successfully “matched” if the proportion of positive votes v_x,y within it exceeds a threshold τᵥₒₜₑ. By aggregating these surfel-level results, we compute the percentage of matched surfels for the entire candidate view j, yielding a robust, coverage-aware overlap score. Finally, we rank all input views based on this surfel overlap score and retain only the top-k candidates. This geometric filtering eliminates irrelevant regions and provides our subsequent attention modules with a highly curated and effective query candidate set: {Tⱼ}^Kⱼ₌₁,{Cⱼ}^Kⱼ₌₁,{Pⱼ}^Kⱼ₌₁,{Fⱼ}^Kⱼ₌₁. More implementation details are provided in Appendix A.1.

    3.3 Coarse Ray-Surface Distance Regressor

    With the relevant views selected, the next challenge is locating the actual surface intersection for the target camera rays. This module aims to seamlessly integrate pointmap- and ray-based representations to directly estimate an initial, continuous coarse surface. To robustly regress this initial surface, we establish a local coordinate system centered at the target query view. As shown in the yellow block of Figure 3, given the target camera pose T_target and intrinsics C_target, we align the candidate views to this target viewpoint and tokenize their pixel-aligned Plücker rays via a convolution layer (Conv) to yield ray embeddings mⱼ for each relevant view j as:

    mⱼ=Conv(ℝ(Tⱼʳᵉˡ,Cⱼ))∈ℝ^hw×d, whereTⱼʳᵉˡ=T_target⁻¹Tⱼ

    		(3)

    Here, Tⱼʳᵉˡ defines the relative transformation to the target viewpoint, and ℝ(·) denotes the operation that casts camera parameters into dense Plücker ray maps. To inject spatial awareness into the visual features Fⱼ (obtained from the backbone in Section 3.1), we condition them with the corresponding Plücker ray tokens using an MLP-based network f_cond and get the reference features F̂ⱼ as:

    F̂ⱼ=f_cond([mⱼ,Fⱼ]),

    		(4)

    where [·] denotes concatenation along the channel dimension.

    Similarly, for the target query view, we cast Plücker rays using its parameters (I_4×4,C_target) and tokenize them into target ray embeddings m_target. To aggregate spatially aligned features from the candidates, we employ a Transformer network f_enc consisting of alternating self- and cross-attention layers. Specifically, in the cross-attention mechanism, the target query ray embeddings act as the queries (Q), while the conditioned candidate features {F̂ⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^K act as the keys (K) and values (V). This allows the target query rays to adaptively fetch relevant geometric information:

    F^*_target=f_enc(Q=m_target; K,V={F̂ⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^K)

    		(5)

    Decoding the aggregated feature map F^*_target yields a ray distance map Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ. This distance map effectively establishes our continuous, albeit coarse, ray-surface representation. Specifically, to locate the 3D surface point p_x,y for a given pixel (x,y) in the target query view, we cast a ray using the known target query camera parameters:

    p_x,y=p_target+Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ_x,y·r_x,y

    		(6)

    where p_target∈ℝ³ is the optical center and r_x,y∈ℝ³ is the normalized ray direction. Both are uniquely determined by the target query pose T_target and intrinsics C_target. More implementation details can be found in Appendix A.2.

    While this coarse surface successfully captures the overall scene geometry and resolves occlusions, it inherently lacks fine-grained, high-frequency local details due to the patch-level resolution of the visual tokens. Therefore, we treat these coarse surface points and their corresponding ray directions as a set of sampled raylets conceptualized by RayletDF [84], denoted as {lₙ=(pₙ,rₙ)}ₙ₌₁^N, which serve as the geometric foundation for our subsequent raylet-based surface module to refine the details.

    3.4 Raylet-based Surface Module

    To elevate our coarse surface to a high-fidelity continuous representation, we must compensate for the missing local geometric details. We achieve this by refining the coarse raylets {lₙ}ₙ₌₁^N through the aggregation of high-resolution local 3D features.

    We first voxelize the initial pointmaps {Pⱼ}^Kⱼ₌₁ and index the corresponding visual features {Fⱼ}^Kⱼ₌₁ obtained in Section 3.3. We then utilize a 3D sparse convolution network (SPConv) [19] to process these indexed features, constructing a robust 3D local feature volume. As shown in the rightmost block of Figure 3, the sparse convolution network produces a set of spatial anchors and their associated local features, denoted as A={aₘ}ₘ₌₁^M. Here, the anchor points are generated through sparse convolution over the voxelized 3D representation, rather than being directly sampled from the original VGGT pointmaps. Each anchor is associated with a learned local geometric feature, which is subsequently used to refine nearby raylets.

    For each coarse raylet lₙ=(pₙ,rₙ) generated from the previous module, we search for its S-nearest anchor points in 3D space, yielding a local neighborhood Aₙ={(a_n,s,f_n,s)}ₛ₌₁^S. To make the network highly sensitive to local geometry, we explicitly calculate the spatial relationships between the coarse raylet and its local anchors. Specifically, we extract the Euclidean distances e_n,s=∥pₙ-a_n,s∥₂ and the relative direction vectors v_n,s=(pₙ-a_n,s)/e_n,s.

    Finally, a refinement network processes the local anchor features alongside these explicit geometric relationships to regress a precise distance residual Δdₙ. This aggregation is formulated as:

    Δdₙ=f_refine([\mathopMEANₛ₌₁^S(f_n,s), e_n,1,v_n,1,…,e_n,S,v_n,S])

    		(7)

    where [·] denotes feature concatenation, and MEAN represents the mean-pooling function applied exclusively to the visual features of the K local neighbors. The final refined surface point is obtained by updating the coarse raylet:

    p^*ₙ=pₙ+Δdₙ·rₙ

    		(8)

    This refinement dynamically carves out the high-frequency details, yielding a continuous, high-fidelity 3D surface. As a byproduct of this continuous ray-based formulation, our method natively supports the analytical derivation of surface normals. Given the input raylet and the final refined distance, we can easily compute a closed-form normal vector, effectively circumventing the noise typical of numerical approximations. We defer the full derivation and other details to the Appendix A.3.

    3.5 Training

    We employ a decoupled two-stage training strategy to train our core modules.

    Stage 1: Coarse Ray-Surface Distance Regression. In this stage, our goal is to establish an accurate global geometric framework. We train the coarse ray-surface distance regressor to predict the continuous coarse depth map Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ. Supervision is provided by the aligned ground truth depth D_gt, using a loss function that combines a pixel-wise ℓ₁ distance with a spatial gradient loss to enforce surface consistency:

    ℓ_coarse=|D_gt-Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ|+∥∇D_gt-∇Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ∥

    		(9)

    Stage 2: Raylet-based Surface Refinement. Once the coarse geometry is reasonably established, we freeze or isolate the first-stage predictions and focus entirely on training the raylet-based surface module. To capture high-frequency geometric details without destabilizing the learned global structure, we predict a residual distance map ΔD. During this stage, we apply a stop-gradient operation to the coarse predictions, formulating the fine-stage loss as:

    ℓ_fine=|D_gt-(sg(Dᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ)+ΔD)|

    		(10)

    where sg(·) denotes the stop-gradient operator. Here, the global residual map ΔD is formed by aggregating the local raylet residuals corresponding to each pixel, i.e., ΔD={Δdₙ}ₙ₌₁^N, where Δdₙ is computed following the local feature aggregation mechanism detailed in Section 3.4. This two-stage training paradigm effectively decouples global topology localization from local surface refinement, thereby enabling high-fidelity 3D reconstructions. More details are in Appendix A.4.

    4 Experiments

    Training Datasets: We train our model on a mixture of 9 datasets, including the training splits of ScanNet [21], GTASfM [79] and ARKitScenes [4], together with the full datasets of BlendMVS [94], WildRGB [86], HyperSim [63], MVS-Synth [37], S3DIS [1] and SceneNN [33] . For evaluation, we use ScanNet++ [95], 7Scenes [66], MultiScan [54], Mushroom [62], Replica [68], and Tanks&Temples [44]. Detailed dataset splits are provided in Appendix A.17.

    Baselines: We compare our approach against five representative baselines: 1) VGGT Projection[78], evaluated via the direct projection of its pointmaps; 2) PriorDA[83], a state-of-the-art depth completion model applied to VGGT pointmaps; 3) CUT3R[80], a feed-forward model utilizing state tokens for novel query views; 4) FLARE[100], the latest feed-forward Gaussian splatting model; and 5) RayletDF[84], a state-of-the-art generalizable ray-based method.

    Metrics: We evaluate surface reconstruction by comparing the predicted ray–surface distance against the ground-truth distance. We report the absolute distance error (ADE, in meters), together with four commonly used metrics [74]: root mean squared error (RMSE), absolute relative distance (Abs Rel), squared relative distance (Sq Rel), and the Threshold accuracy (δ≤1.25) which measures the percentage of predictions that fall within the specified threshold of the ground truth.

    For normal evaluation, we follow the metrics used in normal estimation [3]. We report both the mean and median angular errors on normal. Additionally, we evaluate performance by measuring the percentage of pixels with an angular error below thresholds of 11.25°, 22.5°, and 30.0°. Detailed computation of all metrics is in Appendix A.7&A.8.

    4.1 Evaluation of Out-of-domain Reconstruction

    In this setting, our model takes 50 unposed input views and predicts ray–surface distances for query rays. For each scene, we uniformly sample 50 images from the test RGB sequence as input views. We further ablate the number of input views in Tables 3& 4.

    We evaluate on ScanNet++, 7Scenes, MultiScan, MuSHRoom, and Tanks&Temples. These datasets are excluded from both the VGGT and our training datasets, thereby forming a strictly out-of-domain evaluation setting. For VGGT Projection[78], we directly project the pointmaps predicted by VGGT into the query view using Open3D [103]. We further combine VGGT projection with PriorDA[83], a state-of-the-art depth completion model, to fill missing regions after projection. For the feed-forward reconstruction model CUT3R[80], we first forward all input views and then query the scene state token to predict query-view point coordinates. For the feed-forward Gaussian splatting model FLARE[100], we render query-view depth maps from the predicted 3D Gaussians. For the ray-based method RayletDF[84], which is originally optimized for Gaussians and point clouds, we retrain it on VGGT-predicted pointmaps from our training datasets for a fair comparison. Standard deviation results are provided in Appendix A.6.

    Results & Analysis: Table 1 and Figure 4 report quantitative and qualitative comparisons on ray-surface distance estimation for all query rays of test images. To assess the contribution of our Raylet-based refinement module, we also report the performance of our coarse ray-surface distance regressor in Table 1, denoted as w/o refine.

    Our method achieves the best ADE across all out-of-domain datasets, outperforming all baselines by a large margin. For example, on ScanNet++, our ADE is 0.132m compared with 0.198m for PriorDA. These results demonstrate the strong generalization ability of FoundSurface on unseen datasets. Compared with the state-token-based model CUT3R, our method preserves finer geometric details, as illustrated in Figure 4. Removing the proposed refinement module substantially degrades reconstruction accuracy, confirming its effectiveness. More results are provided in Appendix A.13.

    4.2 Evaluation of Surface Normal Accuracy

    We further evaluate the normal estimation performance of FoundSurface and all baselines. Since some baselines, such as PriorDA, cannot directly produce analytical surface normals, we additionally compute normals from the predicted depth maps using numerical differentiation for reference.

    Results & Analysis. As shown in Table 2 and Figure 5, our method achieves the best performance using only depth supervision, demonstrating the effectiveness of FoundSurface as a robust surface representation. Additional qualitative comparisons are provided in Appendix A.10.
